extract: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
blurb: In a garden one night [Augustine](/authors/saint-augustine) and a gang of boys strip a neighbour's pear tree bare, not because they are hungry but because the theft is forbidden and that is the whole of the pleasure. He spends pages on it, turning the small crime over and over, because he has understood something no one had written down before: that a person can love wrongdoing for its own sake, with nothing to gain. _Confessions_ is addressed start to finish to God, every sin laid out with terrible exactness, the years with a woman he loved and never named, the prayer that begged for chastity and added, but not yet. To read it is to overhear a mind accounting for itself to the one who already knows. Augustine was the first writer in the West to treat the self as a depth instead of a surface, and every memoir of a soul in crisis since has been written in the room he built. The restlessness of his famous opening never settles. It only moves.

title: The Bacchae
author: Euripides
extract: There are many forms of divine things; and the Gods bring to pass many in an unexpected manner
blurb: A stranger arrives in Thebes, smiling, golden-haired, easily caught and chained, and the young king who cages him has no idea he has just imprisoned a god. This is Dionysus come home in disguise, and Pentheus, who rules by reason and refuses to bow, will learn what it costs to deny the wild thing in human nature. [Euripides](/authors/euripides)' last play follows the women of Thebes up the mountain into ecstasy, drumming, dancing, suckling wild animals, and then turns that rapture to horror: lured into a dress to spy on them, Pentheus is torn apart by his own mother, who carries his severed head down the slope in triumph, certain it is a lion's, until the frenzy clears and she sees. Nothing in Greek theatre is more terrifying than her slow waking. The god is beautiful and pitiless, real in a way Pentheus learns too late; the play knows the worship we refuse will have us anyway.

title: Omeros
author: Derek Walcott
extract: This is how, one sunrise, we cut down them canoes.
blurb: At dawn the fishermen fell the gommier trees they will hollow into canoes, the poem's first act of making, and from there [Derek Walcott](/authors/derek-walcott) does something audacious. He hands a St. Lucian fisherman the name Achille, gives his rival the name Hector, and makes the woman they both love a housemaid named Helen. This is not parody but a claim, pressed in Dante's terza rima across St. Lucia, Boston, London, and the African coast Achille rows back to in a vision of his stolen ancestors: that a man hauling a pirogue carries the same epic weight as anyone at Troy. The wound at the poem's centre belongs to Philoctete, a gash from a rusted anchor that will not close, the whole history of the Middle Passage festering in one shin. Listen to how the verse braids English and Creole until neither tongue could say alone what the two say together. The sea here keeps every name the history books let drown.

title: Tristram Shandy
author: Laurence Sterne
extract: I wish either my father or my mother, or indeed both of them, had minded what they were about when they begot me.
blurb: The book begins at the exact moment of its hero's conception, and immediately derails: mid-act, Mrs Shandy asks whether her husband has remembered to wind the clock, and Tristram blames every misfortune of his life on the interruption. That is the engine of the whole thing. Tristram sets out to write his life and cannot get near it, because telling any one minute breeds three more minutes worth telling, and because nobody in the house will stop talking. Nine volumes pass; he is barely born. What looks like chaos is the tenderest argument about people ever smuggled into a joke. Uncle Toby, gentle and wounded, lives forever inside the siege that maimed him, rebuilding it in miniature on the bowling green; Walter spins theories about noses and Christian names that no fact will ever confirm. [Laurence Sterne](/authors/laurence-sterne) gives you a blank page, a black page, a marbled page, and a hand-drawn squiggle for a plot, and somehow it is the most loving book in English about how hopelessly we each live trapped inside our own heads.

title: Joseph and His Brothers
author: Thomas Mann
extract: Very deep is the well of the past. Should we not call it bottomless?
blurb: A young man is thrown into a pit by his older brothers, sold to passing traders, and carried down into Egypt where he will rise from slave to vizier and back to redeemer of the family that betrayed him. [Thomas Mann](/authors/thomas-mann) began this tetralogy in 1926 and finished it in California in 1943, sixteen years and four volumes spanning the rise of Nazism and his own exile, and called it the longest single project of his life. Mann took the few hundred verses of Genesis and unfolded them into nearly two thousand pages of psychology, anthropology, and the slow ironic music of myth becoming history. Joseph the dreamer learns the cost of being beloved by God. The Bible compresses; Mann opens out, fugal, immense.

title: One Thousand and One Nights
author: Anonymous
extract: And Shahrazad perceived the dawn of day and ceased to say her permitted say.
blurb: Dawn is a death sentence. The king has buried a wife every morning for three years, and tonight the turn is Scheherazade's, except she has begun a story she will not finish before the light comes, and a king who must know how it ends cannot kill the only mouth that can tell him. _One Thousand and One Nights_ is the great proof that narrative is not ornament but survival: every tale she spins, of Sinbad swallowed by whirlpools, of djinn loosed from sealed brass, of caliphs prowling Baghdad in disguise to glimpse the lives their palaces hide, is also an argument made beneath the sword that a story can purchase one more sunrise. The pleasure is bottomless, a door opening onto a door opening onto a door. What you carry away is not a book but a discovery: that to be listened to is to be spared, and that the right tale, told well, can hold a blade in the air.

title: My Name Is Red
author: Orhan Pamuk
extract: I am nothing but a corpse now, a body at the bottom of a well.
blurb: A corpse calls up from the bottom of a well, and so begins one of the strangest, most ravishing murder mysteries ever written, narrated in turn by the dead man, a gold coin, a dog, a tree, the colour red itself, and Death. In the snowbound Istanbul of 1591, the Sultan's miniaturists are secretly illuminating a book in the forbidden Frankish manner, with its scandal of perspective and portraiture, its vanity of an individual hand, and one of them has killed to bury the blasphemy. Beneath the whodunit runs the real wound: a war between two ways of seeing the world, the Persian master who paints a horse as God remembers it and goes blind in holy perfection, against the Venetian who paints what one mortal eye happens to see. Threaded through is the patient, aching courtship of Black and the widow Shekure. [Pamuk](/authors/orhan-pamuk) makes you feel that to choose a style is to lose your soul, and to fall in love is to risk it anyway.

title: Faust
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
extract: My worthy friend, gray are all theories, and green alone Life's golden tree.
blurb: [Goethe](/authors/johann-wolfgang-von-goethe)'s scholar has read everything and feels nothing. He stands among his books at midnight, learned past all use and dead to the world, until the devil offers a bargain and Faust names stranger terms than the legend ever dared: not his soul outright, but a wager that no single moment will ever feel so perfect he begs it to stay. Mephistopheles takes the bet certain it will be easy. Across two parts and sixty years of writing, Goethe proves it is not. Part I narrows to one ruined girl, Gretchen, tender and doomed by the love Faust brings her. Part II opens onto everything at once: an emperor's court, ancient Greece, drowned land won back from the sea, a mind that cannot stop reaching. What it finally knows is the most generous claim literature ever dared, that to strive without rest, even into wreckage, is itself the thing worth saving. Gray are all theories, Goethe writes, and green alone life's golden tree.

title: Metamorphoses
author: Ovid
extract: My design leads me to speak of forms changed into new bodies.
blurb: She runs from the god, and just as his breath reaches the back of her neck the change overtakes her: bark climbs her thighs, her fingers stiffen into twigs, her hair shivers into leaves, and Apollo, pressing his mouth to the warm new wood, feels her heart still beating somewhere underneath. Daphne into laurel is one of hundreds. [Ovid](/authors/ovid) threads the whole of pagan myth into a single unbroken poem, from the first sorting of chaos to the streets of his own Rome, and everywhere the same thing happens: a person pushed past the edge of what a body can hold, and the body giving way to it. Narcissus thins to a flower over his own reflection, a weaver's pride hardens into a spider, a raped girl is silenced into a bird. The wonder is how tender Ovid stays toward each one. Nothing in him holds its shape, and that, he seems to know, is exactly what it is to be alive.

title: The Magic Mountain
author: Thomas Mann
extract: Time has no divisions to mark its passage, there is never a thunder-storm or blare of trumpets.
blurb: Up where the air is thin and the snow never wholly melts, a sanatorium keeps its patients to a routine of rest cures, temperature readings, and five vast meals a day, and time quietly stops behaving. Hans Castorp comes for a three-week visit to his consumptive cousin and stays seven years, never quite deciding to, the way an idle afternoon can swallow a whole season before you notice. _The Magic Mountain_ does not describe that slippage; it performs it, lavishing a hundred slow pages on a single early week and then folding entire years into a sentence, until you have lost your own grip on how long you have been up here reading. The Berghof becomes a miniature Europe, feverish and brilliant and arguing itself toward ruin: the humanist Settembrini against the fanatic Naphta, a glass door that keeps slamming, an X-ray that shows Hans his own living hand as a skeleton. He absorbs the mountain's long, seductive education in death, and then the flatland calls him down into the guns of 1914.

title: The Lord of the Rings
author: J.R.R. Tolkien
extract: Not all those who wander are lost.
blurb: There is a road that runs from a green hill in the Shire all the way to a mountain of fire, and the creature who must walk it is a hobbit who would rather be home by his own hearth with a second breakfast. _The Lord of the Rings_ rests on one impossible, beautiful idea: that the single object powerful enough to enslave the world can be unmade only by hands too small and too ordinary to want what it offers. [Tolkien](/authors/jrr-tolkien) set this against a world of such depth that it aches, full of Elves who remember the world's first morning, of kingdoms fallen to grass, of languages he invented whole before he wrote a line of the story. The quest is not strength beating evil but endurance outlasting it; at the mountain's very edge even goodness gives out, and the world is saved by mercy rather than might. Few books have made the love of one servant for his master feel like the last brave thing left alive.

title: The Idiot
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
extract: Beauty will save the world.
blurb: There is a moment, in the seconds before a seizure takes him, when Prince Myshkin feels every jarring thing in existence fall into one harmony so perfect he would give his whole life for it. He arrives in Petersburg from a Swiss clinic carrying no cunning and no self-defense, only a clarity so total that the people around him read it as idiocy. [Dostoevsky](/authors/fyodor-dostoevsky) set himself the hardest task in all of fiction, to put a genuinely good man on the page, and his discovery was stranger than failure: goodness like this is not beaten by the world's cruelty but by what it does to those who need it most. To love the ruined Nastasya Filippovna is to insist she is worth saving, and that is the one tenderness she cannot bear. The novel moves at a fever, scenes erupting in drawing rooms and on railway platforms, confessions blurted to strangers, every evening ending in some fresh public wound. Beauty will save the world, Myshkin believes, and the book spends six hundred pages testing whether the world will let it.

title: Six Characters in Search of an Author
author: Luigi Pirandello
extract: When the characters are really alive before their author, the latter does nothing but follow them in their action.
blurb: A theatre company is slogging through a dull rehearsal when six strangers appear at the back of the house and walk down the aisle, asking to be staged. They are not actors. They are a family, unfinished, abandoned by the writer who dreamed them up and then put down his pen, and they have come to act out the scene that made them: the afternoon a Father, in a house of ill repute, reached for a girl he failed to recognise as his own Stepdaughter. [Luigi Pirandello](/authors/luigi-pirandello)'s argument is quietly terrifying. A character is realer than the actor who plays them, he insists, because a character is locked forever in the single moment that defines them, while the actor goes home and becomes someone else by supper. The Manager tries to mount the story; the characters keep interrupting to say the performance is a well-meaning lie. By the end a shot has been fired, and no one, onstage or in the seats, can tell whether the death was real or only beautifully rehearsed.

title: The Waves
author: Virginia Woolf
extract: Against you I will fling myself, unvanquished and unyielding, O Death!
blurb: Between every chapter the sun climbs and sinks over an empty shore and the waves come in, over and over, indifferent to the six lives unfolding in the spaces between. Bernard, Susan, Rhoda, Neville, Jinny, and Louis speak only in soliloquy, never once to each other, carrying their separate minds from the smell of a childhood garden to the weariness of old age. The book withholds almost everything a novel promises, no scenes, no dialogue, no narrator to tell you what to feel, and hands back something stranger and finer: the pure rhythm of being alive, six consciousnesses beating like one tide. When Percival, the seventh, the friend who never speaks, falls from his horse in India, his death reaches each of them as a separate wound, and you understand that love can go on existing as the shape of an absence. Rhoda, who says she has no face and no self to gather, carries the novel's terror; Bernard, at the last, flings himself at death unvanquished, pulling all six voices into one final charge against the dark.

title: American Pastoral
author: Philip Roth
extract: The Swede. During the war years, when I was still a grade school boy, this was a magical name in our Newark neighborhood.
blurb: Newark's golden boy had a nickname that sounded like a blessing: the Swede, the blond Jewish athlete every kid in the neighborhood worshipped from a distance. Seymour Levov grows up to claim everything the postwar promise offered: the glove factory, the beauty-queen wife, the stone house in the country. Nathan Zuckerman, half-inventing the life he can only guess at, tells the story because the wreckage demands a witness. The wreckage is Merry, the Swede's stuttering daughter, who plants a bomb at the village store to protest Vietnam and kills a man, then vanishes into the rage of her own country. What [Roth](/authors/philip-roth) grasps, and what leaves a bruise, is that the Swede's ruin grows straight out of his goodness. A gentler father, less patient, less loving, might have seen his child coming. _American Pastoral_ is the novel of how the dream curdles from the inside, how the story you tell yourself about your life keeps telling itself right up until the blast.

title: Ward No. 6
author: Anton Chekhov
extract: In the hospital yard there stands a small lodge surrounded by a perfect forest of burdocks, nettles, and wild hemp.
blurb: Behind the hospital, past a forest of burdock and nettle, stands the lodge they call Ward No. 6, and inside it Dr. Andrei Ragin discovers the one man in town worth talking to: Gromov, a patient, who insists with furious clarity that pain is real and must be fought. Ragin disagrees. He is a reader, a gentle stoic who has persuaded himself that a mind well stocked with Marcus Aurelius can be serene in any cell, that suffering is finally a matter of where you choose to stand. [Chekhov](/authors/anton-chekhov), who was a doctor, lets this idea sound almost wise, and then he does the cruelest and most honest thing in the story: he has Ragin declared mad and locked in the ward himself. Nikita the guard beats him with the same bored efficiency that has kept the others docile for years. The philosophy that survived every argument does not survive a single blow. Detachment, it turns out, was only ever the luxury of the man holding the key.

title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Brontë
extract: Reader, I married him.
blurb: There is a laugh in the upper corridor of Thornfield Hall that no one will explain, and a governess who refuses to stop asking. Jane is plain, poor, and orphaned, raised on cruelty and told her whole life that she is nobody, and she narrates her own story as if daring you to look away. She falls in love with Rochester, her brooding master, and he with her, until the morning their wedding shatters on the secret he keeps locked upstairs: a wife, mad, kept like an animal in the attic. Jane could stay as his mistress and be adored. Instead she walks out into the rain with nothing, because the one thing she will not surrender is the self that says _I am no bird; and no net ensnares me_. [Brontë](/authors/charlotte-bronte) wrote a love story whose deepest passion is a woman refusing to be possessed, and the fire of that refusal has never gone out.

title: Gimpel the Fool
author: Isaac Bashevis Singer
extract: I am Gimpel the fool. I don't think myself a fool. On the contrary.
blurb: The children of Frampol tell Gimpel the orphan baker that his dead parents have risen from the grave, that the Messiah has come, that a cow flew over the roof and laid brass eggs, and every time he goes to look. The whole village has made his believing into a game. [Singer](/authors/isaac-bashevis-singer) wrote the story in Yiddish while the Yiddish-speaking world was being annihilated, and he chose this willing fool to carry the one thing the clever could not save. Its quiet argument is that Gimpel's endless gullibility and his faith are the same substance, that the neighbors sharp enough to see through every lie have also armored themselves against every grace. Late in his life the wife who betrayed him for years comes to him in a dream, her face blackened, and what she confesses turns his lifetime of being deceived into something close to holiness. He ends his days as a wandering teller of tales, poor and unafraid, certain that somewhere past all this lying waits a world where even Gimpel cannot be fooled.

title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
author: Lewis Carroll
extract: We're all mad here. I'm mad. You're mad.
blurb: On a July afternoon, rowing three little girls up the river, an Oxford mathematician began making up a story to pass the time, and one of them, Alice Liddell, begged him to write it down. What he gave her was a country where logic has not been abandoned but obeyed too well: a Queen who hands down the sentence before the verdict, a trial whose evidence arrives after the judgment, a croquet match played with live flamingos and hedgehogs that wander off mid-stroke. Charles Dodgson could invert reason precisely because he taught it, and the deep joke of Wonderland is that its madness is consistent. Alice keeps her manners and her common sense and finds neither is any defence against a world where words mean whatever the speaker needs them to and a single bite of mushroom rewrites who you are. The Caterpillar's question is not idle. Who are you, when nothing will hold still long enough to tell you?

title: The Rainbow
author: D.H. Lawrence
extract: She was the doorway to him, he to her.
blurb: Under the moon, a man and a woman gather sheaves of cut corn across a stubble field, walking toward each other and away, lifting and setting down in a rhythm that is a courtship before either has spoken of love. _The Rainbow_ is full of such scenes, where bodies say what the Brangwens cannot, and [Lawrence](/authors/dh-lawrence)'s prose moves with them: incantatory, looping, swollen with the rush of sap and blood until you feel the sentence breathe. Three generations of one Midlands family reach for the same thing, each further than the last, from Tom and the Polish widow who stays forever partly beyond him, through Anna and Will's long bruising marriage, to Ursula, who wants a whole self the land could never give. Seized and burned as obscene on publication, its real scandal was never sex but Lawrence's conviction that industrial England had torn body from spirit, and that the wound could heal. The arc of colour Ursula sees at the close is no promise of heaven but proof that a better world is owed, still waiting to be built.

title: The Lover
author: Marguerite Duras
extract: One day, I was already old, in the entrance of a public place a man came up to me.
blurb: It begins with a stranger who tells her, decades later, that he finds her ravaged face more beautiful than the one she wore as a girl. From that astonishing remark [Marguerite Duras](/authors/marguerite-duras) circles back to the Mekong, to the ferry from Sadec, where at fifteen and a half she stood in a man's flat-brimmed fedora and gold lamé heels and let a wealthy Chinese man step from his black limousine to look at her. What follows is the affair, told in fragments that retreat and return, the narrator slipping between the first person and the third as if she cannot decide whether the girl is herself or someone she once watched from across the years. The family is poor and half-mad, the love is real and impossible, and Duras refuses to pretend the girl was only its victim: she knows exactly what she wants. The prose does not reconstruct desire so much as keep it burning. To remember, here, is to want again.

title: Herzog
author: Saul Bellow
extract: If I am out of my mind, it's all right with me, thought Moses Herzog.
blurb: He writes letters he will never send. To the dead, to the living, to Nietzsche, to Eisenhower, to his analyst, to God, scrawled on scraps and composed in his head, a brilliant man cracking apart and unable to stop explaining himself. Moses Herzog has lost his wife to his best friend, lost the thread of his life, and the only thing his great learning can do is narrate his own collapse with unbearable wit. Few novels have so exactly caught the particular agony of the over-educated heart, the way intelligence becomes a torment when feeling overwhelms it, the way a mind talks and talks because it cannot bear what has happened to the marriage beneath it. And yet the book is funny, gorgeously, helplessly funny, [Bellow](/authors/saul-bellow)'s sentences spilling and looping with a vitality no breakdown can kill. To read it is to feel a mind save itself by the sheer act of putting everything into words, and to recognize, with a jolt, how much of your own grief you have tried to think your way out of.

title: Macbeth
author: William Shakespeare
extract: Out, out, brief candle! Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player that struts and frets his hour upon the stage.
blurb: On a blasted heath, three witches stop a soldier coming home from war and hand him a crown he has not imagined wanting. The prophecy does its damage not by tempting Macbeth but by making the waiting unbearable, the throne suddenly owed him, Duncan suddenly in the way. It is the shortest of [Shakespeare](/authors/william-shakespeare)'s tragedies and the most airless, each murder breeding the next with barely a breath between bloodied scenes. The marvel is the music he gives his killers: Macbeth watching a dagger float toward a hand not yet bloodied, then measuring his despair as tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow creeping in its petty pace; Lady Macbeth, who steadied his nerve for the first killing, scrubbing in her sleep at a spot all the perfumes of Arabia cannot sweeten. He goes numb where she goes haunted, the bold one undone by conscience, the hesitant one past feeling. No play has ever made damnation sound so much like poetry, or shown so exactly how a man talks himself across the line he swore he would not cross.

title: The Plague
author: Albert Camus
extract: What's true of all the evils in the world is true of plague as well. It helps men to rise above themselves.
blurb: First the rats come up to die in the open, on stairwells and in the street, and the town of Oran is too comfortable to read the warning. Then the gates close, the city is quarantined from the world, and Dr. Bernard Rieux begins the work that fills the book: tending the dying, not out of heroism but because the alternative would be unthinkable. [Camus](/authors/albert-camus) strips every consolation away. There is no divine plan, no reward, only the daily refusal to let people suffer alone, and he insists this stubborn decency is the only sanity left when the world stops making sense. The novel's most unbearable hour comes when a child dies slowly in front of a priest who has called the plague God's justice, and that God does not survive the bedside. Camus wrote Oran as occupied France, but the last pages reach further: the bacillus never truly dies, only waits, patient in cupboards and old papers, ready to rouse its rats again in some happy, forgetful city.

title: Romance Sonámbulo
author: Federico García Lorca
extract: Green, how I want you green. Green wind. Green branches.
blurb: Verde que te quiero verde. Green, how I want you green. The line arrives like a spell before you know what it means, and for the length of [Lorca](/authors/federico-garcia-lorca)'s most famous ballad you never quite will. A girl the colour of the sea dreams on a balcony under a gypsy moon, her flesh green, her eyes cold silver, while somewhere a wounded man rides back through the mountains toward her, bleeding from the gates of Cabra. What binds them, whether he arrives in time, what the green even is, Lorca refuses to say, and said he could not say himself. This is a poem you understand with your skin before your mind, its green wind and cold silver carrying a dread you cannot name. Read it aloud in either tongue. Let the refrain deepen and darken each time it returns, until the last green branch closes over something you were never quite shown. Few poems have made mystery this beautiful, or beauty this unsafe.

title: The Flowers of Evil
author: Charles Baudelaire
extract: Hypocrite reader! -- You! -- My twin! -- My brother!
blurb: Read the first poem and [Baudelaire](/authors/charles-baudelaire) reaches out of the page to name you: "Hypocrite reader, my fellow, my brother." Before a single flower has bloomed you are implicated, a fellow citizen of the boredom and the appetite the book is about to anatomise. What follows is not a scatter of lyrics but a built cathedral of them, climbing from Spleen and Ideal up through the gaslit Parisian streets, the wine, the flowers themselves, and at last Death. Baudelaire's genius is a kind of alchemy: he gathers the mud of the modern city, its hospitals and gutters and bought women and bottomless afternoons, and turns it to gold, refusing the old lie that beauty and corruption keep separate rooms. A French court convicted six of these poems of offending public morality, which only proved his point. He had dissolved the wall between the sacred and the squalid, and modern poetry walked through the gap he left.

title: Antigone
author: Sophocles
extract: Many wonders there be, but naught more wondrous than man;
blurb: A handful of dust is all it takes. Polynices fell attacking his own city, and the new king of Thebes has ruled that the traitor's body stay above ground, food for the dogs and the noon sun, a punishment built to outlast death. His sister Antigone scatters dust over him anyway, sealing her fate in an act briefer than the sentence that describes it. What makes [Sophocles](/authors/sophocles)' play unbearable is that neither of them is wrong. Antigone obeys the gods of the dead, who were old before any throne existed; Creon is holding a city together after civil war, and a king whose edicts mean nothing rules nothing. The play takes no side. It destroys them both and keeps Creon on stage long after the girl is walled alive into her rock tomb, so he can total what his principle has cost. Twenty-five centuries on, no one has untied the knot: the law of the city stands, and the city is empty of everyone worth saving.

title: A Raisin in the Sun
author: Lorraine Hansberry
extract: What happens to a dream deferred?
blurb: On the kitchen windowsill of a cramped South Side apartment, Mama keeps a feeble little plant that has never once had enough sun, and she waters it anyway. Into this household, where five Youngers share a bathroom down the hall and a child sleeps on the living-room couch, comes a ten-thousand-dollar insurance check, the whole of a dead man's life turned into cash. Everyone wants it for a different dream. Walter Lee, who drives a rich white man's car, wants a liquor store and the dignity of being his own man; Beneatha wants medical school; Mama wants a house with a patch of yard, in a neighborhood that happens to be white. [Lorraine Hansberry](/authors/lorraine-hansberry) knew that street from childhood, when her own father moved the family past a hostile line and fought the case to the Supreme Court. So when a soft-spoken man arrives offering good money for the Youngers to stay where they belong, the play holds its breath, and so will you. Watch what Walter Lee decides to do with his father's life.

title: Cry, the Beloved Country
author: Alan Paton
extract: Cry, the beloved country, for the unborn child that is the inheritor of our fear.
blurb: A lovely road runs from Ixopo up into the grass-covered hills, and the novel that opens on it is built like a psalm, its sentences rising and falling with the cadence of Zulu speech and the old English Bible. Stephen Kumalo, an aging Zulu parson, leaves those hills for Johannesburg to look for his sister and his son, and learns that his boy has killed a man in a house-breaking gone wrong. The dead man was white. He was also, unbearably, the one white South African who had given his life to the cause of the country's black poor. [Paton](/authors/alan-paton) draws the two fathers, one black and one white, each hollowed by the same act, slowly toward one another across a grief far larger than the law that keeps them apart. Read a page aloud and you will hear a whole wounded country mourning through a single old man's voice. Few novels have loved a land so fiercely while refusing to look away from what it does to its own.

title: The Tin Drum
author: Günter Grass
extract: Even bad books are books and therefore sacred.
blurb: Listen for the drum. On his third birthday Oskar Matzerath decides the world of grown men is not worth growing into and throws himself down the cellar stairs, fixing his body at a child's height forever. From that knee-high vantage he watches Danzig go under: the flags climb the poles, the neighbours join the Party, the Jewish toyseller who supplied his drums is gone, and the only honest witness left is a boy too small to be blamed and too clear-eyed to look away. He carries two instruments, a tin drum that hammers the buried years back into the present and a scream pitched to shatter glass, every smug windowpane that would rather stay whole and silent. [Günter Grass](/authors/gunter-grass) wrote the grotesque the way the century demanded, comedy and horror fused so close you cannot laugh without flinching. Narrating it all from a mental asylum, Oskar keeps the time the nation preferred to forget it ever kept.

title: The Divine Comedy
author: Dante Alighieri
extract: All hope abandon ye who enter here.
blurb: Midway along the road of life, the path simply gives out: the poet wakes in a dark wood, no memory of how he strayed, three beasts barring the way back. What saves him is a descent. Down through nine circles of Hell he goes, past popes and Florentine neighbors fixed forever in weather Dante built to fit their sins, the lustful blown like starlings on an endless wind, the traitors locked in ice. Virgil walks him through the dark; Beatrice, the girl he loved and lost when she died at twenty-four, waits to carry him up. This is the astonishment of it: a single exiled poet mapped the entire afterlife, Hell and Purgatory and Paradise, and set his own grief at its center, all in the Florentine speech he was helping to invent. He climbs until language nearly fails him, and then names what he sees: the Love that moves the sun and the other stars.

title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
author: William Wordsworth
extract: I wandered lonely as a cloud that floats on high o'er vales and hills.
blurb: Ten thousand daffodils crowd the margin of a lake, tossing their heads in a wind off the water, and a wanderer who came upon them by chance stands and watches a whole field dance. [William Wordsworth](/authors/william-wordsworth) took the scene from a walk with his sister Dorothy in the Lake District; her journal recorded the same dancing daffodils, and he made of it something stranger than a nature poem. The flowers are only the occasion. What the poem is really after is what happens later, alone, when the mind is empty or low and the daffodils come flashing back unbidden upon what he calls the inward eye, and the heart that thought itself solitary fills and dances with them. This is the quiet, radical claim under the famous opening line: that beauty truly attended to is never spent, only banked, waiting to be spent again. Joy, he insists, can be saved.

title: Snow Country
author: Yasunari Kawabata
extract: The train came out of the long tunnel into the snow country.
blurb: The train comes out of the long tunnel into the snow country, and the earth lies white under the night sky. A dilettante from Tokyo, Shimamura, watches a girl's face float in the dark train window, a far-off light flaring for an instant inside her eye, and never quite recovers from the beauty of something he cannot keep. In a hot-spring town buried in snow he takes up with Komako, a geisha who loves him with a fierceness that has nowhere to go, who keeps a diary no one will read and studies for a life that will not come. [Kawabata](/authors/yasunari-kawabata) names such devotion wasted effort, and makes the waste unbearably lovely: a woman pouring everything into a man too cool to be warmed, in a place so white and silent it seems to be erasing them both. Few books have wrung so much tenderness from futility, or left a love this whole and this hopeless glittering in the snow.

title: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
author: Matsuo Bashō
extract: The months and days are eternal travellers; the years that come and go are also wayfarers.
blurb: The months and days are travellers of eternity, [Bashō](/authors/matsuo-basho) writes, and the years too are wayfarers, and then he sells his hut, packs almost nothing, and walks out of Edo to prove it. What follows is a five-month journey on foot into the deep north of Japan, set down as haibun: passages of prose that reach for a place, broken open by a single haiku that holds it still. At Hiraizumi he stands in the grass where a great clan ruled and was annihilated, and instead of mourning them he gives us summer grasses and the dreams of dead soldiers, three lines carrying more grief than any chronicle. The pleasures are small and exact, a moon over pines, the islands of Matsushima, weeks of rain on a mountain road. _The Narrow Road to the Deep North_ is one of the shortest masterworks ever made, and that is its claim: attend to the passing world closely enough, and the attention is what lasts.

title: A Hunger Artist
author: Franz Kafka
extract: I always wanted you to admire my fasting.
blurb: There was an age when a man could grow famous by eating nothing, when crowds gathered at a barred cage to watch him fast and butchers stood guard day and night so he could not sneak a meal. [Kafka](/authors/franz-kafka)'s hunger artist is the last practitioner of this dying art, held to forty days by an impresario who knows that is where interest peaks. When fasting falls out of fashion he is moved to a circus stall on the way to the menagerie, where the crowd rushes past toward the animals and no one bothers to change the board counting his days. He goes on starving, unwatched, longer than anyone has. Then comes the confession that turns the whole thing inside out: he was never worth admiring, because he fasted only since he could never find a food he liked. Kafka wrote this as tuberculosis closed his own throat, correcting proofs while eating became impossible. When the artist dies they put a young panther in his cage, joy roaring through its body, and the crowd presses close, unable to look away.

title: Don Juan
author: Lord Byron
extract: Man's love is of man's life a thing apart, 'Tis woman's whole existence
blurb: [Byron](/authors/lord-byron) rhymes "intellectual" with "hen-peck'd you all," and that one outrageous chime tells you the game: a comic epic forever winking at its own verse. The Juan here is not the predatory seducer of legend but its mirror image, a sweet, passive, beautiful young man who is shipwrecked, sold into a harem, hurled through a Russian siege, and bedded by an empress, never once doing the seducing. The hijacking is the joke. The real hero is the narrator, a voice of bottomless wit who can turn, between punchlines, startlingly tender, writing that man's love is of his life a thing apart while woman's is her whole existence, then deriding English cant in the very next breath. Digression is not a flaw but the argument, a mind too alive to sit still inside a story. Byron died at Missolonghi with the poem broken off mid-canto, and no tidier ending could have been honest to it.

title: Death Fugue
author: Paul Celan
extract: Black milk of daybreak we drink it at evening we drink it at midday and morning we drink it at night.
blurb: In a death camp, prisoners are ordered to play dance music while others shovel a grave in the air, and from that obscenity [Paul Celan](/authors/paul-celan) built a poem that refuses to console. Its refrain, black milk of daybreak, is drunk at morning and noon and evening and night, the impossible phrase wheeling back the way a subject wheels through a fugue, gathering a weight it should not be able to carry. A commandant writes home to Germany, calls golden-haired Margarete to mind, plays with his serpents, and orders the prisoners to play death more sweetly, for death is a master from Deutschland. Celan, whose mother was shot and whose father died in the camps, refused both the false comfort of testimony and the lie of silence. By the close, Margarete's golden hair set against Shulamith's hair of ash, _Death Fugue_ will not let you stand apart from the dead.

title: Huckleberry Finn
author: Mark Twain
extract: All right, then, I'll go to hell.
blurb: Two days downriver and the raft has slipped past Cairo in the fog, which means it is carrying Huck and Jim deeper into slave country instead of out of it, and Huck still cannot decide whether to turn his friend in. The wonder of the book is the voice: a barefoot, half-schooled boy telling his own story in the river dialect of the antebellum South, funny and sharp and wholly unable to see that he is the only decent soul in the frame. [Twain](/authors/mark-twain) crowds the banks with America at its worst, two grifters working the river towns, genteel families shooting each other over nothing, a father drunk and dangerous, until cruelty reads as the ordinary weather of the place. So when Huck resolves to help Jim run, he is certain he is damning himself, and you watch a boy do the bravest thing in American literature while believing it the worst. Few novels have made goodness this funny, or this costly to the one who carries it.

title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau
extract: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life.
blurb: Twenty-eight dollars and twelve and a half cents: that is what it cost [Henry David Thoreau](/authors/henry-david-thoreau) to build a cabin in the woods by Walden Pond, and he gives you the figure down to the half-penny, board by board, because the whole book turns on a single audacious sum. The price of anything, he insists, is the amount of life you exchange for it, and most of us, he means you, have overpaid for things we never wanted. So he went to the pond to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts and see what they had to teach. What follows is two years compressed into one turning year, ice thickening and thawing on the pond, rows of beans hoed clean, the dawn arriving as if for the first time. The prose measures everything and worships everything at once. Close it and the question stays lodged: what is your own life costing you, and did you ever agree to the price?

title: Don Quixote
author: Miguel de Cervantes
extract: In a village of La Mancha, the name of which I have no desire to call to mind.
blurb: On a plain in La Mancha, a thin old man levels his lance at a row of windmills, certain they are giants with flailing arms, and charges. He is wrong, of course. He is wrong about almost everything: the roadside inn is a castle, the farm girl Dulcinea a princess, a barber's brass basin the golden helmet of a hero. He has read so many tales of knighthood that his mind has cracked open, and out of the crack pours something the saner world has lost. Beside him trots Sancho Panza, fat and proverb-stuffed and helplessly devoted, and theirs may be the tenderest friendship in all of literature. The miracle is that you start by laughing at the madman and end unable to laugh, because his delusion is only the wish that the world were braver and kinder than it is. No book is funnier, and few are this kind. [Cervantes](/authors/miguel-de-cervantes) will not tell you whether to mock the knight or kneel to him, and by the end you cannot do either alone.

title: Anne of Green Gables
author: L.M. Montgomery
extract: Isn't it splendid to think of all the things there are to find out about?
blurb: Matthew Cuthbert drives to the Bright River station for a boy to help with the farm, and comes home instead with a skinny orphan girl who has already renamed the pond along the road the Lake of Shining Waters. Marilla wants to send her back. Anne Shirley talks her out of it in one afternoon, simply by being unbearably, hilariously herself: breaking a slate over a boy's head for calling her carrots, dyeing her hair green trying to make it black, getting her bosom friend disastrously tipsy on what she swears was only raspberry cordial. What she does, without meaning to, is teach a rigid, unloved farmhouse how to love out loud. [L.M. Montgomery](/authors/lm-montgomery) understood that imagination in a child who has had nothing is not whimsy, it is survival, and that the plainest life turns luminous the moment someone insists on calling it by a better name. By the last page, whatever it costs her to grow up, you will want to have been raised at Green Gables too.

title: The Tao Te Ching
author: Laozi
extract: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao.
blurb: The book opens by warning you off itself. The Way that can be spoken is not the eternal Way, the name that can be named not the eternal name. From that single refusal [Laozi](/authors/laozi) builds 81 short verses that keep circling a thing they admit language cannot hold, the Tao, the current running under everything that is. He never argues so much as shows. A wheel is useful for the empty hole at its hub, a cup for the hollow it cups, a room for the space the walls leave alone; water, the softest thing there is, wears the hardest stone away by yielding rather than striving. The Classical Chinese is so spare that each line can be turned a dozen ways, and read slowly the paradoxes stop sounding like riddles and start sounding like the truest account of how things actually move. Nothing in it raises its voice, and that is the point: it persuades the way water does, by going low and outlasting everything harder. Few books ask so little of you and rearrange so much.

title: Meditations
author: Marcus Aurelius
extract: No more talking at all about what sort of person a good man is: be one.
blurb: In a campaign tent on the Danube frontier, the ruler of the known world wrote himself reminders he never meant another soul to read. [Marcus Aurelius](/authors/marcus-aurelius) could command legions, raise temples, and end a life with a word, and the only thing he could not trust was his own character under the weight of all that power. So he kept a private notebook, in Greek, and filled it with corrections: rise though the bed is warm, do not rage at fools, remember that the man who wronged you this morning is your kinsman, remember above all that you will die and soon. There is no audience here, no pose, only an emperor talking himself back toward decency one entry at a time. That is what makes it beautiful and almost unbearable at once. Two thousand years later you are reading a powerful man's quarrel with himself, and the wisest book ever written about how to live turns out to be the one its author never meant for you to see.

title: Self-Reliance
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
extract: A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds.
blurb: Trust thyself, [Emerson](/authors/ralph-waldo-emerson) writes, and every heart vibrates to that iron string. _Self-Reliance_ is the sound of a man refusing, line by line, to be smaller than his own conviction. The essay's genius is its aim: not the timid or the dull but the respectable conformist, the charitable joiner, the person so eager for approval that they have quietly traded away their own judgment and called it virtue. Emerson names that surrender cowardice, however gentle the motive, and insists that nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of your own mind. The sentences arrive like struck flints, "imitation is suicide," "to be great is to be misunderstood," each one daring you to flinch. And then the trap: to nod along with Emerson is to find a new master to obey, the very failure he is warning against. The only way to prove him right is to close the essay and stop listening to him.

title: The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier and Clay
author: Michael Chabon
extract: To me, Clark Kent in a phone booth and Houdini in a packing crate, they were one and the same thing.
blurb: On the cover of the first issue, the Escapist socks Adolf Hitler across the jaw. Josef Kavalier draws that punch again and again, the only blow he can land from Brooklyn while his family waits in occupied Prague for an exit that keeps not arriving. He himself had escaped the city sealed inside a coffin beside the Golem of Prague, and in that Brooklyn bedroom he and his cousin Sammy Klayman build a whole mythology out of the one thing neither of them can actually do: save anyone. [Michael Chabon](/authors/michael-chabon) writes comic books as if they were a form of prayer, panel after panel, and lets the real cost of the war arrive without asking permission, when Joe's little brother Thomas drowns on a ship that never reaches New York. What lingers is not the costume but the escape artistry underneath it, two boys inventing a hero because the world would not let them be one, and a love story that keeps slipping its own disguises until, finally, it can't.

title: Anna Karenina
author: Leo Tolstoy
extract: Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
blurb: A train pulls into a snowbound Moscow station, a carriage door opens, and Anna steps down into the one glance that will undo her. She has everything the world counts: beauty, wit, an important husband, a place at the centre of Petersburg society. What takes it all from her is not love and not scandal alone but the exact arithmetic of both, a world that winks at a husband's affairs and bolts every drawing-room door against a wife who dares the same. [Tolstoy](/authors/leo-tolstoy) lays a second life alongside hers, Levin out on his estate, scything hay beside his peasants, groping toward a God he cannot name and a happiness he half-distrusts. The wonder of it is the mercy: no one is a villain here, everyone is right inside their own pain. You will dread the final hundred pages and turn them anyway, unable to look away from where the train is going.

title: The Negro Speaks of Rivers
author: Langston Hughes
extract: My soul has grown deep like the rivers.
blurb: A voice speaks that bathed in the Euphrates when dawns were young, built its hut beside the Congo, raised the pyramids above the Nile, and heard the Mississippi sing beneath Abe Lincoln. It is one 'I,' and it is a whole people, carrying the memory of every river Black life has known across the full length of human time. [Langston Hughes](/authors/langston-hughes) wrote it at seventeen, in the few minutes it took his train to cross the Mississippi at dusk, and the poem still moves like deep water, unhurried and immense. Watch what it does with the muddy river turning gold in the sunset, how a despised history is lifted into something ancient and luminous. One line returns, quiet and absolute, a current running beneath all the rest: My soul has grown deep like the rivers. Few poems say so much, so softly, about where a person comes from and how unfathomably far back that reaches.

title: The Communist Manifesto
author: Karl Marx & Friedrich Engels
extract: A spectre is haunting Europe -- the spectre of Communism.
blurb: A spectre is haunting Europe, the pamphlet announces in its first breath, and the line still carries the thrill of something about to happen. What follows is not the screed a reader braces for. Before [Marx](/authors/karl-marx) and Engels indict the bourgeoisie, they praise it, marveling at a class that has torn down every ancient wall, dissolved every fixed relation, profaned everything once held holy, and conjured in a single century more wealth than all the ages before it. The famous verdict, all that is solid melts into air, is delivered almost with wonder. That is the strange power of these fifty pages: they make the world they condemn thrilling to behold, then argue that its own restless engine has built, in the worker, the force that will end it. The prescription has been fought over for nearly two centuries. The portrait of a world that cannot stop dissolving its own ground has been harder to wave away. It closes on a summons that still lifts the hair on your neck: you have nothing to lose but your chains.

title: The Blue Flower
author: Penelope Fitzgerald
extract: Jacob Dietmahler was not such a fool that he could not see that they had arrived at his friend's home on the washday.
blurb: The whole house is hung with washing the day Fritz's friend arrives, the year's linen steaming from every banister, and into this clamour of a great untidy German family the novel sets down its impossible fact: Friedrich von Hardenberg, the young philosopher who will become the poet Novalis, has fallen in love with Sophie von Kuhn. She is twelve. She is not clever, not musical, not pretty in any way worth recording; she plays cards and says nothing memorable, and his family receives the engagement with appalled courtesy. [Penelope Fitzgerald](/authors/penelope-fitzgerald), writing her last and finest novel in her late seventies, never once explains the love, because no one can. She assembles 1790s Saxony out of glimpses instead, chapters barely a page long, the salt-mine country and the racket of a vast household, until a whole world stands built from what she leaves out. The blue flower of Romantic longing, that unreachable ideal, turns out to be a girl who coughs and will not live long. The ache was never the flower. It was the wanting.

title: The Prince
author: Niccolò Machiavelli
extract: it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with.
blurb: It is much safer to be feared than loved: the sentence arrives without heat, without apology, the way a surgeon names the thing that has to be cut. That coolness is the whole unsettling genius of _The Prince_. For centuries the books written for rulers told them how to be good; [Machiavelli](/authors/niccolo-machiavelli), stripped of office and tortured by the Medici he would then dedicate it to, sat down to tell them instead how to survive, and the gap between those two instructions is the nerve he keeps pressing. A prince who insists on virtue among men who have none, he argues, will be destroyed, and cruelty used well and quickly is a kind of mercy. The examples come like evidence in a brief, Cesare Borgia, Moses, Romulus, never ornament. What lingers is not the shock of the conclusions but the calm, the sense of a man describing the world exactly as it is while everyone around him agrees to pretend otherwise. Read it once and you will hear its level voice under every speech a powerful man ever gave.

title: Finnegans Wake
author: James Joyce
extract: riverrun, past Eve and Adam's, from swerve of shore to bend of bay, brings us by a commodius vicus of recirculation back to Howth Castle and Environs.
blurb: riverrun, past Eve and Adam's, from swerve of shore to bend of bay. The book opens mid-clause, on a lowercase word, picking up a sentence the final page left hanging, because the last line breaks off and loops back to the first. [James Joyce](/authors/james-joyce) gave seventeen years and most of his failing eyesight to this one closed circle, inventing a language nobody had spoken, where each word is three or four words crushed into one, punning across a dozen tongues at once. Do not read it the way you read a novel. Say it aloud, and the sense arrives the way it does in a dream, sidelong, through sound, before the waking mind can grab it. A Dublin publican sleeps above his bar and dreams the whole guilty history of the species in a single night; his wife is the River Liffey, and on the closing page she widens into the sea and is gone, only to rise again as riverrun at the top of the book. Nobody finishes it. Stand in it once and let the river carry you.

title: To the Lighthouse
author: Virginia Woolf
extract: What is the meaning of life? That was all - a simple question; one that tended to close in on one with years.
blurb: Candles are lit, the boeuf en daube carried steaming to the table, and around it on a Scottish island Mrs. Ramsay watches her family and guests cohere, for one hour, into something that feels eternal. She is the gravity of the house, the warmth every restless longing bends toward, and looking at the candlelight she thinks that of such moments the thing is made that endures. Then [Woolf](/authors/virginia-woolf) does the most devastating thing in modern fiction: she empties the house. The years pour through the abandoned rooms, the war arrives, and Mrs. Ramsay's death is set down inside square brackets, a world ended in a subordinate clause while the wind keeps lifting the curtains in the dark. Years later Lily Briscoe comes back to the easel she abandoned before the war, the canvas unfinished, the woman who once filled it now gone to a shape of absence. To take up that brush at all is the book's whole faith: that against everything time carries off, one evening at a table, one line drawn true, might be made to hold.

title: The Interpretation of Dreams
author: Sigmund Freud
extract: At any rate the interpretation of dreams is the via regia to a knowledge of the unconscious in the psychic life.
blurb: The first dream [Sigmund Freud](/authors/sigmund-freud) takes apart in these pages is one of his own, a patient's throat examined, an illness that might be his doing, a guilt he refuses to simply sleep off. He dismantles it syllable by syllable, until the dread resolves into a wish too shameful to admit while awake. This is the book's gambit: a dream is never nonsense but a coded letter from the part of us that wants what it must not, smuggled past the inner censor by a dreamwork that condenses and displaces until the desire is unrecognizable even to the dreamer. To prove it, Freud offers the strangest evidence any science ever ran on, his own sleep, his ambitions and rivalries and small humiliations laid open as specimens. Here, reading Sophocles, Freud first lays out the desire he will later call the Oedipus complex, and hands the next century its language for the hidden self. The dream, he writes, is the royal road. Walk it once and you will not look at your own mind the same way again.

title: Where the Mind Is Without Fear
author: Rabindranath Tagore
extract: Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high
blurb: Seven times a clause opens with the word Where, and each names a condition of a country worth waking into: a mind without fear, knowledge free, reason that has not lost its way into the dreary desert sand of dead habit. [Rabindranath Tagore](/authors/rabindranath-tagore) first wrote this prayer in Bengali, then rendered it himself into the English that carried him to the 1913 Nobel, the first in Literature ever awarded outside Europe. It is less a poem about freedom than a held breath before it, a whole nation imagined into being one clause at a time and released only in the final line, when the grammar turns at last to command and asks his motherland to wake into that heaven. Written under empire, it reads now wherever a wall goes up between people. Say that closing sentence aloud, and feel how few words it takes to carry the size of a people's hope.

title: Gravity's Rainbow
author: Thomas Pynchon
extract: A screaming comes across the sky.
blurb: Somewhere over wartime London a V-2 rocket is already falling, faster than its own sound, so the scream arrives after the blast and the dead never hear the thing that kills them. [Pynchon](/authors/thomas-pynchon) takes that arc, up and over and down, as the shape of everything in _Gravity's Rainbow_: a vast descent through the bombed-out Zone of a collapsing Germany, where an American lieutenant named Slothrop is hunted because his body somehow knows where the rockets will fall before they do. He goes looking for the reason and finds instead the cartels who fuelled both armies, who never cared which flag won, who were only ever building the next rocket. The book is paranoid the way a mystic is devout, certain that everything connects, and never once wrong. It is filthy, hilarious, grief-stricken, and stuffed with more equations and dirty songs than a novel should be able to hold. By the last pages Slothrop has come apart into rumour, and only the arc remains, perfect and indifferent, still pointing down at all of us.

title: One Art
author: Elizabeth Bishop
extract: The art of losing isn't hard to master; so many things seem filled with the intent to be lost that their loss is no disaster.
blurb: Start small: a ring of door keys, an hour badly spent, the fluster of a name you can no longer summon. _One Art_ teaches loss the way you might teach a child to swim, beginning in the shallows and wading out, until [Elizabeth Bishop](/authors/elizabeth-bishop)'s catalogue of things gone has swelled to her mother's watch, three beloved houses, two cities, two rivers, an entire continent. All the while the refrain keeps insisting, with a calm that should make us nervous, that the art of losing isn't hard to master. Then the last stanza reaches the loss the whole poem has been circling without naming, a person, a voice, a loved gesture, and the villanelle's patient machinery very nearly holds. It is the parenthesis that gives her away: Bishop breaks off her own performance to order herself, mid-line, to write it. That small broken command is the sound of a heart refusing the very lesson it spent nineteen lines pretending to master.

title: Fahrenheit 451
author: Ray Bradbury
extract: It was a pleasure to burn.
blurb: "It was a pleasure to burn," [Ray Bradbury](/authors/ray-bradbury) begins, and for a few pages you believe him: kerosene in bright arcs, a house lit like a torch, its books curling to black moths on the porch. Guy Montag is a fireman in an America where firemen no longer put out fires; they start them, burning whatever a nation of screens has decided is too dangerous to keep. Then a girl asks him, simply, whether he is happy, and the question will not let him go. This is not a people whose books were taken away. It is a people who burned their own, because feeling anything at all had grown unbearable beside a wall that asks nothing of you. Montag's wife swallows her sleeping pills and cannot remember doing it; the men who pump her stomach are as bored as if they were fixing a drain. By the time Montag runs, the city behind him is doomed, and the last hope is a handful of people in the woods, each becoming a book so that something survives the fire.

title: The Leopard
author: Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa
extract: If we want things to stay as they are, things will have to change.
blurb: Don Fabrizio, Prince of Salina, climbs to his observatory at night because the stars are the only things in Sicily that will not betray him by changing. Below, in 1860, Garibaldi's redshirts are landing, and the feudal world his family has ruled for centuries is quietly ending. His clever nephew Tancredi offers the formula that will let the aristocracy survive by surrendering: for everything to stay the same, everything must change. [Lampedusa](/authors/giuseppe-tomasi-di-lampedusa), the last prince of his own dying line, wrote this while himself near death, and that doubling gives the book its terrible authority. Fabrizio is not fooled. He knows the new world that absorbs his class is genuinely smaller, coarser, less beautiful, and he watches it arrive with a grief too lucid for nostalgia. Read it for the prose that moves like a Sicilian afternoon, slow and golden and already mourning the light it is losing.

title: A Farewell to Arms
author: Ernest Hemingway
extract: The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places.
blurb: In the late summer of that year the troops march past a house on a river, and the dust they raise powders the leaves of the trees so they fall early. That is how the book begins, in a prose so clean it seems to have had everything inessential burned off it, every word load-bearing, every short sentence a held breath. Frederic Henry, an American driving ambulances for the Italian army, finds Catherine Barkley in a war he no longer believes in, and what starts as a way to pass the nights becomes the only thing either of them has. [Hemingway](/authors/ernest-hemingway) writes their happiness so plainly that you trust it completely, which is the trap, because the rain keeps falling and Catherine is afraid of the rain. Few novels know so exactly that the world breaks everyone, and that it kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially. Read it for the tenderness that survives all the way to the last cold page.

title: The Great Gatsby
author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
extract: So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.
blurb: Out across the dark water a single green light burns at the end of a dock, and on the lawn opposite a man stands alone, arms stretched toward it, trembling. Jay Gatsby throws enormous parties for hundreds of strangers and drifts through none of them; the whole gold-lit machine exists to summon back one woman he loved in Louisville five years gone, who married old money while he was away at the war. The wonder of the book is that Gatsby chases not a future but a past already polished past anything the living Daisy could ever be, and [Fitzgerald](/authors/f-scott-fitzgerald) sees clean through to the ruin in it: Tom and Daisy are careless people who break things and retreat into their wealth, and the green light was never a place to arrive at, only a direction to keep facing. And then there are the sentences. Read the last page aloud, feel the current take you, boats borne back ceaselessly into the past, and try to set the book down.

title: Sons and Lovers
author: D.H. Lawrence
extract: He walked towards the faintly humming, glowing town, quickly.
blurb: Mr. Morel locks his wife out on a summer night after a drunken quarrel, and Gertrude stands alone in the garden, breathing in the scent of the tall white lilies until she and the unborn child inside her seem to melt together into the moonlight, one nervous, aching sensitivity already shared before he is even born. That child is Paul, and D. H. [Lawrence](/authors/dh-lawrence) follows him into manhood in a Nottinghamshire coal town, where his mother's thwarted hopes fasten onto him so completely that neither Miriam's tenderness nor Clara's hunger can ever claim him. This is the exact anatomy of a love that gives everything and asks everything back, of a son who cannot leave even when he tries. When cancer finally takes his mother, it is Paul who measures the morphine into her milk and sits with her until she goes still. What is left, on the last page, is a young man walking off the dark fields toward a town glowing faintly against the sky, choosing, for once, to walk toward the light instead of away from it.

title: The Shahnameh
author: Ferdowsi
extract: I suffered during these thirty years, but I have revived Iran with the Persian language.
blurb: For thirty years [Ferdowsi](/authors/ferdowsi) wrote in a Persian he scoured clean of the Arabic that had arrived with conquest, raising a poem the size of a library to house a civilization that had already vanished. _The Shahnameh_ runs from the world's first king to the fall of the last, generation upon generation of kings and heroes, and it has served ever since as the memory Iran keeps of itself. Its great engine is a terrible symmetry: the mightiest are undone not by enemies but from within, the ruin always cut to the exact measure of the gift. Nowhere does this land harder than when Rostam, the unbeaten champion of the age, fights a young warrior who has crossed a continent to find the father he never knew, and learns whose blood is on his hands only as the boy dies. Because the empire it exalts was ash when Ferdowsi began, every blaze of glory arrives already shadowed by its end. The poem mourns the very thing it sings.

title: The Republic
author: Plato
extract: Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy
blurb: Imagine a ring that makes you invisible. Glaucon sets it on the table early and asks the only question that matters: stripped of every reward, with no chance of being caught, would you still choose to be just, or is decency merely the price we pay for fear? Socrates refuses the easy answer and instead builds an entire city in speech, hoping to find justice written large enough to read, mapping the soul's three voices (reason, spirit, appetite) onto three classes until justice reveals itself as a kind of inner health and injustice a sickness its sufferer cannot feel. At the book's heart waits the Allegory of the Cave, where prisoners chained since birth take shadows on a wall for the whole world, and the one who escapes finds the climb toward the sun so blinding the others would kill him before they would follow. By the end, the tyrant who seems to have seized everything carries the most ruined soul in the city. A quarrel about fairness has become the first true map of the human interior.

title: Max Havelaar
author: Multatuli
extract: I am a coffee-broker, and live at No. 37 Laurier Canal, Amsterdam.
blurb: A stack of yellowing pages lands on the desk of Batavus Droogstoppel, an Amsterdam coffee broker with no patience for stories, who spends the whole book complaining about the one he has been handed. Buried inside it is the testimony of Max Havelaar, a Dutch colonial officer in Java who documented exactly what the coffee, sugar, and indigo filling Dutch warehouses cost the people forced to grow them, and tried to stop the theft from inside the government that profited by it. [Multatuli](/authors/multatuli)'s most devastating chapter is the one he buries deepest: Saïdjah, whose family's buffalo is seized by tax collectors, who leaves for Batavia to earn the money for another, and returns three years later to find Adinda's village destroyed and nothing of her left but a name among the dead. By the final pages Multatuli has abandoned his narrators altogether, stepping forward in his own voice to address the King of the Netherlands directly and demand that he act. Few books have ever meant, quite this literally, to bring down an empire.

title: The Catcher in the Rye
author: J.D. Salinger
extract: A book that, when you're all done reading it, you wish the author that wrote it was a terrific friend of yours.
blurb: Where do the ducks in the Central Park lagoon go when the water freezes over? Holden Caulfield keeps asking it, of cab drivers, of the night, of anyone who'll listen, and the question gives him away: under all the scorn is a sixteen-year-old frightened of what becomes of small things when the cold comes. Newly expelled from his fourth school, he spends three December days wandering New York rather than going home, and the whole book is his voice talking to you, funny and aggrieved and able to spot a phony across a room while missing the one he's becoming. The grief he won't name is his dead brother Allie, whose baseball mitt was covered in poems in green ink. He dreams of standing at the edge of a cliff in a field of rye, catching children before they fall into whatever ruined him. You finish it wishing he were a friend you could call.

title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
extract: No man, for any considerable period, can wear one face to himself, and another to the multitude, without finally getting bewildered.
blurb: The town means the letter as a brand. Hester Prynne, handed a scrap of cloth that marks her for life as an adulteress, takes up her needle and works it in gold thread, fantastic and gorgeous, until the badge of her shame becomes the most beautiful thing in drab Puritan Boston. That single act of defiance is the whole book in miniature. [Hawthorne](/authors/nathaniel-hawthorne) lets her wear the worst the magistrates can devise out in the open, year upon year, until it stops being a sentence and becomes simply hers, while the minister Arthur Dimmesdale, who shares the sin and hides it, is eaten from within by the secret he cannot speak. The wild child Pearl, born of that sin, is the one soul in town who cannot be taught to pretend. What _The Scarlet Letter_ knows, and never stops knowing, is that a shame carried in the open can be outlived, and that the letter at last indicts not the woman who wears it but the people who pinned it on.

title: My Last Duchess
author: Robert Browning
extract: That's my last Duchess painted on the wall, Looking as if she were alive.
blurb: The Duke of Ferrara draws a curtain back to show a stranger the portrait of his dead wife, and the polished courtesy of his voice never once falters as he explains, by degrees, why she had to die. She smiled too readily, he complains: a sunset, a bough of cherries someone broke for her in the orchard, his own nine-hundred-years-old name, every kindness earned the same warm look, and he would not stoop to ask her to ration it. So he gave commands, and then all smiles stopped together. [Browning](/authors/robert-browning) hands you one long unbroken speech and lets the speaker damn himself inside his own good manners, each silky aside a confession he has no idea he is making. The horror of _My Last Duchess_ is not the murder but the poise: a connoisseur already appraising his next bride while a bronze Neptune tames a sea-horse on the wall, the dead woman smiling now for no one but him, and only when he chooses to draw the curtain.

title: The Rape of the Lock
author: Alexander Pope
extract: What mighty contests rise from trivial things.
blurb: A pair of scissors closes on a curl of hair, and [Alexander Pope](/authors/alexander-pope) spends five cantos treating the snip as if Troy had fallen. Belinda wakes, and the morning ritual at her dressing table becomes a sacrament: combs, pins, "Puffs, Powders, Patches, Bibles, Billet-doux" laid out like an altar, an army of invisible sylphs deployed to guard her looks and the reputation locked inside them. The heroic couplets are the real marvel here, each snapping shut like a clasp, every closing rhyme a small lethal verdict, the antithesis balanced so finely you can hear the wit cut. Pope wrote it to laugh two feuding Catholic families back into friendship after a real lord did steal a real lock, and beneath the glitter he makes a graver argument: that the cruelties of the drawing room (the slight, the theft, the ruined name) wound as deeply as anything on the plains of Ilium. By the last canto the stolen curl rises into the night sky as a star, and the comedy, without ever saying so, has turned to something close to grace.

title: Les Misérables
author: Victor Hugo
extract: The supreme happiness of life consists in the conviction that one is loved.
blurb: Nineteen years in the galleys for stealing a loaf of bread, and days out of prison the convict steals again, the silver from the one house that fed him. When the police drag him back, the bishop tells them the silver was a gift, and presses on him the two candlesticks he 'forgot.' Everything in [Victor Hugo](/authors/victor-hugo)'s vast novel pours out of that single act of mercy: Fantine selling her hair and then her teeth for a daughter she cannot reach, Éponine taking a bullet in the rain for a boy who loves someone else, a barricade rising in a Paris that will not be saved. Hugo halts the story for the whole of Waterloo and the depths of the Paris sewers because he is making one furious case, that no soul is forever what its worst hour made it. Inspector Javert, who has built his life on the opposite belief, cannot survive being proven wrong, and walks into the Seine. Read it for the candlesticks, and for everything a man spends a life trying to be worth.

title: Things Fall Apart
author: Chinua Achebe
extract: He has put a knife on the things that held us together and we have fallen apart.
blurb: The boy calls him father. When the oracle decrees Ikemefuna must die, Okonkwo is warned to take no part, and then, afraid of seeming weak, cuts the boy down himself. This is the man at the center of the book: Okonkwo of Umuofia, who threw the wrestler Amalinze the Cat, built wealth and a great compound out of nothing, and spent his life outrunning the memory of a gentle, debt-ridden father he could not forgive. [Chinua Achebe](/authors/chinua-achebe) renders the Igbo world with a precision that needs no anthropology, its courts and oracles and proverbs carrying the argument of centuries, a civilization that owes no one an explanation. Then the missionaries arrive, offering a god who will take in the outcast and the failed, and the seams begin to give. What devastates is that the very hardness that made Okonkwo great makes him the wrong man to meet the change. _Things Fall Apart_ does not mourn a lost paradise but a living world, whole and self-sufficient, and a world is the harder thing by far to watch come undone.

title: Where Are You Going Where Have You Been?
author: Joyce Carol Oates
extract: The place where you came from ain't there any more, and where you had in mind to go is cancelled out.
blurb: A gold convertible rolls into an empty driveway one Sunday afternoon, the family off at a barbecue, and the young man who unfolds from it never once climbs the porch steps; he doesn't need to. Arnold Friend runs the whole encounter from the gravel, talking fifteen-year-old Connie toward him through the mesh of a screen door, and [Joyce Carol Oates](/authors/joyce-carol-oates) lets the horror live in that thin, unlatched distance: him outside, Connie inside, the afternoon going airless as his soft, relentless patter does all the work no hand needs to do. Connie has spent her summer sure that being looked at is a power she gets to spend; what she cannot yet see is that Arnold Friend is where that whole economy was always heading, its smiling terminus, maybe the devil himself in boots stuffed to fake the shape of human feet. By the time she reaches for the latch, the title's two questions have folded into one, and the answer has been waiting at the screen door all along.

title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
author: Douglas Adams
extract: In the beginning the Universe was created. This has made a lot of people very angry and been widely regarded as a bad move.
blurb: Arthur Dent stands in his dressing gown in front of bulldozers come to demolish his house, unaware that within minutes the planet itself will be demolished to make way for a hyperspace bypass. [Douglas Adams](/authors/douglas-adams) adapted this novel from his own 1978 BBC Radio 4 series, publishing it in 1979 as the opening volume of what became a five-book trilogy. Ford Prefect smuggles Arthur off Earth seconds before the Vogon fleet vapourises it; they are picked up by the stolen Heart of Gold, captained by the two-headed Zaphod Beeblebrox and crewed by Marvin, an android with a brain the size of a planet and the disposition of a wet weekend. The cosmos is administered by mice and prefaced by Vogon poetry. The number is 42; the universe declines to elaborate.

title: Medea
author: Euripides
extract: I would gladly take my stand in battle array three times o'er, than once give birth.
blurb: "I would rather stand three times in the front line of battle," Medea tells the women of Corinth, "than bear one child." She has borne two of Jason's sons, and by the play's end she will have killed them both. What makes this unbearable is not madness but clarity. Jason has left her for a Corinthian princess and come to explain, reasonably, that the match benefits them all; he expects thanks. Medea, who once killed her own brother and abandoned her homeland to follow him, plans her answer in daylight, reasoning every step aloud. She sends the bride a poisoned gown, then turns to the children, because she knows nothing will wound him more. The speech where she holds the boys, wavers, and chooses anyway gives us the first mind in Western drama to argue itself toward the unforgivable rather than stumble there through frenzy. Twenty-five centuries on, every tragedy that sets a lucid mind at the edge of the worst thing it could do is working in this play's shadow.

title: Crime and Punishment
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
extract: Pain and suffering are always inevitable for a large intelligence and a deep heart.
blurb: An axe, an old pawnbroker, a theory that some men are permitted to kill.
