Raskolnikov, a starving ex-student in a St. Petersburg July so hot the city itself seems delirious, talks himself into the murder to prove he is one of the extraordinary few who stand above the moral law. Then he discovers what no theory accounted for: that the mind keeps its own ledger, and a conscience cannot be reasoned out of existence. What follows is less a chase than a slow tightening, Raskolnikov circling the truth, the detective Porfiry circling him, until the only relief left is to be caught. [Dostoevsky](/authors/fyodor-dostoevsky) writes fever from the inside, the swarming streets and the cold sweat and the half-mad logic that feels, line by line, exactly like your own worst three a.m. And then, impossibly, he offers a way back, through the love of a woman who has nothing and forgives everything.

title: Dream of the Red Chamber
author: Cao Xueqin
extract: When falsehood stands for truth, truth likewise becomes false, Where naught be made to aught, aught changes into naught.
blurb: Every spring the peach blossoms fall across the Grand View Garden, and Lin Daiyu cannot stand to see them trampled into the mud: she gathers the fallen petals and buries them in the earth, weeping for the flowers and, without knowing it, for herself. Her grief over a handful of blossoms is the grief [Cao Xueqin](/authors/cao-xueqin) pours over a whole vanished world. He grew up inside one of Qing China's great households, his family imperial textile commissioners for three generations, then watched the wealth and the long seasons of poetry contests and chrysanthemum wine fall away. Into the Jia family's garden he set everything he could not bear to lose: a recipe, a riddle, the remedy for a cough, and at its heart Baoyu, the boy born with a jade in his mouth, who loves Daiyu as if they had known each other before either was born. His family means him for someone steadier. She burns her poems, page by page, in the brazier. To build a world this tenderly, the novel knows, is the longest way of saying goodbye.

title: The Diary of Samuel Pepys
author: Samuel Pepys
extract: And so to bed.
blurb: The Great Fire is racing toward his street, and [Samuel Pepys](/authors/samuel-pepys) is in his garden digging a pit to bury his wine and a Parmesan cheese. That single act holds the whole genius of the diary: catastrophe and supper on the same scale, the burning of a city weighed against a cheese. For nine years he wrote Restoration London down in private shorthand he never meant a soul to read, and that secrecy is what makes him immortal: the playhouses, the scheming at the Navy Board, the guilty fumblings he hid from his wife Elizabeth, the Plague tolling its dead, all in one plain, hungry, unguarded voice. No one had ever set a life down with so little distance between the page and the man. To read him is to live inside the seventeenth century at the grain of an ordinary Thursday, never knowing which Thursday the books will keep. He stopped in 1669, fearing the writing was costing him his sight, and the most watchful man of his age fell silent rather than go blind. And so to bed.

title: Doctor Zhivago
author: Boris Pasternak
extract: They walked and walked and sang Eternal Memory.
blurb: A candle burns in a frosted window on a Moscow street, and a young man passing in the snow carries the image away without knowing it will one day become a poem. [Boris Pasternak](/authors/boris-pasternak) was a poet first, and he wrote his only novel in secret over a decade, certain the Soviet state would never let it be printed; smuggled to Italy, it reached the world he could not. Yuri Zhivago, doctor and poet, is swept through revolution and civil war and forced labor, drawn again and again across the frozen Urals to Lara, in reunions that are always also farewells. What makes the book unbearable is not the history but its refusal to let history erase the private heart: the candle, the snow, the kerosene light, all the small radiances a century meant to extinguish. At the end Zhivago's poems remain, the only thing the cold could not take.

title: Confessions of Zeno
author: Italo Svevo
extract: I am the doctor who is sometimes spoken of in rather unflattering terms in this novel.
blurb: Every page of this confession is a lie, or so the doctor who publishes it insists in his opening note, furious that his patient quit analysis and mocked the whole undertaking on the way out. Zeno Cosini was told to write his life story as a cure for his smoking, and he cannot stop lighting one last cigarette: he marks the date on the wall each time, U.S. for ultima sigaretta, and breaks the promise again by morning. He falls for the beautiful sister, is refused, and somehow proposes his way into marrying the plain one instead, and she becomes the one part of his life he never manages to ruin. Every excuse he invents is more delightful than the truth it hides, and slowly you realize his sickness is only everyone's, dressed less carefully. [Svevo](/authors/italo-svevo) lets him diagnose himself sane at the very end, right before predicting, with a straight face, the bomb that will finally scour the disease of life from the earth.

title: Hurricane Season
author: Fernanda Melchor
extract: They reached the canal along the track leading up from the river, their slingshots drawn for battle and their eyes squinting, almost stitched together
blurb: Buzzards wheel over an irrigation canal outside the Mexican village of La Matosa, where a gang of boys wading through the reeds find the bloated body of the woman everyone called the Witch. From there the novel spirals backward through the voices of the town to reckon with her murder, each chapter a single unbroken sentence that runs for pages without a paragraph to catch your breath. [Fernanda Melchor](/authors/fernanda-melchor) writes in a torrent, obscene and biblical at once, the filth and fury of La Matosa pouring out in a rhythm you cannot stop reading even as it appalls you. This is not a whodunit; everyone knows who is dead. It is an anatomy of what poverty, superstition, and inherited cruelty do to the people caught inside them, told without a shred of mercy or a single false note. Sophie Hughes's English carries every degree of the storm. You surface from it shaken.

title: The Sound and the Fury
author: William Faulkner
extract: I give you the mausoleum of all hope and desire.
blurb: The title comes from the blackest speech in _Macbeth_, the one about a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing, and [Faulkner](/authors/william-faulkner) takes it literally. The novel opens inside the mind of Benjy Compson, who cannot tell this morning from thirty years past, for whom his sister Caddy survives only as the smell of trees and an ache he has no words to hold. The same ruin of one Southern family is then told again, and again, and again: by Quentin, drowning in time at Harvard; by Jason, mean and grasping; and at last by Dilsey, the Black servant who endures because she never believed the Compson name was worth a thing. To read it is to climb out of Benjy's dark, mind by mind, into the still light of Dilsey's Easter morning. And at the centre of every voice stands Caddy, the lost girl her brothers circle and none can keep, whom the novel itself loves too much to ever let speak for herself.

title: The Metamorphosis
author: Franz Kafka
extract: One morning, when Gregor Samsa woke from troubled dreams, he found himself transformed in his bed into a horrible vermin.
blurb: He wakes on his back, hard as armour, his thin legs waving helplessly above him, and his first clear thought is not terror but the train he is about to miss for work. [Franz Kafka](/authors/franz-kafka) gives literature its most monstrous premise and then flatly refuses to explain it; the real horror is never that Gregor Samsa has become an insect, but that his family adjusts. Watch the love curdle into housekeeping: the locked door, the rotting scraps shoved under it, the sister whose violin he loved learning to flinch. This is the most exact thing ever written about being wanted only for what you provide, and about what remains of a person once the providing stops. Few books are so quietly unbearable about the small room you are kept in, the apple festering in your back, the morning they decide everyone would be lighter if you were simply gone.

title: The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
day: International Day of Innocent Children Victims of Aggression
extract: But they seem to know where they are going, the ones who walk away from Omelas.
blurb: Picture a city in summer, bells ringing, swallows over the rooftops, horses garlanded for the festival race, a place so happy you suspect at once that it must be a lie. It isn't. [Le Guin](/authors/ursula-k-le-guin) then shows you the one cost: in a broom closet beneath the city sits a child, naked, fed on a half-bowl of cornmeal, never spoken to, and everyone in Omelas knows it is there. The whole radiant happiness of the place rests on that single, unredeemed misery, and they have agreed to it. This is the most quietly devastating thought experiment in American fiction, a story that hands you the oldest bargain in ethics and watches your face. Most stay, having reasoned themselves to peace. A few rise from the table and walk out the gate, on into a darkness even the author cannot describe. You will know, before the last line, exactly which one you are.

title: Nature
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
extract: I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all; the currents of the Universal Being circulate through me.
blurb: Cross a bare common at twilight, the snow still standing in the puddles, nothing lucky in your day, and feel a gladness rise that borders on fear: this is where [Emerson](/authors/ralph-waldo-emerson) begins. Then comes the sentence that started a literature. Standing on open ground, his head bathed in the blithe air, he feels the small self dissolve until he is nothing and sees everything, a transparent eyeball through which the currents of the universe pour. _Nature_ is the founding document of American thought, the essay that told a young country it need not borrow its religion or its poetry from the Old World, because the woods past the door were scripture enough. Emerson wonders what we would do if the stars came out one night in a thousand years, how we would believe and adore, then reminds us they come out every night and we have stopped looking up. Read it and you start looking again.

title: Buddenbrooks
author: Thomas Mann
extract: And -- and -- what comes next?
blurb: In the old gilt-edged book where the Buddenbrooks have recorded four generations of their births and deaths, little Hanno takes a pen and draws two clean lines beneath his own name. Asked why, he can only say he thought nothing more was coming. He is right. [Thomas Mann](/authors/thomas-mann)'s chronicle of a Lübeck grain dynasty is a study of how a family dies not from catastrophe but from refinement: each generation inherits the firm along with a finer, more trembling nervous system, until the commercial nerve thins entirely into music and longing and the wish to be left alone. Thomas the Senator reads Schopenhauer one winter night and tastes, for an hour, the dissolution of the self into something vast; by morning he is back at his desk, and it saves no one. The terrible tenderness of the book is that it loves what is killing them. To grow this beautiful, Mann saw, is to grow unfit to live.

title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot
extract: The growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts.
blurb: Edward Casaubon has poured his life into a book called the Key to All Mythologies, a great work he will never finish, and Dorothea Brooke, ardent and not yet twenty, marries him certain she can help him carry it. That mismatch is where _Middlemarch_ begins, before [George Eliot](/authors/george-eliot) widens the lens to hold a whole Midlands town: the gifted young doctor Lydgate, whose reforming ideals wear away under debt and his wife's lovely, immovable will; the banker Bulstrode, whose piety papers over an old crime; Fred Vincy, waiting slowly to deserve Mary Garth. Eliot knows every one of them from the inside, with a sympathy so exact it can name the very hour an idealism begins to shrink. She wrote that if we truly felt all ordinary human life we would hear the grass grow and the squirrel's heart beat, and die of the roar that lies on the other side of silence. No other novel takes you so close to that roar, or sends you back into your own small life so much gentler for having heard it.

title: The Tempest
author: William Shakespeare
extract: We are such stuff As dreams are made on; and our little life Is rounded with a sleep.
blurb: The sea heaves, a ship splits on the rocks, and a man on the shore has conjured the whole tempest from nothing, then watches his enemies wash up alive on his island. Prospero, exiled Duke turned sorcerer, has waited twelve years for this hour: the spirit Ariel at his command, the brother who betrayed him within reach, his daughter Miranda about to meet her first young man. And then, at the height of his power, he gives it all up. He breaks his staff, drowns his book, and forgives. The isle, Caliban tells us, is full of noises, sounds and sweet airs that give delight and hurt not, and the whole play shimmers with that strange music. Hear Prospero say we are such stuff as dreams are made on, and our little life is rounded with a sleep, and you are hearing [Shakespeare](/authors/william-shakespeare) himself lay down his art. No farewell in the language is gentler, or more complete.

title: Bleak House
author: Charles Dickens
extract: London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall. Implacable November weather.
blurb: Fog everywhere: fog up the river, fog down the river, and at its densest heart the High Court of Chancery, where the suit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce has dragged on so long that no living soul can say what it was first about. This is [Dickens](/authors/charles-dickens) at his angriest and his grandest, the book where the antagonist is not a person but a process: a court that swallows fortunes and lifetimes at its own glacial pace, patient, impartial, and bottomless. Around that pit he assembles a whole nation. A great lady at Chesney Wold keeps a secret that could ruin her; a boy named Jo who sweeps a crossing and, knowing nothing and taught nothing, carries disease between the classes that swear they never touch. Two voices share the telling, one rising above the machine to watch it whole, the other Esther Summerson, who can measure the worth of everyone in England except herself. You come to it for the fog, and you leave unable to get it back out of your lungs.

title: The Adventures of Augie March
author: Saul Bellow
extract: I am an American, Chicago born - Chicago, that somber city - and go at things as I have taught myself, free-style
blurb: Everyone in Augie March's Chicago has plans for him: the imperious Grandma Lausch, ruling the household of his nearly blind mother; the crippled, brilliant Einhorn, who runs the ward's loans and numbers from a wheelchair; Thea, who drives him to Mexico to hunt iguanas with a trained eagle. [Saul Bellow](/authors/saul-bellow) called them "reality instructors," and the book is the long, joyous record of how each one recruits Augie and how each one loses him. What makes _The Adventures of Augie March_ feel like a window thrown open is the voice: a high-low American speech that vaults from Heraclitus to street-corner patter inside one sentence, going at things, as Augie says, free-style. Bellow had written two careful, buttoned novels before this; here he let the language run, and American fiction was never quite so polite again. Augie never settles, never lets himself be completed, and the book never asks him to. Refusal, it turns out, is the freedom this whole rushing book is in love with.

title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens
extract: My father's family name being Pirrip, and my Christian name Philip, my infant tongue could make of both names nothing longer or more explicit than Pip.
blurb: In a shuttered room where every clock stopped at twenty to nine, a jilted bride sits in her yellowing wedding dress beside a cake gone gray with cobwebs, and a blacksmith's boy is brought in to play for her amusement and to fall hopelessly in love with the girl she is raising to break men's hearts. That boy, Pip, comes into a secret fortune and goes to London to become a gentleman, certain he knows who his benefactor is. He is wrong, and the error costs him nearly everything that ever loved him. What _Great Expectations_ does that no Victorian novel quite matches is to let a man narrate his own snobbery from the inside: the older Pip tells the whole story in retrospect, so every page of his rise carries the aftertaste of his shame at Joe, the gentle blacksmith who loved him without wanting a thing in return. The cruelty of the book is that the hindsight repairs nothing. Pip sees exactly how he failed the man who raised him, and the seeing only sharpens the grief.

title: Nightwood
author: Djuna Barnes
extract: Life is not to be told, call it as loud as you like, it will not tell itself.
blurb: Nora Flood comes to Doctor Matthew O'Connor in the small hours and begs him to tell her everything he knows about the night, and the old fraud, an unlicensed gynaecologist in a wig and a soiled nightgown, talks until the light comes. He is talking her through grief. She has lost Robin Vote, the somnambule who drifts through these pages like a beast still half learning to be human, adored by everyone and held by no one. [Djuna Barnes](/authors/djuna-barnes) wrote one woman's obsession with another in a baroque, incantatory splendour T. S. Eliot set beside Elizabethan tragedy, prose so dense with image you stop and read a sentence twice for the dark shine of it. This is what it is to love something that cannot love you back and will not be kept, told in a register nearer prophecy than confession. It ends where such love goes, somewhere below speech and below the human, and Barnes lets you feel the descent coming long before it arrives.

title: Blood Meridian
author: Cormac McCarthy
extract: War is the ultimate game because war is at last a forcing of the unity of existence. War is god.
blurb: Riders cross a desert lit like the floor of hell, the sun coming up red over the mountains, and [McCarthy](/authors/cormac-mccarthy)'s prose tolls after them in long Old Testament cadences that make you stop and read the line twice. These are the Glanton gang, scalp-hunters turned loose on the Texas-Mexico borderlands of the 1840s, and at their center rides Judge Holden: hairless, enormous, impossibly learned, the most frightening figure in American fiction, who holds that war is the eternal condition of man, that war is god. The novel refuses every consolation the western ever promised. No justice waits out in the dust, only the violence and the going on, set down in sentences so beautiful they feel like a kind of blasphemy. What stays with you is not the slaughter but the judge's argument, made in that vast and unhurried voice, that the world has always run on blood and that he is merely its high priest. Close the book and the desert is still there, the dance still turning, and you cannot quite say he was wrong.

title: The Library of Babel
author: Jorge Luis Borges
extract: The universe (which others call the Library) is composed of an indefinite and perhaps infinite number of hexagonal galleries
blurb: Picture a library with no walls and no end: identical six-sided rooms repeating in every direction, each shelf holding books of exactly four hundred and ten pages, each page a lattice of the same twenty-five symbols. [Borges](/authors/jorge-luis-borges) asks one annihilating question. If the shelves hold every possible arrangement of those symbols, then somewhere on them sits every book that could ever be written: the true history of your death, the faithful catalogue of the whole Library, and a hundred thousand near-perfect lies that differ from the truth by a single comma. The men who live there once wept with joy at this, then went mad hunting for the one page that would justify their lives. What makes _The Library of Babel_ unbearable and gorgeous is how it turns a mathematician's daydream into a portrait of us, small creatures adrift in a total order we cannot read. An old librarian, going blind a few galleries from where he was born, sets down one last conjecture, and for a held breath the dread of the place turns into something close to grace.

title: Mrs Dalloway
author: Virginia Woolf
extract: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
blurb: Mrs Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself, and with that sentence the whole of London opens like a flung-back window: a June morning after the war, Big Ben booming the hours into the air, a single ordinary day stretched wide enough to hold an entire life. Clarissa is giving a party tonight. But the prose refuses to stay with her, slipping from mind to mind across the city, into the thoughts of an old lover, a passing stranger, and Septimus Warren Smith, a shell-shocked young veteran who hears the dead singing in Regent's Park and can no longer bear the weight of being alive. [Woolf](/authors/virginia-woolf) finds the deepest things in the smallest gestures, the way a whole life can turn on a kiss remembered for thirty years. When word of a death reaches the lit, crowded party, you understand what the shimmering day has been building toward, and why ordinary happiness can suddenly feel like grace.

title: Ulysses
author: James Joyce
extract: yes I said yes I will Yes.
blurb: Everything happens on one ordinary Thursday in Dublin: a man eats a kidney for breakfast, attends a funeral, drifts through pubs and a newspaper office and a maternity hospital, and walks home well after midnight. [Joyce](/authors/james-joyce) poured the whole of a human mind into the passing hours, every flicker of memory and appetite and grief caught as it happens, until the inside of a head becomes the largest place there is. The book changes voice with every chapter, ventriloquizing newspaper headlines, a religious catechism, the entire history of English prose itself, daring you to keep up and rewarding you when you do. And it ends inside Molly Bloom, half-asleep beside her husband, her thoughts running on without a single full stop toward the most famous yes in all of literature. Few books have loved one human life this completely. Give it the patience it asks for, and a single Dublin day opens into the whole of being alive.

title: The Tartar Steppe
author: Dino Buzzati
day: World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought
extract: Perhaps this was the good fortune that other men vainly sought throughout the whole world.
blurb: To the north of the Bastiani Fortress lies only the steppe, a pale emptiness running to a horizon where, every soldier believes, the Tartars will one day appear. Giovanni Drogo arrives at this last outpost certain his posting is temporary, certain real life is waiting somewhere else. Then he begins to watch that horizon. A year passes, then several, then decades, each swallowed by the same conviction that the great event, the battle that will redeem every idle hour, is finally drawing near. [Buzzati](/authors/dino-buzzati)'s cruelty is also his tenderness: Drogo is never lazy and never a coward, only faithful to a future that recedes one season at a time. You watch an entire life spent in readiness for a moment that may never arrive, and somewhere in the waiting you catch your own reflection, the meaning always just past the edge of the plain, the years going by while you keep your post and tell yourself the time is nearly here.

title: Fathers and Sons
author: Ivan Turgenev
extract: A nihilist is a man who does not bow down before any authority, who does not take any principle on faith.
blurb: Bow to no authority, take no principle on faith, accept nothing you cannot weigh or dissect: that is the creed Yevgeny Bazarov carries into his friend's family estate, frog specimens in hand, certain that love and art and aristocratic honour are so much sentimental rot. [Turgenev](/authors/ivan-turgenev) gave this young man's faith its name, nihilism, and built him so completely that radicals and conservatives alike read the book and felt betrayed. The wonder of it is the tenderness. Turgenev loves Bazarov even as he dismantles him, and the instrument of the dismantling is Anna Odintsova, a widow whose unhurried composure strips the materialist of his own and leaves him in love against every conviction he owns, appalled by what he feels. Here is the recognition that aches: the certainty of the young, and the moment it cracks. Read it for the man undone by the single thing he swore was an illusion, the feeling he could not lay open on a table.

title: Beloved
author: Toni Morrison
extract: 124 was spiteful. Full of a baby's venom.
blurb: A house on the edge of Cincinnati shakes with the rage of a dead infant. "124 was spiteful," the novel begins, and the venom belongs to a baby whose mother once cut her throat rather than let a slavecatcher carry her back into bondage. When the ghost returns in the flesh, a glutted, devouring young woman who calls herself Beloved, Sethe gives herself over to the daughter she killed, starving to feed a love that has no bottom. [Toni Morrison](/authors/toni-morrison) wrote the unspeakable arithmetic of slavery from the inside: what it costs a mother to decide her child is better dead than owned, and what a life built on that choice does to the one who made it. The prose moves like grief itself, circling the thing it cannot say until it must. Few novels have looked so steadily at the worst love is capable of, or insisted so fiercely that the people who survived deserve to be remembered by name.

title: Nausea
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
extract: I exist. It is soft, so soft, so slow. And light: it seems as though it suspends in the air.
blurb: He stoops to pick up a pebble at the edge of the sea, means to skip it across the water, and finds he cannot: the thing in his hand has turned obscene, too solid, too there. So opens the diary of Antoine Roquentin, a historian washed up in a grey French port, watching the ordinary furniture of the world shed its names one by one, until a chestnut root in the public garden rears up before him as pure, naked existence, soft and black and monstrous, meaning absolutely nothing. This is the queasy vertigo [Sartre](/authors/jean-paul-sartre) named nausea: the discovery that nothing had to be, that you yourself are superfluous, that the tidy story by which a life seems to add up is paint brushed over a void. It should be unbearable, and very nearly is. Yet the book keeps one small light burning, a worn record turning in a café, a melody so clean it seems to exist as nothing around it does. You will not look at a chestnut tree, or your own hand, the same way again.

title: The Bhagavad Gita
author: Vyasa
extract: Let right deeds be Thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them.
blurb: Two armies stand drawn up for slaughter, conch shells ringing, and a warrior asks his charioteer to halt the horses in the empty ground between them. There Arjuna looks at the enemy and recognises his grandfather, his teachers, his cousins, and he cannot lift his bow. What follows is not a battle but a conversation: the charioteer is Krishna, god walking the earth as a friend, who refuses to let Arjuna's grief off easily. Across seven hundred Sanskrit verses he turns one man's failure of nerve into the largest questions there are: what dies when the body falls, how to act in a world you did not make, why work done without hunger for its reward is the only freedom. Then, asked for proof, Krishna grants Arjuna divine sight, and the soldier sees every world and every age blazing inside the god's countless mouths. The wonder of the _Bhagavad Gita_ is that it holds the cosmos and a single trembling man in one breath, and tells you, without raising its voice, that you are standing on Arjuna's field already.

title: All Quiet on the Western Front
author: Erich Maria Remarque
extract: This book is to be neither an accusation nor a confession, and least of all an adventure.
blurb: A pair of good leather boots passes from one dying boy to the next, each new owner inheriting them the moment the last is buried, a small grim economy that outlasts every man who laces them. This is the world [Remarque](/authors/erich-maria-remarque) hands you, the Western Front seen not by a general but by Paul Bäumer, a German schoolboy of nineteen who marched off because a teacher swore it was glorious, and who spends his short life learning what the teacher never had to. What sets this book apart from every other war story is its refusal to console. Paul lies trapped in a shell crater beside a French soldier he has just stabbed, finds in the dead man's pocket that he was a printer named Gérard Duval with a wife and child, and pleads forgiveness from a corpse. The enemy was a boy too. Remarque tells it in prose so flat and clear it leaves nowhere to look away, and the close is the cruelest stroke of all: the title is the lie the dispatches send home.

title: Requiem
author: Anna Akhmatova
extract: Can you describe this? And I said: I can.
blurb: Outside a Leningrad prison, a woman has stood in the same line for seventeen months, holding a parcel for a son who may already be dead, when the woman beside her, lips blue with cold, whispers, "Can you describe this?" and [Akhmatova](/authors/anna-akhmatova) answers, "I can." Out of that promise comes _Requiem_, the cycle she could not write down because possessing it on paper would have meant her own arrest, and so she gave it line by line to a few trusted friends to carry in memory while the paper burned. It is the great poem of the Stalinist terror, told not from the cells but from the women left at the gate, and it will not keep the grief to itself: this is not one mother's anguish but a whole country's, queuing in the snow. Read it and you stand in that line too, learning what it costs to remember out loud when remembering is forbidden.

title: Miss Julie
author: August Strindberg
extract: I have climbed to the top of a column and sit there without being able to tell how to get down again.
blurb: The count is away, the midsummer bonfire is burning in the yard, and his daughter has come down to the kitchen to dance with the servants. Julie tells the valet Jean a recurring dream: she has climbed to the top of a high column and cannot get down again, only longing to fall. Jean dreams the reverse, of lying beneath a tall tree he aches to climb. Two dreams, one falling and one rising, and [Strindberg](/authors/august-strindberg) sets them loose in a single room over one unbroken night to grind against each other. He prefaced the play insisting his people were not types but living contradictions, half-noble and half-brutal by turns, and Julie and Jean prove him right at every line: she is never only the count's daughter, he is never only the boot-black. That is what makes the warm kitchen so dangerous. When the class line they cross snaps back into place, it falls on the one who had the farther height to lose, and the count's bell, ringing through the wall, settles the rest.

title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
extract: Water, water, every where, Nor any drop to drink.
blurb: For no reason he can ever name, a sailor lifts his crossbow and kills the white bird that had followed the ship through the Antarctic fog, and everything after is the price. The wind dies, the ship hangs as idle as a painted ship upon a painted ocean, water on every side and not a drop to drink. [Coleridge](/authors/samuel-taylor-coleridge) wrote _The Rime of the Ancient Mariner_ in the diction of an old medieval ballad, and it still moves like a fever you cannot wake from. The crew hang the albatross around his neck; then two hundred of them die and leave him alone with the corpses under a staring moon. What finally breaks the curse is not prayer or penance but an involuntary jolt of wonder, the moment he watches the water snakes coil and flash and blesses them without meaning to. And even then the tale is never done: doomed to wander and retell it, he stops a stranger on the way to a wedding, holds him with a glittering eye, and you, reading, cannot leave.

title: Berlin Alexanderplatz
author: Alfred Döblin
extract: He stood outside the gates of Tegel Penitentiary, a free man.
blurb: Tram numbers, weather bulletins, the day's cattle prices from the slaughterhouse, a hymn, a headline about a killing three streets over: all of it pours into the prose without warning, because this is what Berlin actually sounded like in the late 1920s, and [Alfred Döblin](/authors/alfred-doblin) refused to turn the volume down. Through that din walks Franz Biberkopf, newly out of Tegel prison and sworn to himself that this time he will stay decent. The city has other plans. It pulls him back among thieves, takes an arm, takes the woman he loves and cannot protect, and grinds his small vow so fine that Death itself steps forward to speak with him. What makes the book unforgettable is that Döblin found a form not for the city but as the city: the same relentless material that batters Franz batters the reader on every page. You finish it knowing exactly how it feels to be one man against a place that does not pause for you.

title: Under the Volcano
author: Malcolm Lowry
extract: No se puede vivir sin amar. (One cannot live without loving.)
blurb: Mezcal in the morning, then more mezcal, and a mind so steeped it reads doom in everything: a torn travel poster, the two volcanoes standing over the town like sentries at the gate of the underworld. Geoffrey Firmin, a disgraced British Consul, drinks his way through a single Day of the Dead in Mexico while his estranged wife Yvonne, just returned, and his half-brother Hugh try to reach the man still alive somewhere inside the ruin. What makes the book unbearable is its lucidity. Firmin is never numb; he understands with awful precision the love being held out to him, and exactly why he cannot close his hand around it. [Lowry](/authors/malcolm-lowry)'s prose comes in great hallucinatory swells, Spanish and English and grief all braided together, and a ravine waits at the edge of town through every chapter. By the end you have watched a man read every omen gathering to kill him and choose, hour by lucid hour, not to be saved.

title: The Man Without Qualities
author: Robert Musil
extract: If there is a sense of reality, there must also be a sense of possibility.
blurb: Vienna, 1913. A committee of the great and the good gathers to plan a jubilee for 1918, a festival of Austrian spirit meant to dazzle the whole of Europe; none of them can know the empire has barely two years left to exist. Into this hum of self-congratulation walks Ulrich, a gifted mathematician who has resolved to take a year's holiday from life itself, having earned every distinction a man could want and found that not one of them touches him. He is the man without qualities, not because he is empty but because he is too full: he holds what [Musil](/authors/robert-musil) calls the sense of possibility so completely that to settle on a single life would feel like quietly murdering all the others. The book thinks as it moves, breaking into essays mid-scene, endlessly deferring the moment when something must at last be decided. Musil gave it twenty years and died in Swiss exile with the final pages unwritten. A novel about a man who cannot commit could close no other way.

title: Sonnets from the Portuguese
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
extract: How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.
blurb: Count the ways. That instruction, from the most famous love poem in English, is usually mistaken for rapture, but read the whole sequence and you find something stranger and more moving: a woman counting because she cannot quite believe the sum. [Elizabeth Barrett Browning](/authors/elizabeth-barrett-browning) wrote these forty-four sonnets in a darkened Wimpole Street room during her courtship with Robert, an invalid who had long since folded away any expectation of being loved, and then was. She published them disguised as translations from the Portuguese, unable to claim such nakedness as her own. The sonnet had spent three centuries as a man's instrument, aimed at a silent, distant beloved; here it turns inward, and its subject is not longing but the slow, frightened work of trusting that the love will hold. Sonnet by sonnet she tests her disbelief against his constancy. By the forty-third she is not rhapsodising. She is counting, because she needs the total to come out true.

title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad
extract: The horror! The horror!
blurb: Dusk gathers on the Thames, and as the great waterway to the ends of the earth goes still, a man named Marlow says the strangest thing: this too has been one of the dark places of the earth. Then he tells how he piloted a battered steamboat up the Congo to fetch a legendary ivory agent named Kurtz, and how every mile of river turned the journey inward. [Conrad](/authors/joseph-conrad) writes the approach as a slow drowning of certainty. The prose grows foggy and hypnotic, the sentences losing their footing as Marlow advances, until what waits upriver is not a man but a hollow where one used to stand. Kurtz has crossed the line civilisation swore it would never cross, and let himself be worshipped as a god to do it. The book will not let you watch from a safe distance; it implicates the calm London evening, and you in it. So when his last words come, the horror, the horror, hear them not as a verdict on the jungle but as one on us.

title: Journey to the End of the Night
author: Louis-Ferdinand Céline
extract: Travel is useful, it exercises the imagination.
blurb: Ferdinand Bardamu signs up for the war on a whim, chasing a passing band down a Paris boulevard, and by nightfall he is loose in a France gone mad with slaughter, having learned the one thing he will carry everywhere after: that he is a coward, and that cowardice may be the only sane answer to a world bent on killing him. From the trenches he flees, to a fever-rotted African colony, to the clanging assembly lines of Ford's Detroit, to a tubercular Paris slum where he hangs out a doctor's shingle among people too poor to be saved. [Céline](/authors/louis-ferdinand-celine) wrote it in a French nobody had dared set on the page, the gutter slang and broken rhythms and trailing ellipses of real speech, and made every polished sentence before him sound embalmed. This is the great novel of looking straight at the worst of us and refusing to flinch, of seeing that we are all traveling the same road into the same dark. Few books are this funny about despair, or this tender toward the ruined.

title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
author: Leo Tolstoy
extract: The previous history of Ivan Ilyitch was the simplest, the most ordinary, and the most awful.
blurb: Open the novella and Ivan Ilyich is already dead. His colleagues, reading the notice between cases, feel first the small private arithmetic of whose promotion now follows, then the relief that it is him and not them. This is the world [Tolstoy](/authors/leo-tolstoy) lays bare: a respectable judge who furnished his life as carefully as his drawing room, every choice correct, tasteful, like everyone else's. Then a bruise in his side begins to ache, the ache will not stop, and it teaches him the one thing he arranged his whole existence never to learn. What torments him is not the pain but the lie kept up around his bed, the cheerful pretense that he is only ill and will surely recover. Only Gerasim, the peasant who holds his legs through the night, tells the truth by refusing to pretend. The most ordinary life, Tolstoy shows, can be the most terrible, and the question that breaks open in the dark, whether he lived as he ought to have, is one you will not put down once you have heard it asked.

title: A Fine Balance
author: Rohinton Mistry
extract: The human face has limited space. If you fill it with laughter there will be no room for crying.
blurb: Four strangers crowd into one small Bombay flat during Indira Gandhi's Emergency: a Parsi widow guarding her hard-won independence, a student down from the mountains, and two tailors, an uncle and his nephew, who fled a village where their caste was a death sentence. They share one stove and bicker like relatives, and slowly, without ever deciding to, become a family. [Rohinton Mistry](/authors/rohinton-mistry) sets this fragile warmth against a state machinery that clears slums with bulldozers, herds men into sterilization camps, and treats the poor as refuse to be swept from the road. What makes the novel unbearable is how completely you come to love these four before the world takes pieces of them, one by one, with a patience that feels almost personal. And still there is laughter at that table, a shared meal at the end of a brutal day. A proofreader tells Maneck you have to hold a fine balance between hope and despair. The book asks whether anyone can hold it when despair owns every advantage, and it refuses to lie to you about the answer.

title: Song of Myself
author: Walt Whitman
extract: Do I contradict myself? Very well then I contradict myself, (I am large, I contain multitudes.)
blurb: "I celebrate myself, and sing myself": the line should land as arrogance and somehow arrives as an embrace. _Song of Myself_, the poem that opens _Leaves of Grass_, turns that first gesture into a promise to the reader, for whatever the speaker assumes, you shall assume, and the wall between two strangers goes thin as paper. Across fifty-two sections of free verse, [Whitman](/authors/walt-whitman) pulls the whole republic into one long breathing line, the carpenter and the prostitute, the runaway slave and the president, no one set above another, because verse without meter refuses to rank a person. A child asks him what the grass is and he answers a dozen ways, each truer than the last, the common green of every dooryard pressed living into your hand. To read it is to feel a single self widen until it has room for everyone inside it, the boast at the poem's close arriving as nothing but the truth: you are large, you contain multitudes.

title: Les Enfants Terribles
author: Jean Cocteau
extract: A blow struck him full in the chest. A dark blow. A blow like a marble fist. A blow like a statue's fist.
blurb: A snowball thrown by Dargelos, the boy every classmate secretly worships, catches Paul full in the chest, and he goes down as though struck by something far heavier than snow. He is carried home to the room he shares with his sister Elisabeth, and stays there, half convalescent, half enthroned, while the two of them build a kingdom from one shared bed, a hoard of junk turned treasure, and a ritual they call the Game: a trance of insults neither can stop until the other cries mercy. [Cocteau](/authors/jean-cocteau) writes their world with the logic of a fairy tale and the nerve endings of adolescence, so that a photograph over the bed, or a phial of poison Paul has kept since childhood, carries the weight of scripture. Friends, lovers, even a sudden fortune wander in from outside and are absorbed or cast out by rules only brother and sister can read. It is a story about how completely two people can seal a world off from the world, gorgeous and airless at once, and the door that closes from the inside.

title: As I Lay Dying
author: William Faulkner
extract: My mother is a fish.
blurb: My mother is a fish, the youngest boy decides, having no other shape to hold his loss in. Addie Bundren has died, and her family loads the pine coffin her eldest son built beneath her window onto a wagon, then hauls it across forty miles of flooded river and scorched road to bury her in Jefferson, buzzards wheeling above the July heat. [Faulkner](/authors/william-faulkner) splinters the telling among fifteen voices, fifty-nine short chapters, each Bundren and bystander speaking in turn, so you assemble the grief and the family's separate, secret hungers yourself. Addie gets a single chapter too, spoken from the far side of death, and it overturns everything you believed about why these people are on the road. The wonder is how he makes a mind audible: the broken syntax of a frightened child, a son's pride as he sets his own shattered leg, a father who longs for new teeth more than he mourns his wife. Grief has rarely been this funny, or this true.

title: The Sun Also Rises
author: Ernest Hemingway
extract: Isn't it pretty to think so?
blurb: Count the drinks. The Pernod, the Fundador, the cold Spanish wine drunk from a leather bag in the sun, the bottles emptied to keep the talking going and the wanting down. Jake Barnes loves Lady Brett Ashley and cannot have her: a wound from the war has seen to that, and the whole novel turns on the ache of a desire that can never be answered. So they drift, this circle of expatriates, from the cafés of Paris to the bullring at Pamplona, where [Hemingway](/authors/ernest-hemingway) writes the running of the bulls and the grace of a young matador with a clean, unhurried attention that feels like prayer. The sentences are short and plain and somehow hold everything the characters will not say. Few books have made so much sorrow out of so little. By the last line you will understand exactly how it feels to want a thing you know you cannot keep, and to say so lightly anyway.

title: Ozymandias
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
extract: Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!
blurb: Somewhere in a desert, two enormous stone legs stand with nothing above them, and half-sunk in the sand nearby lies a shattered face still wearing a sneer of cold command. The pedestal keeps its inscription perfectly: "My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings; Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!" The command survives; the works do not. The kingdom is gone, the boundless and bare sands stretch away in every direction, and the one thing the centuries chose to spare is the boast that everything around it has turned to mockery. [Shelley](/authors/percy-bysshe-shelley) fits the whole death of empire into fourteen lines, and folds inside them a quieter marvel: the unnamed sculptor who read a tyrant's contempt so well that his hand outlived the man, the throne, and the civilization that built it. Every power that has called itself eternal has a desert like this one waiting. Here is the poem that knows the way there.

title: The Overcoat
author: Nikolai Gogol
extract: In the department of - but it is better not to mention the department.
blurb: Akaky Akakievich loves the alphabet. A copying clerk in a St. Petersburg department too dull to name, he has no ambition beyond a clean transcription, certain letters his favourites, and the work brings him a private rapture that needs nothing else. Then a tailor tells him his coat is past mending, and the saving begins: months without supper, without candlelight, the future narrowed to one garment he can almost feel on his shoulders. When the coat finally comes it is the happiest day of his life, and [Gogol](/authors/nikolai-gogol)'s narrator, who has been mocking this little man for pages, suddenly cannot keep it up. There is a moment when a young clerk's joke falters and he hears, underneath it, I am your brother. That is the whole revolution of the story. The coat is stolen, the city that never noticed Akaky shrugs, and out of his death something walks back through the snow to collect what it is owed. Russian literature's tenderness for the overlooked begins here, improbably, in laughter.

title: Housekeeping
author: Marilynne Robinson
extract: My name is Ruth. I grew up with my younger sister, Lucille, under the care of my grandmother, Mrs. Sylvia Foster.
blurb: A glacial lake sits at the heart of Fingerbone, and it has already taken two of this family: the grandfather, when his train slid off the bridge one night and vanished without a ripple by morning, and years later the mother, who borrowed a car and drove it calmly into the same black water. Ruth and her sister Lucille are passed between relatives until their aunt Sylvie arrives to keep house, though Sylvie keeps it the way water keeps a shape. She sleeps in her coat, eats in the dark, lets the leaves drift in through doors left open, and saves the rinsed tin cans she will never use. [Marilynne Robinson](/authors/marilynne-robinson)'s first novel understands that ordinary housekeeping is a quiet refusal to grieve, a daily insistence that absence is manageable, and that Sylvie's failure at it is a deeper fidelity to the dead. The prose runs long and luminous, all cold light and rising water, until you feel the pull of the lake yourself, and the terrible tenderness of a girl who would rather drift than forget.

title: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter
author: Carson McCullers
extract: In the town there were two mutes, and they were always together.
blurb: They come to him one at a time, and they tell him everything. A girl who hears whole symphonies no one else can hear, a Black doctor worn thin by a lifetime of injustice, a half-drunk agitator nobody else will listen to, the watchful man behind the café counter: each finds a way to John Singer, a deaf-mute in a small Georgia mill town, and pours out a life. They are certain he understands them, because he never tells them otherwise. [Carson McCullers](/authors/carson-mccullers) was twenty-three when she caught the cruellest thing about loneliness, that a silence we fill with our own longing can feel more like being heard than any answer ever could. And Singer, who holds the whole town's confidence, is himself in love with another mute shut away in a state asylum, a man who barely knows he is alive. The novel moves at the pace of a long Southern summer, gathering its quiet griefs without hurry. By the last page you see it plainly: everyone here is talking, tenderly, into a face that cannot answer back.

title: Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair
author: Pablo Neruda
extract: Tonight I can write the saddest lines.
blurb: Tonight I can write the saddest lines, a boy of nineteen tells himself, and a century of readers have whispered the same words back into their own dark rooms. Here [Pablo Neruda](/authors/pablo-neruda) makes a woman out of landscape, a body of white hills and white thighs that looks, he writes, like a world lying in surrender, and turns the oldest ache there is into something that feels like it happened to you last week. The poems move from the heat of having someone to the cold of the bed where she used to lie, and the closing Song of Despair goes down like a ship sinking with all its cargo of memory. He never pretends the grief is noble. He just says it, plainly: I no longer love her, that's certain, but maybe I love her. To read this is to be nineteen and wrecked by someone all over again.

title: The Myth of Sisyphus
author: Albert Camus
extract: One must imagine Sisyphus happy.
blurb: The boulder reaches the summit, balances a moment, and rolls back down the far slope. Sisyphus turns and walks after it, and it is in that walk down, [Camus](/authors/albert-camus) tells us, that the man is most alive, the hour of consciousness in which he sees his whole fate and is not crushed by it. The essay opens with a sentence that has frightened readers for generations, that the only truly serious philosophical question is suicide, and from there it refuses every comfort that would let us look away. Camus calls this collision the absurd: a mind that aches for meaning set against a universe that will not answer. To leap toward God, or reason, or hope, he names philosophical suicide, an escape from the confrontation rather than a passage through it. Written in occupied Paris, where despair held every card, the book chooses revolt, not the vanishing of the rock but the refusal to be beaten by it. One must imagine Sisyphus happy, it ends, and walking down the mountain beside him, you believe it.

title: Reflections on the Revolution in France
author: Edmund Burke
extract: Half a dozen grasshoppers under a fern make the field ring with their importunate chink.
blurb: [Burke](/authors/edmund-burke) remembers Marie Antoinette glittering at Versailles and grieves that ten thousand swords did not leap from their scabbards to defend her; the age of chivalry is gone, he mourns, and a colder age of calculators has come in its place. _Reflections on the Revolution in France_ is the great cry against the faith that reason alone can raze a civilization and build a better one from the bare ground. Burke had cheered the American colonists and spent years prosecuting the plunder of India, so his fury at Paris stunned the friends who took him for a friend of liberty. What he defended was the inherited wisdom no philosopher can recover from first principles, a partnership, he calls it, between the living, the dead, and those yet to be born. He wrote it before the guillotine had taken a single head, naming the Terror and the soldier-despot who would follow, and watched the future arrive exactly as he had said. You can resist every line and still feel the chill of a man who could see in the dark.

author: Roberto Bolaño
extract: Reading is like thinking, like praying, like talking to a friend, like expressing your ideas, like listening to other people's ideas.
blurb: In a Mexican border city the bodies of women keep turning up, in vacant lots, in the desert, behind a school, and the files pile up unsolved. [Roberto Bolaño](/authors/roberto-bolano)'s enormous posthumous novel circles that fact in five movements and never lets you forget it is there. Four European scholars chase a vanished German novelist across continents; a philosophy professor comes apart in the desert heat; an American reporter flies in to cover a boxing match and feels a wrongness he cannot name. Then arrives the part about the crimes, nearly three hundred pages in the flat, exhausted language of a coroner's report, one murdered woman after another, until the catalogue becomes the most damning thing fiction has dared to attempt. Bolaño wrote it knowing he was dying, and the book refuses every consolation a smaller one would reach for. It cannot redeem what it shows you. It only asks, with terrible patience, that you do not look away.

title: Paradise Lost
author: John Milton
extract: Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven.
blurb: Hurled flaming out of Heaven, Satan lifts his head from a lake of fire and, surveying the ruin of everything he was, decides he would rather rule this pit than kneel in paradise. [Milton](/authors/john-milton) gives the Devil the grandest voice in the language, and the terrible thrill of the poem is how much you feel his defiance before you learn to distrust it. From that burning floor the poem opens outward to hold the whole cosmos at once: the war in Heaven, the void of Chaos, the making of the world, and two naked people in a garden who have been told not to eat one thing. It is written in blank verse that rolls like an organ, clause piling on clause until a single sentence carries the weight of a falling empire. Milton set out to justify the ways of God to men, and wrote instead the most magnificent account of loss we have: the morning two people walk out of Eden, hand in hand, into the world that is ours.

title: The Odyssey
author: Homer
day: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey Opens in Cinemas
extract: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy.
blurb: A goddess offers a man immortality on an island where nothing can ever harm him, and every evening he sits on the shore and weeps, staring out at the water toward a rocky little kingdom and a wife who has aged ten years without him. That refusal is the secret heart of _The Odyssey_: not whether Odysseus can outwit the Cyclops or sail past the Sirens, but whether an ordinary mortal life, brief and grief-prone, is worth more than never dying at all. [Homer](/authors/homer) gives us not the warrior at Troy but the strategist at the end of his patience, a man who survives by thinking faster than any god expects, who even walks into the land of the dead to ask the way home. When he reaches Ithaca at last he announces nothing. He bends a bow no one else can string and kills every man who has been eating his food and courting his wife. The cunning that took Troy and the cunning that takes back a house are the same cunning, and the poem knows it.

title: Persuasion
author: Jane Austen
extract: You pierce my soul. I am half agony, half hope.
blurb: Eight years ago Anne Elliot let herself be talked out of the only love she would ever feel, and she has been quietly paying for it ever since. She is twenty-seven now, her bloom faded, treated as furniture by a vain father and a colder sister, when Frederick Wentworth, the naval officer she once refused, comes back rich and admired and seemingly indifferent to her. _Persuasion_ is [Austen](/authors/jane-austen)'s last finished novel and her most autumnal, the one where the wit cools into something close to grief: its heroine is not too clever for her own good but too constant, and the book lives inside her steady, unregarded mind while everyone around her mistakes her for no one. Austen wrote it knowing she was ill, and the ache of a second spring, of bloom recovered late, runs all through it. When Wentworth finally sets down his pen and lets Anne read what he could never say aloud, the irony falls away completely, and so does the reader's composure.

title: The Emperor of Ice-Cream
author: Wallace Stevens
extract: Let be be finale of seem.
blurb: Call the roller of big cigars. The poem opens like an order shouted into a busy kitchen, and at once the room is loud with the living: a muscular man whipping concupiscent curds in cracked cups, boys hauling flowers in last month's newspaper, girls loitering in their everyday dresses. [Wallace Stevens](/authors/wallace-stevens) loved a word the way a child loves sugar, and he lets these consonants clatter and melt on the tongue. Then, in the cold back bedroom, a dead woman lies under a sheet she once embroidered with fantails, her horny feet protruding, in the poem's own unsparing phrase, to show how cold she is, and dumb. Set the riot of appetite against the silent corpse and ask which one rules. Stevens answers without blinking: against death there is no king and no god, only the body's hunger for sweetness while it can still taste. The only emperor is the emperor of ice-cream.

title: L'infinito
author: Giacomo Leopardi
extract: So my mind sinks in this immensity: and foundering is sweet in such a sea.
blurb: A young poet climbs a lonely hill outside a small provincial town, and a hedge blocks his view of the horizon. That is all that happens. From that one obstruction [Leopardi](/authors/giacomo-leopardi) builds the most astonishing fifteen lines in Italian, because the hedge hides the world and the mind is suddenly free to imagine what lies past it: interminable spaces, superhuman silences, a depthless calm so vast the heart nearly recoils in fear. Then the wind stirs the branches, and the sound of this living moment rings against that imagined eternity, until the seasons, dead and present, come flooding in. _L'infinito_ is not about a view. It is about the strange sweetness of being overwhelmed, the mind consenting to drown in something larger than itself. The poem carries you to the edge of thought and lets you go, and its final line has lived in the memory of Italian readers for two centuries: to founder, it says, is sweet in such a sea.

title: The Old Man and the Sea
author: Ernest Hemingway
extract: A man can be destroyed but not defeated.
blurb: Far out where no other boat will follow, an old Cuban fisherman feels a great fish take his bait in the dark, and for two days and nights he holds the line across his shoulders while the marlin tows his skiff toward the open Gulf. Santiago has gone eighty-four days without a catch, and he comes to love the fish even as he kills it, calling it brother, grieving that the same pride binds them both. [Hemingway](/authors/ernest-hemingway) pares every sentence to the bone, the prose so clean and unhurried it moves like the sea itself, and the old man's murmured talk to the bird, to the boy, to his own cramping hand carries a tenderness his hard life never let him say aloud. Then the sharks come for what he has earned, and you watch a triumph turn to wreckage while the man inside it stays unbroken. He brings home only a skeleton lashed to his skiff, and falls asleep dreaming of lions on the long beaches of his youth.

title: King Solomon's Mines
author: H. Rider Haggard
extract: On a dark night a single star is better than nothing.
blurb: A dying Portuguese, frozen in a mountain cave three centuries ago, tears a strip from his shirt and draws a map in his own blood: a desert, two peaks the shape of a woman's breasts, and beyond them the mines of Solomon. Allan Quatermain, an old elephant hunter who insists he is a coward and no hero, follows that dead man's map with two Englishmen hunting a lost brother, into unmapped country no traveller has crossed and returned. What waits is a hidden kingdom under a one-eyed tyrant, and Gagool, a witch so ancient she seems to have outlived her own death, guarding a treasure chamber that turns into a tomb. [Haggard](/authors/h-rider-haggard) wrote the book that taught adventure how to dream: the blank space on the map, the long trek into it, the great door of stone swinging shut. Every lost-world story since walks in Quatermain's dusty boots. Read it for the oldest, purest pleasure fiction offers, the pull of the horizon and the dread of what lies past it.

title: Moby-Dick
author: Herman Melville
extract: Call me Ishmael.
blurb: A man with one leg, who lost the other to a white whale, stands on the deck of a Nantucket whaler and nails a gold coin to the mast: it belongs to the first sailor who sights the beast that maimed him. From this [Herman Melville](/authors/herman-melville) builds something far larger than a sea chase. The Pequod carries men of every race and faith toward a creature that has stopped being an animal and become the face of everything indifferent and enormous that a person can hate: God, the ocean, the blank white nothing behind the world. The prose swells like Shakespeare let loose on the Atlantic, lurching from a chapter on the colour white into sermons, soliloquies, the dense beautiful tedium of how to butcher a whale. You feel the wave gathering long before it breaks. Few books reach so high and pull the whole sky down with them.

title: The Count of Monte Cristo
author: Alexandre Dumas
extract: All human wisdom is summed up in these two words,--'Wait and hope.'
blurb: Edmond Dantès has everything a young man could want: a ship to captain, a girl to marry, a future bright as the Marseille harbour at dawn. Then, at his own betrothal feast, four men who envy him put their names to a lie, and he vanishes into the Château d'If, the island fortress from which no prisoner returns. What he finds there, whispered through stone by a dying priest, is a fortune beyond counting and the name of every man who buried him alive. The rest is the most patient revenge ever written: a stranger of impossible wealth arriving in Paris years on, gracious, smiling, holding every thread in his gloved hand. [Dumas](/authors/alexandre-dumas) built it as pure thrill, and it thrills, but beneath runs a darker question, whether any ransom can buy back a stolen life, and where a wronged man stops being the hand of Providence and starts playing God. Wait and hope, the novel says at its close. By then you will know the cost of both.

title: Brave New World
author: Aldous Huxley
extract: But I don't want comfort. I want God, I want poetry, I want real danger, I want freedom, I want goodness. I want sin.
blurb: In a sunlit nursery, infants crawl toward bowls of roses and bright picture books, and then the floor shrieks with electricity until they learn to recoil from flowers and reading for life. This is happiness, engineered. [Huxley](/authors/aldous-huxley) imagines a civilization that has solved the human problem by deleting it: babies decanted from bottles into fixed castes, every want met, every grief dissolved on the tongue by a gram of soma, mothers and fathers and solitude and old age all scrubbed away. It is a paradise, which is exactly the horror. When a man raised on Shakespeare outside the system wanders in, he asks for the one thing it cannot grant him: the right to be unhappy, to grow old, to love something he might lose. No book has guessed more chillingly that the cage might be soft, scented, and gladly chosen, that we would not be tortured out of our freedom but comforted out of it.

title: The Seven Madmen
author: Roberto Arlt
extract: What's known as madness is simply what most people aren't accustomed to thinking.
blurb: Caught embezzling from the sugar company, Remo Erdosain waits in his employer's office to be denounced as a thief, and the last floor of his life gives way. A bill collector lost in the grey machinery of Buenos Aires, he falls instead into the orbit of the Astrologer, a charlatan-messiah plotting to topple society with a secret order bankrolled by a chain of brothels and held together by a manufactured religion. What makes the book unbearable and alive is not the conspiracy but the man beneath it: Erdosain in his "anguish zone," so humiliated, so hungry to matter, that any crime looks like a door out of nothing. [Roberto Arlt](/authors/roberto-arlt) wrote in a rough, unschooled Spanish that his polished contemporaries scorned, and that rawness is exactly the point, prose that sweats and stammers and burns. Few novels have caught so precisely the vertigo of a soul that would rather detonate the world than go on being no one.

title: The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas
author: Gertrude Stein
extract: Only three times in my life have I met a genius and each time a bell within me rang.
blurb: 'I was born in San Francisco, California,' the book begins, plainly, as if this really were one woman telling her own quiet life, though it is not. [Gertrude Stein](/authors/gertrude-stein) wrote every word of it in the voice of Alice B. Toklas, the woman she had shared a life with for decades, and it is the first book Stein ever let herself write in sentences a stranger could follow. Alice tells you early on that she has met exactly three geniuses: the philosopher Whitehead, Picasso, and Gertrude Stein, and says it without blinking, because of course it is Stein saying it about herself. Behind that joke, half of modern art passes through their rooms at rue de Fleurus, Picasso repainting a face from memory until it stops resembling the sitter and starts looking true. Only in the final lines does Stein confess the trick outright: she has written it as simply as Defoe wrote _Robinson Crusoe_, in someone else's mouth, because it was the only way she could finally say what she meant about the woman beside her.

title: Wolf Hall
author: Hilary Mantel
extract: "So now get up." Felled, dazed, silent, he has fallen; knocked full length on the cobbles of the yard.
blurb: "So now get up." Those are the first words the book gives Thomas Cromwell, not yet grown, half-conscious on the cobbles of his father's yard, blood in his mouth, a boot drawing back for one more kick. He gets up. He walks to Dover, crosses to the Continent, fights as a young mercenary, trades cloth in Antwerp, and comes home a lawyer, a fixer, and finally the most powerful commoner in England, the mind Henry VIII cannot do without. [Hilary Mantel](/authors/hilary-mantel) writes it all in the close, unbroken present tense, so that six centuries collapse and you are inside Cromwell's skull as he calculates, remembers, grieves, and watches everyone watching him. The wonder of _Wolf Hall_ is how completely it inhabits a man history flattened into a villain, restoring his ledgers, his dead children, his tenderness, his ruthlessness, in the same unhurried breath. It ends with Thomas More's severed head and a girl's name not yet spoken. Cromwell notes both, and does not look away.

title: Mahabharata
author: Vyasa
extract: What is found here may be found elsewhere. What is not found here will not be found elsewhere.
blurb: Two vast armies face each other across the plain of Kurukshetra, cousin against cousin, and the finest archer alive lets his bow slip from his hand: the men he has been brought here to kill are his uncles, his teachers, the boys he grew up beside. Into that paralysis his charioteer leans close and begins to speak, and the charioteer is God. The _Bhagavad Gita_ is only one current in the largest river of story ever told, a poem that swallows a dice game in which a king gambles away his kingdom, his brothers, and his wife; a thirteen-year exile; a war that ends with the earth emptied of its young men. It says of itself that whatever is found here may be found elsewhere, but what is not here exists nowhere, and after living inside it you believe the boast. It is the whole of human wanting, and the terrible bill that wanting comes to.

title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
author: Anonymous
extract: He who has seen everything, I will make known to the lands.
blurb: For seven days Gilgamesh would not bury his friend. He sat beside Enkidu's body, waiting for him to wake, and only when a worm fell from the dead man's face did the king of Uruk understand what death was. He had been two-thirds divine, terrifying, a tyrant who took the brides of his city on their wedding nights, until the gods shaped Enkidu from clay to be his match, and the two men fought and then loved each other like brothers. Now Gilgamesh runs. He crosses the desert in lion-skins, passes the scorpion-guardians of the mountains, rows across the waters of death to reach the one man who survived the flood and was granted life without end. He even finds the plant that restores youth, falls asleep beside a pool, and lets a serpent eat it. He comes home with nothing but the walls of his city. The oldest written story in the world was already about the only thing no power can buy: more time with the people we cannot keep.

title: If This Is a Man
author: Primo Levi
extract: Consider if this is a man who works in the mud, who does not know peace, who fights for a scrap of bread.
blurb: Consider whether this is a man, the opening poem demands: one who labors in the mud and fights for a crust of bread. [Primo Levi](/authors/primo-levi) wrote it after eleven months in the Auschwitz subcamp at Monowitz, a chemist's exact eye turned on the machinery built to unmake the human being. He watches a guard snatch an icicle from his thirsting mouth and answer his "why" with "Hier ist kein warum," here there is no why, and you understand in one stroke a whole world emptied of reason. What astonishes is the calm: no rage, no vengeance, only the patient witness of a scientist cataloguing how a person is reduced to a number, a hunger, a thing that competes for soup. And then, against all that, a half-remembered canto of Dante recited to a friend, proof that some unkillable scrap of the man survives. Read it for the cold, miraculous mercy of being told the exact truth.

title: Wide Sargasso Sea
author: Jean Rhys
extract: They say when trouble comes close ranks, and so the white people did. But we were not in their ranks.
blurb: "Our garden was large and beautiful as that garden in the Bible," Antoinette says of the estate where she was raised, "but it had gone wild." She is a white Creole girl on a Jamaica that has just freed the people her family once enslaved, hated by the Black islanders for what her name means and scorned by the English who come to buy what is left of it. [Jean Rhys](/authors/jean-rhys), born in Dominica, wrote _Wide Sargasso Sea_ to give a country, a childhood, and a sanity to the woman Charlotte Brontë left raving in an attic: the first Mrs Rochester, the madwoman of _Jane Eyre_. The Englishman Antoinette marries is never named here. He renames her Bertha, carries her across the ocean to a cold locked room, and calls the result madness. Rhys calls it a sentence, handed down by empire and by marriage, and her prose holds you in the wide warm sea between her island and his England, so lush and disorienting you feel the ground soften and give way.

title: Notes of a Native Son
author: James Baldwin
extract: On the 29th of July, in 1943, my father died. On the same day, a few hours later, his last child was born.
blurb: On the morning his father was buried, [Baldwin](/authors/james-baldwin) rode to the graveyard through streets carpeted with the smashed plate glass of the Harlem riot. His father had died the day the family's youngest child was born, and the funeral fell on Baldwin's nineteenth birthday, so that private mourning and a city on fire collided in one unbearable week. Out of that coincidence he builds his greatest essay: a portrait of a proud, paranoid, bitter preacher of a father, and the slow terror of discovering that the very bitterness that helped kill the man had taken root in the son. Watch him hurl a water glass at a New Jersey waitress who will not serve him, and feel the rage he says no Black American is without, a fever to be lived with or surrendered to. The prose moves with the cadence of the pulpit he was raised in. It closes by handing you two commandments you must somehow keep at once, and you carry them out of the book.

title: Nostromo
author: Joseph Conrad
extract: Any one can declaim about these things, but I pin my faith to material interests.
blurb: On the Golfo Plácido, a gulf so black a man cannot see his own hands, Nostromo rows a lighter heavy with silver into the dark to keep it from a revolution. He is the most trusted man in Sulaco, an Italian capataz whose entire fortune is what the docks believe of him: that he cannot be bought. [Conrad](/authors/joseph-conrad) invented a whole South American republic, Costaguana, its mountains and feuds and ruined idealists, only to set one silver mine at its heart and watch what the metal does to everyone who touches it. Charles Gould gives his soul to the lode until his wife Emilia loses the husband to the institution he becomes. And the silver, once buried, begins its slow work on the one incorruptible man, who can neither return it nor stop guarding it. Conrad tells it all out of order, the cost felt before the accounting, so you grasp too late what material interests truly take: not a man's honesty, but the self he most needed to believe in.

title: The Good Soldier
author: Ford Madox Ford
extract: This is the saddest story I have ever heard.
blurb: "This is the saddest story I have ever heard." So John Dowell begins, and the strangeness takes a moment to land: he was there for all of it, the sadness is largely his own, and he is the one person who still cannot see it. Across nine years of taking the waters at a German spa, two couples keep a flawless picture of Edwardian decency while Florence Dowell carries on an affair with Edward Ashburnham, the good soldier of the title, a man whose honour answers to every code the world can see and none that it cannot. Leonora, Edward's wife, has known the whole time. Dowell, telling it backward from the rubble of all four lives, will not quite let himself know even now. To read him is to feel his most soothing sentences as the ones burying the most, and to do the work he refuses, assembling from each calm digression a ruin that was always in plain sight. The saddest story is the one he cannot bear to finish hearing.

title: Song of Solomon
author: Toni Morrison
extract: You wanna fly, you got to give up the shit that weighs you down.
blurb: In a dusty Virginia town, children clasp hands and circle and sing a rhyme nobody can explain, a song about a man named Solomon who rose into the air and flew, and Milkman Dead, who came south chasing a rumor of gold, slowly understands that the nonsense is the only surviving record of his own great-grandfather. _Song of Solomon_ takes hold of the African American legend of the Flying Africans, the enslaved who, the story goes, simply rose from the fields and went home across the water, and asks the question the legend buries: Solomon flew to freedom and left twenty-one children earthbound behind him. [Morrison](/authors/toni-morrison) weighs names like gold here. Dead was a drunk soldier's slip of the pen in a Freedmen's ledger; Pilate carries hers in a brass box at her ear because her father, who could not read, copied the shape from the Bible. The book ends at the lip of a leap, where surrender to the air is freedom and abandonment in one motion, the old choice made again.

title: Slaughterhouse-Five
author: Kurt Vonnegut
extract: So it goes.
blurb: Beneath Dresden, in a cellar under the slaughterhouse numbered five, a young American prisoner waits out the night the sky catches fire and the city overhead burns to ash. Billy Pilgrim survives, and afterward comes unstuck in time, skidding without warning between his captivity, his daughter's wedding, his own death, and the planet Tralfamadore, whose aliens insist that all moments exist at once, so the dead are never gone, only elsewhere on the line. Each time death arrives, and it arrives on nearly every page, the book answers only "So it goes," three flat words that are not a shrug but the sound of a man who walked through the ashes and found no language equal to them. [Kurt Vonnegut](/authors/kurt-vonnegut) needed more than twenty years to write this, and what he made is less a war novel than a wound in the shape of one. Read it and you will never hear those three words the same way again.

title: Rebecca
author: Daphne du Maurier
extract: Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again.
blurb: An R curls across the flyleaf of a book, the notepaper, the sheets on the bed she died in: proof of a woman who is nowhere in this house and everywhere in it. The second Mrs de Winter arrives at Manderley without a name of her own, and spends the novel trying to become someone in a house built around the memory of a woman she never met. [Daphne du Maurier](/authors/daphne-du-maurier)'s cruelty is exact: the heroine's jealousy is not of a rival but of a ghost, a dead woman so vivid and so admired that being alive starts to feel like the lesser condition. Then the truth arrives, and it does not console. Maxim did not love Rebecca. He killed her, and everything the book has let the reader believe about their marriage collapses into that single fact. What lingers isn't the twist but the ache underneath it: how easily a person can be erased by someone else's legend, and how much of love is really just the fear of being unremembered.

title: The Master & Margarita
author: Mikhail Bulgakov
extract: Manuscripts don't burn.
blurb: A black cat the size of a man boards a Moscow tram and politely offers to pay his fare, and somehow this is among the gentler things the Devil and his retinue do to a city that has officially decided he cannot exist.
