[Mikhail Bulgakov](/authors/mikhail-bulgakov) wrote _The Master & Margarita_ in secret across the 1930s, burning one draft and rewriting it from memory, revising until the morning he died, certain no censor would ever let it pass. So the book became its own proof that in Stalin's Moscow, where a careless word could make a man disappear, the truth could still be set down. Two stories twine together. One is a capital turned to glorious chaos by Woland's magic; the other is ancient Jerusalem, where Pontius Pilate condemns an innocent he longs to save and learns that cowardice is the one sin that never lets him sleep. When the Master's burned novel is laid whole on the table again, the Devil only shrugs. Manuscripts don't burn.

title: Steppenwolf
author: Hermann Hesse
extract: For madmen only, and one price only--your mind.
blurb: Somewhere on a wall in a grey northern city a sign flickers into being: Magic Theatre, for madmen only, and the price is your mind. Harry Haller, a greying intellectual lodging in a tidy bourgeois house he both reveres and can't stop sneering at, has spent years certain he is two creatures sharing one skin: the man who weeps at Mozart and the wolf of the steppes who would tear the whole comfortable world to pieces. [Hesse](/authors/hermann-hesse) lets that diagnosis stand just long enough to take it away. Hermine, a dancer who refuses to treat his despair as sacred, teaches him to waltz, to laugh, to suspect his sharpest self is not his only one. The book's quiet, devastating claim is that no one is two natures; everyone is a thousand, and to call yourself a single type is to lock the rest of yourself in a cell you furnished. Read it the next time you have decided which animal you are.

title: Oblomov
author: Ivan Goncharov
extract: Mechanically and at random he traced some letters in the dust with his finger. There resulted the word Oblomovstchina.
blurb: The dressing gown is Persian, vast, worn soft from years of wear; the divan has long since taken the shape of its owner. For something close to a hundred and fifty pages, Ilya Ilyich Oblomov, a Russian gentleman of thirty-two with a steady income and an estate going quietly to ruin, tries to get out of bed and cannot. Visitors come and go, each busier and hollower than the last, while [Goncharov](/authors/ivan-goncharov) watches his hero fail to rise with a tenderness that slowly becomes the argument: this stillness is worth our whole attention. Oblomov even gave a word to the language, Oblomovism, for the sweet paralysis of a man who would rather dream his life than live it. Yet the book loves him far too much to leave it a diagnosis. When Olga nearly wakes him, and he nearly lives, you lean toward the page; when he sinks at last into the warm, fed, undemanding calm of a widow's house, the grief is real, because he understood exactly what he was trading away, and chose the divan anyway.

title: Hamlet
author: William Shakespeare
extract: To be, or not to be, that is the question.
blurb: Who's there? The play begins with a question flung into the freezing dark, a sentry on the battlements of Elsinore challenging a shape he cannot name, and the whole tragedy turns out to be that question asked over and over, of a ghost, of a murderer, of the self. The ghost gives a prince one task: avenge a father poisoned by the uncle who now wears his crown and shares his mother's bed. Hamlet believes it, knows what is required, and cannot move. He thinks instead, more nakedly and more beautifully than anyone in the language had thought aloud before, until thought itself becomes the thing that stays his hand. When he stands alone and weighs being against not being, he is not really asking about death; he is asking whether a mind this awake can ever simply act. The answer takes five acts and leaves the stage strewn with the dead, and you feel the bodies coming long before they fall.

title: Hills Like White Elephants
author: Ernest Hemingway
extract: The hills across the valley of the Ebro were long and white.
blurb: Heat off the dry hills, a bamboo bead curtain stirring across the doorway, two glasses sweating on a station table in the valley of the Ebro while a man and a girl wait for the express to Madrid. They order beer, then Anis del Toro, then beer again, and around every drink circles the one thing he wants and she does not: an abortion, a word [Hemingway](/authors/ernest-hemingway) never lets either of them say. He calls it simple, just to let the air in, nothing really at all; she looks at the long white hills and says they look like white elephants, then quietly takes it back. In five pages you watch how gentle reasonableness becomes a kind of force, how a person can be talked toward something while both pretend the choice is hers. This is the iceberg made flesh, everything that matters held just below the surface, the silence saying what no speech could. The hills stay across the valley, long and white, and no one crosses them.

title: The Time Machine
author: H.G. Wells
extract: There is no difference between Time and any of the three dimensions of Space except that our consciousness moves along it.
blurb: Put a finger on a small brass lever, and watch the model wink out of the present like a soap bubble. That parlour trick, performed for a skeptical dinner party, is how _The Time Machine_ begins, but the trick is the least of what [Wells](/authors/hg-wells) does. He sends his Traveller forward to the year 802,701, where the leisured classes have softened into the childlike Eloi who graze in the sunlight, and the workers have descended into the Morlocks, pale things in the dark who climb up at night to feed on them. That is the famous parable, and it is not the deepest thing here. The machine carries him further still, to a cold red beach beneath a swollen dying sun, where nothing stirs but a few crab-shaped horrors in the failing light. Wells understood before anyone that deep time does not honour our dramas; it swallows them. The Traveller comes back with two white flowers a dead girl pressed into his pocket, the only proof he ever held anything at all.

title: Auto Da Fé
author: Elias Canetti
extract: The best definition of a home was a library.
blurb: Peter Kien, the world's foremost living sinologist, owns twenty-five thousand books and has arranged his own mind to match them, shelf for shelf, so that neither a fact nor a doubt is ever out of place. He has no wife, no friends, until he watches his housekeeper Therese handle one of his books as though it might bruise, mistakes her carefulness for reverence, and marries her within the week. It is the single worst piece of reading he will ever do. Therese and the caretaker Pfaff, a retired policeman with a taste for cruelty, strip the apartment bare and put him on the street, where a hunchbacked chess hustler named Fischerle attaches himself to the ruined scholar like a man who has finally smelled money. Kien's brother, a celebrated Paris psychiatrist, arrives just in time to rebuild the library and leaves before he can see what a man who has shut out the whole world finally does with a box of matches and twenty-five thousand books he loved more than any person alive.

title: Midnight's Children
author: Salman Rushdie
extract: I was born in the city of Bombay... once upon a time.
blurb: At the precise instant India wins its freedom, just past midnight on the fifteenth of August, a baby tumbles into the world handcuffed to history, and the clocks, Saleem Sinai swears, joined their palms in salute. He is one of 1,001 children born in that first enchanted hour, each one gifted, and Saleem, blessed with the most enormous and leaking of noses, can gather them all inside his head: a telepathic parliament of every future India might have been. Years later, cracking apart and pickling his memories in a Bombay factory while his lover Padma begs him to hurry, he tells the impossible thing in one torrential rush of clause upon clause, as if the subcontinent were trying to speak at once. _Midnight's Children_ is the rare book that swallows a nation whole and never stops being funny, tender, and heartbroken. When the Emergency comes for the children one by one and their gifts go dark, you feel what Saleem has known since the clocks saluted him: a self and a nation can be the same wound, and bleed together.

title: To His Coy Mistress
author: Andrew Marvell
extract: Had we but world enough, and time, this coyness, Lady, were no crime.
blurb: Had we but world enough, and time, the poem begins, and for a few luxurious lines it lets us believe we do: a hundred years to praise her eyes, two hundred to adore each breast, thirty thousand for the rest. Then comes the most famous swerve in English love poetry, "But at my back I always hear / Time's wingèd chariot hurrying near," and the spell of leisure shatters. [Marvell](/authors/andrew-marvell)'s seducer is too honest to flatter; he argues, and the argument is death itself. The grave is a fine and private place, he warns her, but none embrace there, and worms will try what her long caution has preserved. What makes the poem ache rather than merely dazzle is that the case for pleasure traps the one who makes it: the chariot is at his back too. By the close he is not pleading but blazing, urging that they tear their pleasures with rough strife through the iron gates of life. Read it once and every clock in the room grows louder.

title: Crow
author: Ted Hughes
extract: But who is stronger than death? / Me, evidently. / Pass, Crow.
blurb: Something is interrogating a newborn thing: who owns these scrawny little feet? Death. This bristly scorched-looking face? Death. These unspeakable guts? Death. And then, at the end of the catechism, who is stronger than death? Me, evidently. Pass, Crow. [Ted Hughes](/authors/ted-hughes) wanted the songs a crow would actually sing, in a language stripped to something super-simple and super-ugly, and what came out was Genesis rewritten as black comedy by a creature to whom the worst has already happened. God tries to teach Crow the word Love, and Crow's gape produces a white shark, then a bluefly, a tsetse, a mosquito, then a man's head and a woman's body locked together in a struggle God cannot pull apart. It is horribly funny until it stops being funny. Hughes wrote these poems in the years after Sylvia Plath's death and abandoned the sequence when a second death made the rest unwriteable, so the myth breaks off mid-creation, exactly where its maker could not follow.

title: Father Goriot
author: Honoré de Balzac
extract: Henceforth there is war between us.
blurb: Old Goriot's room at the Maison Vauquer reeks of boiled cabbage and threadbare gentility, and among its shabby lodgers he sits nightly, once a vermicelli merchant, now selling off his silver plate to keep his daughters in silk. Anastasie and Delphine married into a Paris that despises their father's trade; he loves them anyway, with a devotion so total it looks less like tenderness than a wound reopening itself daily. Watching from the next room is Eugène de Rastignac, a law student with an empty purse and a hunger to rise, caught between Goriot's ruinous love and the escaped convict Vautrin's offer of a shortcut paved with someone else's blood. [Balzac](/authors/honore-de-balzac) built Paris as a machine that runs on devotion, and Goriot is the fuel: he dies delirious, calling for the daughters he ruined himself loving; their answer is two empty carriages bearing only the family crest. Rastignac buries him almost alone, then turns to look down at the glittering city and squares himself to take from it exactly what it just taught him to want.

title: Pensées
author: Blaise Pascal
extract: The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
blurb: "The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me." The man who wrote that line had already built a calculating machine and worked out the mathematics of chance. Then a single night in November 1654 converted him absolutely, and he sewed the record of it onto a scrap of paper hidden in the lining of his coat, found only after he died. _Pensées_ is the rubble of the defense of Christianity he never lived to finish, gathered from scattered notes by editors who could not agree on their order. That disorder is the argument. Here is the keenest mind of its century turning its instruments on faith and reaching the exact place where the instruments give out: why a person must wager on God, why we fill every waking hour with noise out of terror rather than pleasure, why the heart keeps reasons that reason will never know. The book never arrives at its conclusion, because its conclusion was always that, by reason alone, no one arrives.

title: At the Mountains of Madness
author: H.P. Lovecraft
extract: I am forced into speech because men of science have refused to follow my advice without knowing why.
blurb: A geologist on an Antarctic expedition crosses a range of unmapped black peaks and finds, in the city beyond, vast cyclopean walls carved with the history of a civilization older than humanity. [H.P. Lovecraft](/authors/hp-lovecraft) serialized this novella in Astounding Stories in 1936, near the end of a life lived in genteel Providence poverty, drawing on Poe and on his own xenophobic dread of what lay beneath the surface of any known thing. The expedition narrator, Dyer, pieces together the murals and the dissection notes left by the Old Ones, the shoggoths, the unspeakable presence still alive in the deeper valleys. Lovecraft's prose strains, repeats, italicizes, runs at the limits of the speakable. The horror is that the universe is indifferent and that we are recent.

title: King Lear
author: William Shakespeare
extract: How sharper than a serpent's tooth it is To have a thankless child!
blurb: Tell me how much you love me, says an old king, and I will measure out my kingdom by the answer. Two daughters lie beautifully; the third, Cordelia, can only say she loves him as a daughter should, no more, no less, and for that honesty she is cast out. _King Lear_ is the play in which [Shakespeare](/authors/william-shakespeare) withdraws every comfort he grants elsewhere: no innocence is shielded, no late repentance buys mercy, no heaven leans down to set things right. Out on the storm-struck heath, Lear loses crown and shelter and finally his reason, and the tempest outside is the smaller of the two. What makes the play unbearable is its refusal of consolation, the way it carries a father to the brink of seeing clearly only to take from him the one thing that recognition might have saved. Few works look so steadily at suffering and find the universe with nothing to say.

title: Macunaíma
author: Mario de Andrade
extract: In the depths of the virgin forest was born Macunaíma, hero of our people.
blurb: Ai, que preguiça! Ah, what laziness. So groans Macunaíma, born full-grown and black in the depths of the Amazon, a child who refuses to speak for six years and then only to curse the labour of being alive. He is a shape-shifter and a glutton, a magnificent liar who loves everything and stays loyal to nothing, and [Mário de Andrade](/authors/mario-de-andrade) names him, gleefully, the hero with no character at all. When a cannibal giant steals the green amulet his forest-goddess love once gave him, Macunaíma sets off for São Paulo, mistaking its skyscrapers and machines for jungle spirits and dragging the folklore of a whole continent behind him. This is the wild founding text of Brazilian modernism, a rhapsody that stitches hundreds of Indian, African and European tales into one impossible map where no river runs where geography swears it should. It is filthy, funny, and finally aching: a country trying to dream itself whole and half-knowing it never quite can.

title: Fairy Tales and Stories
author: Hans Christian Andersen
extract: "But the Emperor has nothing at all on!" said a little child.
blurb: A tin soldier with one leg falls from a windowsill into a gutter, sails out to sea in a paper boat, and is swallowed by a fish bought at market and brought home. [Hans Christian Andersen](/authors/hans-christian-andersen), the cobbler's son from Odense who walked to Copenhagen at fourteen with nothing, began publishing these tales in 1835 and continued for nearly forty years, inventing the literary fairy tale as a form distinct from the folk tales the Grimms had collected. The little mermaid trades her voice for legs that walk on knives; the ugly duckling shivers through one winter; the emperor parades naked while a child speaks. Cruelty and tenderness sit on the page without apology. The stories know what children know and adults forget.

title: Rickshaw Boy
author: Lao She
extract: A rickshaw, a rickshaw had been his rice bowl. He'd bought one and lost it. He'd bought another and sold it.
blurb: To run through the streets of old Peking with a fare behind you, lungs burning, the whole city a blur of dust and heat, and to know that the rickshaw beneath your hands belongs to someone else: this is the life Xiangzi means to escape. Strong and honest, he wants one thing only, a rickshaw of his own, and he saves for it with a purity of purpose that breaks your heart precisely because you can feel the city gathering to take it from him. [Lao She](/authors/lao-she) wrote in the living speech of Beijing's poor, and the novel keeps a tenderness and rough humor even as its logic tightens like a noose. This is naturalism at its most humane and most pitiless: the study of a good man robbed by soldiers, cheated by a police spy, and pushed into a marriage he never chose, until decency itself becomes a thing he can no longer afford. Few books make you love a man so much while showing you, step by unbearable step, exactly how a society destroys him.

title: In Cold Blood
author: Truman Capote
extract: The village of Holcomb stands on the high wheat plains of western Kansas.
blurb: On a November night in 1959, two men drove across the wheat plains of western Kansas toward a farmhouse they had never seen, acting on a cellmate's tip that the place held a safe full of cash. There was no safe. They cut the telephone wires, tied the Clutter family one by one, and shot all four through the head for a few dollars and a portable radio. [Truman Capote](/authors/truman-capote) read a few paragraphs in the newspaper, went out to Holcomb, and stayed six years. What he built, _In Cold Blood_, he called the nonfiction novel: every fact checked, every name real, yet written with the inwardness fiction allows, until the reader is carried straight through the locked door and into the mind of Perry Smith, the small, broken, oddly gentle man who pulled the trigger. By the end you grieve for killers whose guilt was never in doubt, and cannot quite forgive yourself for it. Capote could not finish the book until Smith and Hickock were hanged, and that long wait shadows every sentence he set down before it.

title: Hopscotch
author: Julio Cortázar
extract: Only in dreams, in poetry, in play do we sometimes arrive at what we were before we were this thing that, who knows, we are.
blurb: On the pavement a child tosses a pebble and hops, square by square, toward the one chalked Heaven at the top. [Cortázar](/authors/julio-cortazar) built a whole novel on that game. _Hopscotch_ begins with two tables of contents: read it straight through and you hold one book; follow the second, leaping between chapters in a prescribed, looping order, gathering up the "expendable" passages most novels would cut, and the same pages become another book entirely, one that doubles back and will not end. In bohemian Paris, Horacio Oliveira loves La Maga and cannot do the single thing she does without effort, which is to simply be alive inside her own life. He has read every philosophy and still cannot reach the center of anything. That center is the square called Heaven: always one toss of the stone away, never landed on by thinking. To read this book is to play the game and feel, exhilarated and undone, how the search and the reading are the same hopeless, holy act.

title: Of Our Spiritual Strivings
author: W.E.B. Du Bois
extract: Between me and the other world there is ever an unasked question.
blurb: A tall newcomer refuses to trade visiting-cards with a boy in a New England schoolroom, one small glance of dismissal, and a child understands for the first time that a vast veil shuts him out from the others' world. From that wound [W.E.B. Du Bois](/authors/web-du-bois) built the truest account we have of what it costs to live behind the veil, the essay that opens _The Souls of Black Folk_. He names the strange doubleness of it, the sense of forever watching yourself through hostile eyes, measuring your own soul by the tape of a world that looks on in contempt and pity, until the self feels split in two. He calls it double consciousness, and once you have read the phrase you will not unsee it. Yet the essay refuses despair. Its longing is to be both Negro and American at once, neither self bleached nor buried, and that ache still sets the terms of how a nation speaks about race.

title: Invisible Man
author: Ralph Ellison
extract: I am an invisible man. No, I am not a spook like those who haunted Edgar Allan Poe.
blurb: Before he has a name, before he understands anything, a boy is shoved blindfolded into a boxing ring to brawl with other Black boys while drunk white men in tuxedos roar, then made to scramble for gold coins scattered across a rug wired to give shocks. That humiliation is the narrator's education, and [Ralph Ellison](/authors/ralph-ellison) spends the rest of the book teaching him the lesson underneath it: a Black man in America is not hidden, he is unseen, real to every institution only as the symbol it needs him to be. A Southern college, a Harlem street-corner, a political brotherhood that wants a voice and not a man, each hands him an identity cut for someone else's face, and each one costs him more. Ellison wrote it in prose that swings and riffs like the Louis Armstrong record the narrator loves, grief turned somehow into invention. He ends underground, in a room he has lit with 1,369 stolen bulbs, blazing against the dark that refused to look at him.

title: Two Treatises of Government
author: John Locke
extract: The state of nature has a law of nature to govern it, which obliges everyone, and reason, which is that law, teaches all mankind.
blurb: Before [Locke](/authors/john-locke), the question of why anyone should obey a king had a settled answer: God placed him there, and authority ran downhill from heaven to Adam to crown. The First Treatise takes that doctrine, in Robert Filmer's confident phrasing, and pulls it apart joint by joint. But the demolition only clears the ground. What Locke builds on it in the Second Treatise is one of the boldest claims any Englishman has set in print: that power runs the other way, upward, from people who entered the world already holding their lives, their liberty, their property, and who lend a government only as much authority as it takes to guard those things. Break the trust and the loan is called in. A people may dissolve a government that turns on them, not as rebels but as creditors. Read it and you are reading the words Jefferson would borrow, almost unchanged, when thirteen colonies decided their king had broken the trust and the loan was theirs to call in.

title: The Year of Magical Thinking
author: Joan Didion
extract: Life changes fast. Life changes in the instant. You sit down to dinner and life as you know it ends.
blurb: A husband sits down to dinner on the evening of December 30, 2003, lifts his glass, and is dead before the soup is cleared, while in another hospital their daughter Quintana lies in an ICU coma. [Joan Didion](/authors/joan-didion) began this memoir nine months later, at sixty-nine, with the reportorial precision she had spent four decades sharpening. Life changes in the instant: that line opens the book and recurs through it like a stuck record, the sentence the mind cannot stop typing because it is true and not yet believable. Didion catalogues the shoes she could not give away, the autopsy reports she requested, the bargains struck with a husband who could not be brought back. Grief, she finds, is not a passage but a place.

title: Emma
author: Jane Austen
extract: Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence.
blurb: You will think yourself smarter than Emma Woodhouse, and that is the trap. Handsome, clever, and rich, she sets about arranging the loves of everyone in Highbury, certain she can read a heart at a glance, and [Jane Austen](/authors/jane-austen) keeps you sealed so snugly inside Emma's head that you misread the village just as she does, charmed the whole way down. Then comes the picnic at Box Hill, where Emma, bored and dazzling, makes a small cruel joke at the expense of harmless, chattering Miss Bates, who is too poor and too kind to defend herself. Mr. Knightley's reproof afterward is so quiet and so exact that the laughter dies in your own throat. That is the wager of the novel: most books let you see more than the heroine, and _Emma_ bets you will see exactly as little. The rebuke that humbles her humbles you, and you close the book knowing yourself a shade better than when you opened it.

title: Letters to a Young Poet
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
extract: Be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves.
blurb: Are these any good? It is the question every beginner aches to have answered, and it is the one [Rilke](/authors/rainer-maria-rilke) refuses, across all ten letters, ever to touch. Franz Kappus was nineteen, a military cadet who had mailed his verses to a poet barely older than himself, and what came back was not a verdict but a redirection. Go into yourself, Rilke tells him; find the hour of deepest quiet, the place where the need to write lives, and ask whether you would die if it were forbidden you. If the answer is no, then do not write. From there the letters keep widening, through solitude and doubt and the long work of love, toward the strange counsel at the book's heart: that a young man should be patient with everything unresolved inside him and learn to love the questions themselves rather than force them shut. Read them young and they quietly reset what you thought a life in art would cost. Few books have ever trusted a stranger so completely with his own becoming.

title: The Enchiridion
author: Epictetus
extract: Some things are up to us and some are not.
blurb: Hold it in one hand and you have already grasped its first claim. The book is small, a manual a soldier could carry to war, and everything it asks turns on a single line drawn through a life. Some things are up to you; most are not. Your judgments, your desires, the use you make of whatever happens, these are yours. Your body, your reputation, the people you love, tomorrow morning, these never were. [Epictetus](/authors/epictetus) learned the distinction the hard way, born a slave in Nero's Rome and lame for life, made to find the one thing no owner can reach. The sayings his student Arrian set down do not soothe; they reorganize a person from the inside, schooling desire away from what can be seized and toward what cannot. Come to it wanting consolation and it hands you something harder and far better instead: the small, unbreakable part of a life that was always only yours to keep.

title: First Love
author: Ivan Turgenev
extract: O youth, youth! little dost thou care for anything; thou art master, as it were, of all the treasures of the universe.
blurb: Zinaida is twenty-one and keeps a parlour of grown men circling her for sport, and into that court drifts the sixteen-year-old from the estate next door, ruined before he knows what has touched him. She is fond of him, which is worse than the teasing she hands the others, because fondness leaves him nothing to fight. [Turgenev](/authors/ivan-turgenev) drew the novella from his own boyhood, and the wound is dressed with a son's exactness. Then a night by the garden wall shows Vladimir who Zinaida truly loves, and it is not a rival of his own age but his own father, elegant and remote, holding her in a register the boy cannot yet imagine. What the book understands is how love first arrives at full adult power, before anyone is ready to carry it. The whip-mark she lifts to her lips, tenderness chosen in the teeth of cruelty, is among the most precise images in nineteenth-century fiction.

title: Native Son
author: Richard Wright
extract: He was their property, heart and soul, body and blood; what they did claimed every atom of him, sleeping and waking
blurb: An alarm clock shrieks, and the first thing Bigger Thomas does that morning is corner a rat against the wall of the cramped one-room apartment his whole family shares, and bring it down with a hurled skillet. Hold the image, because the whole novel lives inside it. [Richard Wright](/authors/richard-wright) wrote the first book by a Black American to climb the bestseller lists, and he did it by refusing every comfort: Bigger kills a white girl, smothering her into silence in the dark because a Black man found in her bedroom is already a dead one. Wright will not let you condemn him cleanly or pity him cleanly, since both responses let you off the hook. Across three movements named "Fear," "Flight," and "Fate," the book insists that a country built to erase a man has left him violence as the only act that feels like choosing. The title is the charge: Bigger is America's native son, and the nation that raised him has no language for what it sees in the mirror.

title: Dangerous Liaisons
author: Pierre Choderlos de Laclos
extract: It is not enough to possess her, she shall give herself up.
blurb: In one of the most famous letters in the book, Valmont composes a love note to the devout Madame de Tourvel while lying with a courtesan, using her body as his writing desk, each pious phrase doubling as a lewd joke the woman he is courting will never catch. That is _Dangerous Liaisons_ in miniature: a war fought entirely on paper, where seduction is a military campaign and tenderness is only another feint. [Laclos](/authors/pierre-choderlos-de-laclos), an artillery officer who wrote only this one novel, lets the letters do the damage; sincerity and its counterfeit grow impossible to tell apart, even by the people writing them. Valmont sets out to ruin Tourvel as a proof of skill and is genuinely undone by her, unable to find the line between his performance and his heart. The Marquise de Merteuil is the colder, finer mind, a woman who forged her intelligence into a blade because her century handed her nothing else to hold. They believe they are the players. The letters they cannot stop writing are the trap.

title: The Name of the Rose
author: Umberto Eco
extract: Books are not made to be believed, but to be subjected to inquiry.
blurb: Seven deaths in seven days, each one answering a trumpet of the Apocalypse, fall upon a snowbound Benedictine abbey, and a Franciscan friar called William of Baskerville arrives to read the bodies the way he reads everything else, drawing a whole story from a smear of ink on a dead man's finger or the print of a horse in fresh snow. [Umberto Eco](/authors/umberto-eco) gives this monastery a library that is a sealed labyrinth, a place where knowledge has been built into a maze precisely so that no one may wander it freely, and somewhere inside waits a single book so dangerous that men kill to keep it shut. What the book argues is that laughter is no sin but a kind of truth, and the fear of that idea is the real murderer here. Eco builds the most ingenious mystery imaginable and then lets its detective reason brilliantly, and not quite rightly, toward an answer that solves less than it mourns. You finish it convinced that a library is the most thrilling and most terrifying room ever made.

title: Gargantua and Pantagruel
author: François Rabelais
extract: Do what thou wilt.
blurb: Our word for the monstrously huge comes from this book's giant, and [Rabelais](/authors/francois-rabelais) earns it. Gargantua is born bellowing for drink, eats entire herds at a sitting, and as a boy works through everything to wipe himself with before pronouncing a live gosling the finest. Yet Rabelais warns in his prologue that the book is a Silenus box, grotesques painted outside and something precious sealed within, and to read it is to pry that box open: beneath the noise and the bawdry a humanist philosophy keeps surfacing. A petty king called Picrochole goes to war over stolen cakes, and the farce sharpens into a study of how paranoia governs. The Abbey of Thélème, Gargantua's utopia, runs on a single rule, _Do what thou wilt_. And the long quest to the Oracle of the Divine Bottle ends with one word of counsel for living: Drink. Rabelais had to coin the word Pantagruelism for what his giants practice, because no smaller term could hold a wisdom that refused to part the body from the soul, or the laugh from the argument.

title: The Swindler
author: Francisco de Quevedo
extract: I sir, was born at Segovia, my father’s name was Clemente Pablo, a native of the same town; may God keep him in heaven.
blurb: At the school of the licentiate Cabra, [Quevedo](/authors/francisco-de-quevedo) starves his pupils so completely that their ribs show through their skin and their eyes retreat into their skulls, and he describes it not with pity but with a comic relish that never once looks away. That relish is the whole book. Pablos is born to a thief for a father and a witch for a mother in Segovia, and spends the rest of his life trying to talk, dress, and swindle his way out of that birth into the ranks of gentlemen. Every trick works for a page and fails by the chapter's end, because in Quevedo's Spain blood shows through velvet the way bone showed through Cabra's starving boys. The prose itself is the con: puns stacked on puns, insults sharpened to a point, sentences that pick your pocket while you're admiring their tailoring. Pablos sails at last for the Indies still believing a new country will finish what cunning could not. It never does. A man who only changes his place, and not his life, changes nothing at all.

title: War and Peace
author: Leo Tolstoy
extract: Well, Prince, so Genoa and Lucca are now just family estates of the Buonapartes.
blurb: Natasha Rostova stands at the edge of her first ball, sixteen and terrified no one will ask her to dance, and [Tolstoy](/authors/leo-tolstoy) gives the moment the same grave attention he gives the cannon at Borodino, because to him they are the same size. That is the secret of _War and Peace_: a girl's held breath and an empire's invasion belong to one continuous fabric of being alive. Five families move through fifteen years of Napoleonic war, and the book follows them so closely that you stop reading about them and simply live beside them, year after year. Prince Andrei lies wounded under a sky so high and endless that everything he believed about glory falls silent. Pierre, rich and adrift, keeps mistaking the shape of meaning and stumbling toward it anyway. Tolstoy's argument, woven into the structure itself, is that no general wins a battle: history is the sum of millions of frightened private wills, all moving at once. You finish it changed, the way you finish a decade.

title: The Sorrows of Young Werther
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
extract: I have possessed that heart, that noble soul, in whose presence I seemed to be more than I really was.
blurb: She is cutting bread for a crowd of younger brothers and sisters the first time Werther sees her, and that is all it takes: he loves Charlotte instantly, completely, hopelessly, for she is already promised to a steady and decent man named Albert. The whole novel is the letters Werther sends a friend, and you can almost watch his hand shake more with each one as the gap between the world he feels and the world that exists widens past bearing. [Goethe](/authors/johann-wolfgang-von-goethe) poured the book out in six weeks at twenty-four, bleeding his own thwarted love for a real Charlotte into every line. What he discovered was a new kind of ruin: a soul undone not by anything life withholds but by the sheer excess of its own longing, a tenderness too vast for any ordinary day to hold. It made him famous overnight and made heartbreak fashionable; across Europe young men wept over it and dressed in Werther's blue coat and yellow waistcoat to follow their hero all the way down.

title: Homage to Catalonia
author: George Orwell
extract: the whole experience has left me with not less but more belief in the decency of human beings.
blurb: In a Barcelona barracks, an Italian militiaman grips [George Orwell](/authors/george-orwell)'s hand so hard that Orwell decides, on the spot, never to see him again, so the moment stays whole. That single, deliberate loss opens the strangest memoir to come out of the Spanish Civil War: Orwell arrived to fight fascism and found, for one unrepeatable season, a city where tipping was illegal and strangers called each other comrade and meant it. Then a sniper's bullet passes clean through his throat, missing the artery by about a millimetre, and he comes back from the front to find his own side hunting his friends as traitors and newspapers at home reporting battles that were never fought. He ends the book back in an England still fast asleep, at peace, oblivious to what is coming, sure the world will not wake until the bombs do it for us. Few writers have paid this much, in blood and in disillusion, to tell the truth this plainly.

title: Skunk Hour
author: Robert Lowell
extract: I myself am hell; nobody's here—
blurb: One dark night, a Tudor Ford climbs a hill above a dying Maine sea town, and the man at the wheel parks to watch the love-cars below, and something in him comes loose. _Skunk Hour_ is the poem where American verse stopped wearing its collar. [Robert Lowell](/authors/robert-lowell) built the opening from gossip and decay, a hermit heiress, a summer millionaire's auctioned yawl, a fairy decorator brightening his shop, all of it holding off the moment the voice cracks open and admits, flatly, 'My mind's not right.' Then the line that made a whole generation of poets go quiet, Milton's Satan spoken from a New England backseat: 'I myself am hell.' What saves the poem from mere despair is the last thing it looks at, a mother skunk marching her kittens up Main Street, jabbing her head in the garbage, refusing to be afraid. Lowell dedicated it to Elizabeth Bishop, whose _The Armadillo_ taught him to end on one small, stubborn animal. Read it once and you carry the smell of it for years.

title: Essays
author: Michel de Montaigne
extract: Que sais-je? (What do I know?)
blurb: When [Montaigne](/authors/michel-de-montaigne) played with his cat, he wondered whether the cat was not playing with him. He wrote the thought down, the way he wrote everything down, in the round tower on his estate where he had withdrawn to study the only human being he could examine without flattery or lying: himself. He called the results essais, meaning attempts, and invented a whole form of writing by beginning from the admission that he did not know. Across more than a hundred of them he catches his own mind in the act, fearful and vain and idle and still grieving a friend years dead, and somehow the wandering composes a whole person. He moves from cannibals to the raising of children to how a man ought to die. The miracle is the voice. Four centuries on, no one in print sounds more like company, turning to you across the table as though doubt itself were a form of friendship.

title: Ode on a Grecian Urn
author: John Keats
extract: Beauty is truth, truth beauty,--that is all Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know.
blurb: Carved on the urn, a lover bends toward a kiss that will never quite land; the girl he reaches for will never age out of being lovely, and the two will hang there, an inch apart, for as long as the marble holds. _Ode on a Grecian Urn_ turns that frozen inch into its whole argument. The piper's melodies are sweeter for being unheard, the boughs sweeter for never shedding a leaf, because art rescues a moment from the decay that ruins everything it touches, and pays for the rescue by denying it fulfilment forever. [Keats](/authors/john-keats) was twenty-three, already nursing the consumption that had taken his brother, and the consolation was not theoretical; he needed the beautiful thing to also be the true thing. When the urn at last speaks, telling us beauty is truth and truth beauty, hear it not as a neat moral but as a dying man refusing to let go of the only equation that might save him.

title: The Social Contract
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
extract: Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains.
blurb: "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains." [Rousseau](/authors/jean-jacques-rousseau) opens with the sentence that would help topple a monarchy, then spends the rest of the book asking the question buried inside it: not how to break the chains, but how to make them just. His answer is the general will, the idea that a people can author the laws they live under and so obey only themselves, that authority drawn from the consent of the governed is the one authority that does not enslave. It is a thrilling, dangerous, impossibly hopeful proposition, that a crowd of strangers might become a single body politic and govern itself without a master. Read it knowing the Bastille fell within Rousseau's century and the men who stormed it carried his sentences in their heads. Few books have argued, this fiercely, that freedom and obedience could be the same act.

title: Their Eyes Were Watching God
author: Zora Neale Hurston
extract: Ships at a distance have every man's wish on board.
blurb: Beneath a pear tree in bloom, a girl watches bees sink into the blossoms and feels the world snap into meaning: the tree married to the wind, every calyx arching to meet the love embrace. That vision becomes the standard Janie Crawford measures every marriage against ever after. She chases it through three husbands. Logan Killicks wants a worker and a mule; Joe Starks, the big-voiced mayor who wills Eatonville out of swamp, wants her silenced on a pedestal inside his store; Tea Cake, younger and broke, takes her down to the Everglades muck to pick beans and dance after dark. [Hurston](/authors/zora-neale-hurston) had spent years gathering the folk speech of the Black South as Franz Boas's student, and the vernacular here is the harvest, no quaint dialect but a full instrument, warm and exact, able to carry a woman's interior weather through the hurricane that breaks the book open. When Janie pulls her horizon in at last like a great fish-net, you have read one of the few novels to let a Black woman want joy and call it enough.

title: Ferdydurke
author: Witold Gombrowicz
extract: I felt that my form was being violated from outside and that I could do nothing about it.
blurb: Imagine waking adult and self-possessed, then watching a professor stroll into your room, click his tongue, and address you as a schoolboy, until the years peel away and your own face goes soft and stupid against your will. That is the morning [Witold Gombrowicz](/authors/witold-gombrowicz) hands his Józef, who spends the rest of the book being shrunk back into childhood by nothing more than what everyone around him expects. The horror is that it works. Gombrowicz had words for the machinery: gęba, the grimace a crowd presses onto you until it becomes your face, and pupa, the rump of an immaturity no one ever outgrows. He stages it everywhere, in a classroom where two boys fight an actual duel of grimaces, in a household weaponising its own modern youthfulness, in a country manor where courting a servant girl curdles into farce. The novel even turns on itself, breaking off into prefaces that quarrel with their own argument. Close it and you will never again be sure your personality is yours.

title: The Life of Samuel Johnson
author: James Boswell
extract: No, Sir, when a man is tired of London, he is tired of life; for there is in London all that life can afford.
blurb: Late one night, straight from a tavern where Samuel Johnson had talked until the small hours, [James Boswell](/authors/james-boswell) sat down and wrote out every word of it before he let himself sleep, terrified of losing a single sentence. He kept doing that for two decades. The result is not really a life; it is a voice, caught closer to full volume than any other mind in English has ever been recorded. You hear Johnson roar and contradict himself and touch every lamppost on the way home and weep over the dread that he would die unforgiven. Boswell loved him enough to leave in the ugliness: the rages, the sloth, the terror of his own mind giving way, the tics no one else thought worth writing down. That refusal to tidy him is the book's whole genius, and its scandal. Two centuries on, open the book anywhere and Johnson is still in the room, arguing too loudly to ignore.

title: To Autumn
author: John Keats
extract: Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness, close bosom-friend of the maturing sun.
blurb: Where are the songs of Spring? [Keats](/authors/john-keats) poses the question near the end and then, almost tenderly, tells himself not to go looking. _To Autumn_ came in September 1819, after he walked the harvested fields outside Winchester, ground he wrote he had never liked so well as that month. It is the last of his great odes and the only one that does not strain to be elsewhere: the _Nightingale_ longs to dissolve into the dark and the _Grecian Urn_ climbs off into cold philosophy, but autumn keeps both feet in the stubble. The first stanza loads the vines until they bend, the second lays the season down asleep on a half-reaped furrow, and the third gathers the choir that is left, the small gnats mourning in the willows, the full-grown lambs bleating from the hills, the swallows massing for a sky they are about to leave. He was twenty-three and had seventeen months to live, and still he does not flinch. The poem simply notices that ripeness and ending are one weather, and chooses to stay out in it.

title: Effi Briest
author: Theodor Fontane
extract: It is really too wide a field.
blurb: Effi Briest is seventeen, still swinging in the garden at Hohen-Cremmen, when her mother calls her indoors to be engaged to a man more than twice her age, once her mother's own suitor. In the grey Baltic town where Baron Innstetten takes her, an old ghost story haunting the house keeps her awake longer than her husband's attentions do, and it is years before a brief affair with Major Crampas gives her one season that feels entirely her own. The unbearable part of [Theodor Fontane](/authors/theodor-fontane)'s novel is not the affair, ended almost as soon as it began, but what follows: Innstetten finds the old letters years later, admits he feels no jealousy or hatred, nothing personal at all, and challenges Crampas to a duel regardless, because honor, dead in him already, still has to be obeyed. For that dead code, Effi loses her husband, her daughter, and her place among people who once loved her, and only at the very end, back in the garden where she began, does anyone dare ask whether the fault was ever truly hers.

title: The Aeneid
author: Virgil
extract: I sing of arms and the man.
blurb: In a temple in Carthage, Aeneas finds the fall of Troy painted on the walls, his own dead among the figures, and weeps before strangers. [Virgil](/authors/virgil) gives the moment the line every Latin student carries: sunt lacrimae rerum, there are tears at the heart of things. That grief is the poem's engine. Aeneas is the founder of Rome and the most unwilling hero the ancient world made, dragged by pietas, that untranslatable fusion of duty, piety, and love, away from all he wants toward a future he will not live to see. He carries his old father from the flames and loses his wife in the smoke. He loves Dido, leaves her at the gods' command, and the leaving kills her. Descending among the dead in Book Six, he watches his father summon the unborn souls of Rome, emperors marched past a man who will never reach the city they build. No epic before it had grasped this: empire and a broken heart can be the same thing, and Rome is bought with all its founder must surrender.

title: Rhinoceros
author: Eugène Ionesco
extract: I'm the last man left, and I'm staying that way until the end. I'm not capitulating!
blurb: A rhinoceros comes thundering through the square of a drowsy French town one Sunday afternoon, and the locals, aperitifs in hand, fall to arguing not about the horror of it but about whether the beast had one horn or two. Then another, and a third. One by one the townspeople turn: skin greening to leather, a horn budding from the brow, the voice thickening into a trumpet, and each new beast insists, reasonably, that this is the most natural thing in the world. [Ionesco](/authors/eugene-ionesco) watched friends in 1930s Romania embrace the Iron Guard, and he never forgot how politely, how sensibly, decent people talk themselves into the herd. The terror of the play is that it is also hilarious, the comedy and the horror the same green skin. At the end stands Bérenger, the shabby, hungover man who never fit anywhere, the last human left, refusing. You will recognise everyone who left him.

title: The Heights of Macchu Picchu (Alturas de Macchu Picchu)
author: Pablo Neruda
extract: Rise up and be born with me, brother.
blurb: 'Del aire al aire, como una red vacía.' From air to air, like an empty net: that is how [Neruda](/authors/pablo-neruda) drifts through the modern world for eleven cantos, hollowed out, finding no life he can hold, until he climbs the Andes to the silent stone city above the clouds. Then the poem turns. He stops marvelling at the ruins and begins to ask who cut these stones, who starved and died raising this splendour, and _The Heights of Macchu Picchu_ becomes a summons to the anonymous dead. This is the twelve-part sequence at the heart of _Canto General_, and its glory is that ascent, out of private despair into a vast act of solidarity, the living poet lending his mouth to the labourers time erased. 'Sube a nacer conmigo, hermano,' he cries, rise up and be born with me, brother, and asks them to speak through his blood. Few poems reach so high to bring so many back.

title: Chaka
author: Thomas Mofolo
extract: The white man is coming, and it is he who will rule you, and you will be his servants.
blurb: By a river, a boy the world has already wronged meets the sorcerer Isanusi, who offers him everything he has been denied: strength, dominion, a name kingdoms will learn to fear. Writing in Sesotho, [Thomas Mofolo](/authors/thomas-mofolo) took the historical Shaka Zulu and made of him something nearer to Macbeth or Faust than to any chronicle, a tragedy of a soul that sells itself away piece by piece. Chaka is a bastard son, beaten and driven from home, and every cruelty done to him becomes fuel; his rise is dazzling, his conquests without end. Then Isanusi names the last medicine, and Chaka murders Noliwe, the one woman he loves, to buy more power, and the wronged boy becomes the thing that wrongs the world. Mofolo watches it all with an unbearable, mourning tenderness, refusing to look away and refusing to stop loving the man he damns. Few books make you pity a monster so completely.

title: A Madman's Diary
author: Lu Xun
extract: Save the children...
blurb: Between the lines of the history he has revered all his life, page after page of benevolence and virtue, a sleepless man finally makes out the two words that were always underneath: eat people. Once he has seen it he cannot stop. The neighbours' grins, the doctor sent to take his pulse, the elder brother who runs the house all become, he is certain, fellow diners waiting their turn at a feast four thousand years old that has always called itself morality. His terror is not delusion but the only clear sight in the country, and the sharpest cut turns inward, the dawning horror that he too, raised at the same table, may already have tasted what they taste. [Lu Xun](/authors/lu-xun) wrote the first great story in everyday Chinese, and the plain new speech was itself the blow, aimed at the lovely old language that taught a civilisation to devour its own and feel righteous doing it. The diary breaks off on a cry that has never stopped sounding: save the children.

title: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
author: T.S. Eliot
extract: I have measured out my life with coffee spoons;
blurb: Let us go then, you and I: the poem opens like an invitation, the evening spread above the half-deserted streets like a patient etherised upon a table. What follows is the inner weather of a man circling one overwhelming question he cannot bring himself to ask, deferring it past the toast and the tea, past the women who come and go talking of Michelangelo, until the asking has become impossible. Every reader who has stood at a doorway polishing the perfect sentence and then walked away having said nothing recognises him exactly. It is built almost entirely of dread: the thinning hair noticed by others, the coffee spoons in which a whole life is measured out, the eternal Footman holding the coat and snickering. [T.S. Eliot](/authors/ts-eliot) wrote it barely out of his early twenties and somehow already knew how a self can congeal into gesture. The verse that opened modern poetry ends among mermaids singing far out at sea, a music he is certain is not for him, and the soft horror of waking into the ordinary and going under.

title: The Portrait of a Lady
author: Henry James
extract: Under certain circumstances there are few hours in life more agreeable than the hour dedicated to the ceremony known as afternoon tea.
blurb: On a long English lawn at Gardencourt, three men take afternoon tea and a young American woman walks toward them with the whole of her life still unspent, certain she will not let anyone choose it for her. Isabel Archer has a fortune she did not seek, a mind that refuses every easy comfort, and two suitors any sensible woman would take; she sends them both away and gives herself instead to Gilbert Osmond, a connoisseur of beautiful objects who has decided she is one. [Henry James](/authors/henry-james) writes her ruin so slowly you feel the air going out of the rooms. Then, in a single midnight chapter, he sits her alone before a dying fire and lets her trace, thought by thought, exactly how a free woman talked herself into a locked house. The terrible tenderness of the book is that it never once lets you stop loving her for it; her ruin is made entirely of her own best qualities, her courage, her refusal to be saved.

title: The Handmaid's Tale
author: Margaret Atwood
extract: Nolite te bastardes carborundorum.
blurb: Scratched into the floor of a closet, in a hand its new occupant will never match to a face, is a line of schoolroom Latin a woman left there before her: nolite te bastardes carborundorum, don't let the bastards grind you down. The closet belongs to a Commander in the Republic of Gilead, and the woman who finds it is called Offred because she now belongs to a man named Fred, forbidden to hold money, forbidden even to read the words she has just discovered. [Margaret Atwood](/authors/margaret-atwood) built Gilead out of the historical record and invented none of its cruelties, and that is the source of its particular dread: you cannot find the moment where this becomes impossible, only the moments where it became convenient. Offred hoards memory the way the starving hoard bread, her stolen name, her daughter's weight in her arms, her husband's face going soft at the edges. Read it once and you will never again trust that the ground beneath an ordinary life is solid.

title: Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas
author: Machado de Assis
extract: To the worm that first gnawed the cold flesh of my corpse, I dedicate as a fond remembrance these Posthumous Memoirs.
blurb: The author is dead, and that is the joke and the liberty of it. Brás Cubas dedicates his memoir to the first worm that gnawed his corpse, then tells the story of his life with the careless candour only a man past all consequence can afford. He pursues a married woman, drifts through an inheritance he did nothing to deserve, dreams up a miracle cure that will finally make his name, and confesses every petty vanity because the grave has made honesty cost him nothing. The chapters are tiny, some a single line, one made of nothing but punctuation, and the narrator keeps breaking off to needle you, the reader he can no longer be bothered to impress. Under all the wit, what aches is the sum it reaches: a charmed, squandered life, seen whole at last by the only man who can no longer fix it. [Machado de Assis](/authors/machado-de-assis) wrote the funniest book ever made from a wasted life, and somehow the saddest.

title: Beowulf
author: Anonymous
extract: LO, praise of the prowess of people-kings of spear-armed Danes, in days long sped, we have heard, and what honor the athelings won!
blurb: Out of the fog-bound moors, where the black mere boils under twisted roots, a shape comes walking toward the lighted hall: Grendel, who cannot bear the sound of men singing and means to silence it tooth by tooth. Against him stands a young warrior who strips off mail and sword to meet the monster bare-handed, because honour will have it no other way. The poem hammers forward on the old alliterative line, two beats and a breath, two beats and a breath, a meter built to be spoken aloud over a fire while the wind worries at the door. There are three fights, each lonelier than the last, and the last sends a grey king alone into a dragon's barrow while his companions slink up the hill. What survives is not the gold, buried cursed beside him, but the grief. _Beowulf_, the oldest long poem in English, already mourns the brave, doomed world that made it, and sings it into the dark anyway.

title: Sailing to Byzantium
author: W.B. Yeats
extract: An aged man is but a paltry thing, a tattered coat upon a stick.
blurb: That is no country for old men, the poem begins, and it means the whole teeming world: the young in one another's arms, the salmon-falls, the mackerel-crowded seas, everything that is born only to die. An aging man, his body a tattered coat upon a stick, can no longer bear to live inside that sensual music, so he sails the seas to the holy city of Byzantium, begging its sages to consume his heart away and gather him into the artifice of eternity. What [Yeats](/authors/wb-yeats) wants is staggering and a little terrifying: to be taken out of nature altogether, to die out of the dying animal of the flesh and be reborn as a thing of hammered gold, a mechanical bird singing on a golden bough to keep a drowsy emperor awake. It is the oldest dream an artist has, made unbearably exact: to trade the warm body that perishes for the cold made thing that lasts, and to wonder, even then, whether it was worth the cost.

title: Civil Disobedience
author: Henry David Thoreau
extract: That government is best which governs least.
blurb: One night in a Concord jail, held for refusing a tax to a government that kept slaves and waged war on Mexico, [Thoreau](/authors/henry-david-thoreau) worked out the most dangerous idea an honest person can have: that obedience to an unjust law is itself a kind of wrong. He will not lend his weight, not even the few coins of it, to a machine he believes is grinding men down. The argument is plain and merciless. If the law makes you the agent of injustice, then break the law; the true place for a just man under a government that imprisons unjustly is also a prison. What gives the essay its strange, quiet force is how personal it makes the question. It does not ask what governments should do. It asks what you will do, alone, when the tax collector knocks. The cell held him one night; the sentences he wrote there reached Gandhi's salt road and a Birmingham jail, and they are still knocking.

title: Underworld
author: Don DeLillo
day: The Shot Heard Round the World
extract: Longing on a large scale is what makes history.
blurb: On October 3, 1951, Bobby Thomson's home run clears the wall at the Polo Grounds and the crowd comes up as one voice, while newspapers that same afternoon carry word that the Soviet Union has tested its second atomic bomb. [Don DeLillo](/authors/don-delillo) opens on that collision of joy and dread, then follows the ball hit that afternoon across forty years, from the boy who vaults the turnstile to catch it to Nick Shay, the man who buys it decades later, having spent the years between in waste management, learning the discipline of burying what he cannot look at directly. The novel moves backward through the second half of the American century, uncovering what a nation throws away to keep smiling: nuclear waste, mob debts, guilt nobody names aloud. _Underworld_ loves its wrecked, ordinary people enough to insist that garbage is the truest record of a civilization, that nothing discarded is ever really gone, only waiting, underground, to be found again.

title: Lolita
author: Vladimir Nabokov
extract: Lolita, light of my life, fire of my loins. My sin, my soul.
blurb: "Lolita, light of my life, fire of my loins." That is how a child rapist asks you to fall in love with him, and the horror of [Nabokov](/authors/vladimir-nabokov)'s novel is how nearly it works. Humbert Humbert, a cultivated European with a gift for the perfect phrase, narrates his years of preying on a twelve-year-old girl in English so voluptuous you catch yourself savouring a sentence before you remember what it is confessing. The prose is not a frame around the crime; it is the crime's silk disguise, the means by which Dolores Haze is talked out of the room while a creature called "Lolita" is invented to replace her. But she keeps surfacing anyway: the girl crying herself to sleep in roadside motels, the child who had a life before this man found her. To read it is to be seduced and then to feel the seduction curdle in your hands, which is exactly what Nabokov built it to do.

title: The Remains of the Day
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
extract: The evening's the best part of the day. You've done your day's work. Now you can put your feet up and enjoy it.
blurb: Downstairs, Stevens pours brandy for the gentlemen of Europe while his father lies dying in an attic room, and he will remember it, without irony, as the proudest evening of his career. That is the whole tragedy of Stevens, butler of Darlington Hall, in miniature: a man who poured himself so completely into the ideal of service that there was nothing left over for grief, or for Miss Kenton, the housekeeper he loved in the only language he allowed himself, which was no language at all. Now, motoring west through the English countryside on the pretext of asking her back, he narrates his life as a ledger of dignity well kept, and the more carefully he balances it the more clearly we see what it cost. [Kazuo Ishiguro](/authors/kazuo-ishiguro) writes Stevens's prose as the very instrument of his repression, each qualifying clause a door closing softly. By the time a stranger on a pier tells him the evening is the best part of the day, the ache is unbearable, because for Stevens the evening is nearly all that remains.

title: The Half-Finished Heaven
author: Tomas Tranströmer
extract: Each man is a half-open door leading to a room for everyone.
blurb: Despondency stops mid-stride. Anguish stops. Even the vulture, wheeling overhead, breaks off its flight, and into that sudden stillness a light comes streaming, so bright the ghosts themselves stoop to take a drink. This is the strange, exalted weather of [Tomas Tranströmer](/authors/tomas-transtromer)'s title poem, fourteen lines in which fear simply lifts and the world stands revealed. Cave paintings surface from the ice-age dark. Strangers walk together in the sun by the hundred. And then the line people carry around for the rest of their lives: each person is a half-open door, leading to a room for everyone. Tranströmer worked as a psychologist among juvenile prisoners and the broken, and he writes grace the way a physician writes a diagnosis, plainly, without a flourish, so you believe it. The heaven of the title is unfinished, still being built. But for the length of this poem the door swings open, the lake becomes a window into the earth, and you are let inside.

title: The Fall of the House of Usher
author: Edgar Allan Poe
extract: During the whole of a dull, dark, and soundless day in the autumn of the year, when the clouds hung oppressively low in the heavens.
blurb: Approach the house and the first wrong thing is its reflection: the grey, decaying mansion sits perfectly doubled in the black tarn below it, as though a second House of Usher were already waiting underwater for the first to come down. [Poe](/authors/edgar-allan-poe) is the writer who discovered that dread can be built before anything happens, that a low sky and a vacant eye-like window and a barely visible crack running from roof to foundation can work so deep into a reader's nerves that the eventual horror feels like recognition rather than surprise. Inside, Roderick Usher trembles with a sensitivity so acute that light, sound, and his own pulse have become torture, while his twin sister Madeline fades toward a death that will not stay a death. The story's terrible insight is that a family and the walls it has never left can fuse into one organism and rot as one. By the last page you understand the crack was never only in the stone.

title: Cousin Bette
author: Honoré de Balzac
extract: Virtue cuts off your head; vice only cuts off your hair.
blurb: Lisbeth Fischer has spent thirty years hemming linen and minding children for a family that has never once wondered what she wants, swallowing every kindness they hand her wrapped in condescension. Her cousin Adeline is beautiful, adored, and married to a Baron who cannot stop ruining her for the sake of younger women. Bette has watched this marriage rot from the inside for so long that patience has curdled into something closer to appetite. When a hard, hungry courtesan named Valérie Marneffe needs an accomplice, Bette finally finds a use for everything she has swallowed, and sets about dismantling the Hulots with the same quiet competence she once brought to their linen closets. [Balzac](/authors/honore-de-balzac) wrote the novel in under two months and it shows in nothing but the ferocity: every page moves like a hand closing around a throat. Few books understand so exactly how an unloved woman's devotion can be the most dangerous thing in the house.

title: Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night
author: Dylan Thomas
day: World Hospice and Palliative Care Day
extract: Rage, rage against the dying of the light.
blurb: Four times the same command returns, each time harder than the last: Rage, rage against the dying of the light. [Dylan Thomas](/authors/dylan-thomas) built that insistence into the bones of the poem by choosing the villanelle, a nineteen-line form on two rhymes whose refrains are forced to recur whether the poet wills them or not. He turned the constraint into a son's argument with death. Across the stanzas he gathers wise men, good men, wild men and grave men, each finding at life's end some reason to resist the dark, until the catalogue narrows to one bed and one face: a father going blind and losing his voice, on what the poem calls the sad height. It does not mourn so much as command. The strangest of love letters, it is a son ordering his dying father not to leave gently but to rage, to curse and bless him with fierce tears, because watching the light go out quietly is the one thing he cannot bear, and the form itself makes that refusal say itself over and over.

title: The Bell Jar
author: Sylvia Plath
extract: I saw my life branching out before me like the green fig tree in the story.
blurb: There is a fig tree in this book, and on every branch a different life Esther Greenwood might choose: a husband, a book of poems, a professorship, a string of lovers in far-off countries. She sits starving beneath it, unable to reach for one without watching the others blacken and drop, so she chooses nothing while the whole tree rots above her head. [Sylvia Plath](/authors/sylvia-plath) drew Esther's prize summer at a New York fashion magazine, and the slow airless descent that follows, from her own hospitalization a decade before she wrote it, and published it under another name. What makes it almost unbearable is the clarity: Esther's wit never dulls and her eye never blurs, so the reader watches a first-rate mind narrate its own vanishing with terrible composure. The bell jar is her word for the glass that lowers over a life, where you breathe the same stale air and look out and cannot, however hard you reach, touch the world on the other side.

title: Fragment 31
author: Sappho
extract: Peer of gods he seemeth to me, the blissful Man who sits and gazes at thee before him,
blurb: Equal to the gods, she calls the man who gets to sit across from the one she loves and simply listen to her talk. That is the whole wound: not his presence but his composure, the ordinary luck of a body that can hear that laughter and stay intact. [Sappho](/authors/sappho)'s body cannot. The poem becomes a catalogue of her own collapse, taken down symptom by symptom as it happens, the tongue gone silent, a thin fire racing under the skin, the eyes blind, the ears roaring, sweat, trembling, a pallor greener than grass, and then the line that has outlived empires, that she is a little short of dying. No one had ever written desire this way before, from inside the falling body, and almost no one has done it better since. The poem breaks off mid-breath, the papyrus torn, the voice cut where the symptoms have already finished their work, and across twenty-six centuries you can still feel the room tilt.

title: The Divan of Hafez
author: Hafez
extract: Arise, oh Cup-bearer, rise! and bring / To lips that are thirsting the bowl they praise,
blurb: Across Iran, at Nowruz and in every hour of doubt, a household opens this book at random and reads whatever ghazal a finger lands on as a message meant for them; no other book of verse on earth is opened as an oracle this way. [Hafez](/authors/hafez) sings of wine and the cupbearer, the beloved's dark curl, the tavern where the honest drunkard shames the preaching hypocrite. The miracle is that you can never settle it: the wine may be a cup in Shiraz or the wine of God, the beloved a boy or the divine, and Hafez holds both inside a single line and refuses to choose, so the poem means more the longer you look. Goethe, reading Hafez in old age, was moved to answer him with a whole Divan of his own. Read one aloud and the nightingale complains to the rose while some private ache of yours is suddenly named in a garden six hundred years gone.

title: The Cairo Trilogy
author: Naguib Mahfouz
day: Naguib Mahfouz Wins the Nobel Prize
extract: Nothing records the effects of a sad life so graphically as the human body.
blurb: For years Amina is not allowed past her own front door; she knows Cairo only through the wooden lattice of an upstairs window, watching the minarets catch the dawn while her husband sleeps off a night she is forbidden to imagine. By day he is the most pious and terrifying of fathers; by night, al-Sayyid Ahmad is the most charming man in the cafés, full of wine and song. [Naguib Mahfouz](/authors/naguib-mahfouz) follows this one household down three generations and a quarter-century, from the 1919 streets where Egyptians rise against the British to the slow loosening of everything the father's word once held absolute. Sons drift toward faith, doubt, and politics; one of them does not come home. What Mahfouz builds, room by room and prayer by prayer, is time itself: the unbearable tenderness of watching a whole world that seemed permanent become the past while you read. By the end you have not read about a family. You have lived inside one and outlived it.

title: Eichmann in Jerusalem
author: Hannah Arendt
extract: The lesson of the fearsome, word-and-thought-defying banality of evil.
blurb: He sat in a bulletproof glass booth in a Jerusalem courtroom, and the woman sent to watch him kept waiting for the monster to surface. Adolf Eichmann had organized the trains that carried millions to the death camps, yet on the stand he produced only officialese and stock phrases, a man who seemed unable to think a single thought that was his own. From those weeks [Hannah Arendt](/authors/hannah-arendt) drew the most disquieting idea of the century: that the machinery of mass murder can run not on towering hatred but on the simple refusal to think, what she called the banality of evil. She does not shrink his guilt or the scale of the dead; she insists, harder, that he was ordinary, that the capacity was clerical, and that this should frighten us more than any demon would. The cost to her was savage; her account of the Jewish councils' cooperation broke friendships she would defend for the rest of her life. The book's enduring terror is that it never lets you set this man apart from yourself.

title: A Tomb for Boris Davidovich
author: Danilo Kiš
extract: I've reached my mature years—why spoil my biography?
blurb: They have already broken him: the lungs, the kidneys, the joints, his body a heap of sores under the rubber truncheons. Yet Boris Davidovich Novsky, old Bolshevik and fierce internationalist, will not sign. He does not fear death. He fears that the false confession his interrogator demands will become the only document to outlive him, and so corrupt forever the biography he spent forty years writing in his own blood. For two weeks the two men wrestle over the wording, each fighting for a single phrase, and Fedukin plays his cruelest card: every day Novsky refuses, another man is shot in his name. [Kiš](/authors/danilo-kis) tells it as archival fact, a true story recovered from the footnotes of the Terror, and that dry documentary calm is what makes it unbearable. Few pages have caught so exactly the vanity and the grandeur of a man who would rather die than let his life be misread.

title: The Importance of Being Earnest
author: Oscar Wilde
extract: To lose one parent, Mr. Worthing, may be regarded as a misfortune; to lose both looks like carelessness.
blurb: Two young men about town have each invented a fictional friend named Ernest, a convenient second self to be summoned or buried whenever pleasure requires an alibi. Both fall in love; both women, by glorious coincidence, have resolved to marry only a man called Ernest; and the lie sets about correcting itself with the serene logic of farce. But nobody reads this play for its plot. You read it to hear the talk, where every line has been polished until it gleams like a verdict, where a baby is mislaid in a handbag at Victoria Station and a horrified woman demands to know which railway line. [Wilde](/authors/oscar-wilde) does not satirise Victorian seriousness from the outside; he climbs inside it and lets it convict itself, sentence by perfect sentence, so the sharpest indictment of an age arrives disguised as the funniest thing ever said over a plate of cucumber sandwiches. By the end you have understood the secret it tells with a straight face: earnestness was never a virtue, only a style, and Wilde simply wrote the better one.

title: Death of a Salesman
author: Arthur Miller
extract: Attention must be paid.
blurb: He comes home early, the two sample cases too heavy, unable to keep the car on the road because his mind keeps sliding into a sunlit past that may never have happened. Willy Loman has sold things his whole life on one article of faith: that to be well-liked is to be worth something, that personality is capital you can bank against the future. [Arthur Miller](/authors/arthur-miller) folds time so that a long-dead hotel-room scene presses through the wall of the present, until you cannot tell what Willy did from what he needed to believe he did. He has staked not only his own dignity but his sons' on a self the world refuses to honour, and his wife, watching him unravel, says the line that holds the whole play upright: attention must be paid. Miller's enormous claim is that this tired drummer, who drove the same New England roads for thirty years, earns the stature of tragedy. The grief is not that Willy fails, but that he believed, to the last, in the thing that was failing him.

title: Howards End
author: E.M. Forster
extract: Only connect the prose and the passion, and both will be exalted, and human love will be seen at its height.
blurb: A wych elm grows outside the house called Howards End with pig's teeth driven into its bark, an old country cure for toothache, and Mrs. Wilcox is the only person in her brisk, telegram-sending family who understands why that matters. E. M. [Forster](/authors/em-forster)'s novel asks what happens when a woman who feels that kind of belonging leaves her house, on a scrap of paper nobody witnesses, to a stranger who understands it too. Margaret Schlegel is that stranger: clever, well-read, allergic to cant, and drawn despite herself into marrying a man who cannot connect the person he is at his desk to the person he is at home. Forster's famous instruction, only connect, sounds simple until you watch what it costs: Margaret's sister falls for a penniless young clerk starving himself on culture he can't afford, and the collision between the families shows exactly how much of England's beauty rests on what it refuses to see. When the fighting is over, the wych elm is still standing, and so, against every odd the novel has raised, is the house.

title: Gulliver's Travels
author: Jonathan Swift
extract: The most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the surface of the earth.
blurb: Children get the sanded-down version: a man tied to the ground by people six inches high. The real book is colder, stranger, and far funnier. Lemuel Gulliver, ship's surgeon, washes ashore four times, and each landfall is a lens ground to a different power. In Lilliput, two empires wage war over which end of an egg to crack, and the joke is how familiar the fervor feels. In Brobdingnag, a giant king studies humanity through a magnifying glass and pronounces it a pest, and you cannot honestly fault his evidence. Then [Swift](/authors/jonathan-swift) removes the comedy: among the serene, reasoning horses of the last voyage, the human creature appears as the Yahoo, filthy and shrieking, and Gulliver can never again unsee it. The triumph is the voice, the flat and reasonable monotone of a man reporting only what he saw, dismantling the whole species without once raising itself. He comes home sane by every measure but the human one.

title: A Season in Hell
author: Arthur Rimbaud
extract: One must be absolutely modern.
blurb: He remembers his life once as a feast where every heart lay open and the wine never stopped, then he sits Beauty on his knees, finds her bitter, and curses her.
