That is how [Rimbaud](/authors/arthur-rimbaud) opens the reckoning that follows: nine chapters begun that spring and finished after his lover Paul Verlaine shot him through the wrist in a Brussels hotel room that same summer, their affair in ruins. He calls himself pagan, beast, damned; he stages his own descent into a hell built from pride and drugs, then turns and renounces the very sorcery, his own dazzling early verse, that had made him a prodigy at sixteen. He paid to have it printed, then never collected the copies; they sat unclaimed in a Brussels warehouse for thirty years while their author walked into the desert and never wrote another line. What he left behind ends not in despair but in a command that has outlived him: one must be absolutely modern.

title: Kubla Khan
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
extract: In Xanadu did Kubla Khan A stately pleasure-dome decree:
blurb: In Xanadu did Kubla Khan a stately pleasure-dome decree: the line arrives already chanting itself, sound running ahead of sense, and you are inside the spell before you have parsed a single word. A sacred river winds through caverns measureless to man down to a sunless sea; a deep romantic chasm slants across a green hill where a woman wails for her demon-lover; ancestral voices prophesy war. [Coleridge](/authors/samuel-taylor-coleridge) swore the whole vision came to him entire in an opium sleep, hundreds of lines composed without effort, until a person from Porlock knocked and the rest dissolved like images on a stream after a stone is thrown in. What he saved breaks off at the instant the speaker aches to rebuild that dome in air from the half-remembered song of an Abyssinian maid. The poem cannot finish what it dreams, and that refusal is its glory: a pleasure-dome built of pure sound, sunny and caverned, already vanishing even as you read it.

title: Lucky Jim
author: Kingsley Amis
extract: Dixon was alive again. Consciousness was upon him before he could get out of the way.
blurb: "Dixon was alive again. Consciousness was upon him before he could get out of the way." That is how [Kingsley Amis](/authors/kingsley-amis) opens the most famous hangover in English fiction, and it tells you everything about Jim Dixon's whole miserable position: a junior history lecturer at a dreary provincial university, trapped between a woman he does not love and a Head of Department who mistakes solemnity for scholarship. The comedy builds by pure accumulation of humiliation, the cigarette that burns a black crater clean through his host's spare-room sheets, the frantic razor-blade repair job, and then the "Merrie England" lecture itself, where nerves and stolen sherry conspire to make Jim's own voice turn traitor in front of the whole faculty, sliding into helpless mimicry as his career burns down around him. Underneath the farce is something that stings: the particular claustrophobia of being polite your way into a life you never chose. Amis lets his hero win anyway, and the ending still feels like a window thrown open.

title: The Consolation of Philosophy
author: Boethius
extract: nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so
blurb: In a prison cell at Pavia, a condemned man is weeping over his ruin when a woman appears at his side and tells him to stop. It is Philosophy herself, come to reason him out of his grief. [Boethius](/authors/boethius) had been consul, the most powerful civilian in Italy, until a charge of treason under Theodoric left him awaiting execution. What he wrote in those last months is neither plea nor prayer but a conversation, alternating prose and verse, in which Fortune's wheel turns exactly as it must, raising and dropping every life without malice, because nothing it lends was ever truly given. Wealth, office, reputation: loans, all of them, and all recalled. Only the reasoning soul holds anything that cannot be seized. For a thousand years the grieving reached for this book, Alfred and Chaucer and Elizabeth I among those who translated it, and found a man at the edge of death still insisting, gently, that the argument held.

title: Lysistrata
author: Aristophanes
extract: No wild beast is there, no flame of fire, more fierce and untameable than woman; the panther is less savage and shameless.
blurb: Twenty years into a war that has buried a generation, the women of Athens and Sparta decide to end it themselves, with the only leverage left to people who cannot vote or fight: they will refuse their husbands the marriage bed until the killing stops. They swear the oath over a shared bowl of wine, seize the treasury on the Acropolis, and wait. What follows is the frankest comedy of desire ever staged, husbands hobbling about in visible agony, a truce finally haggled out over the body of a naked girl who stands in for the map of Greece. But [Aristophanes](/authors/aristophanes) wrote it while Athens was bleeding itself white in a war it would go on to lose, and the laughter carries a wound: the suspicion that the people who pay for the slaughter are the only ones with any reason to stop it. Bawdy, furious, and tender about the ordinary life that war devours, it hands the whole catastrophe of empire to the people history never thought to ask.

title: The Canterbury Tales
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
extract: Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote, the droghte of March hath perced to the roote.
blurb: Say the first line aloud and something startling happens. "Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote" is six hundred years old, yet you can almost hear yourself inside it, English being born on the tongue. [Geoffrey Chaucer](/authors/geoffrey-chaucer) sets thirty pilgrims on the road from a Southwark inn to Becket's shrine at Canterbury, hands them a game (each tells a tale, the best wins supper), and then does the thing no one had done in English: he lets every sort of person speak as fully themselves. The Wife of Bath, five times married, talks for eight hundred lines before she deigns to begin her story, arguing and flirting and refusing to be ashamed of any of it. The Pardoner hawks pig bones as the relics of saints, thunders a sermon against greed, and knows precisely what he is. No tale can be peeled from its teller; each story is a confession the speaker never means to make. The whole muddy road becomes England talking to itself, bawdy and holy and gloriously alive, in the language we still speak.

title: Woodcutters
author: Thomas Bernhard
extract: While the others were crowding round the actor, who had sunk into the wing chair, I retreated into the darkest corner of the anteroom.
blurb: Sitting in the wing chair. The phrase returns again and again through this novel, a compulsion the narrator cannot suppress, because he never once stands up: across an entire Viennese dinner party he stays fixed in a dark corner, watching former friends he has spent years despising arrange themselves to receive a famous Burgtheater actor. The occasion is grief. Joana, a dancer from their old circle, has hanged herself that morning, and the mourners honour her the only way they know how, by performing. [Bernhard](/authors/thomas-bernhard) delivers it in one unbroken churn of prose, contempt circling back on itself, gathering force with each repetition until the rhythm becomes its own ugly, hypnotic music. Then the cruelty turns inward, because the man cataloguing every fraud in the room cannot say why he keeps returning to these people, why he is still here at all. By the time he rises and resolves to set it all down, the novel has folded him into its own verdict: the obsessive attention he wields against them is the very thing it is made of.

title: Birthday Letters
author: Ted Hughes
extract: But the jewel you lost was blue.
blurb: For more than three decades [Ted Hughes](/authors/ted-hughes) said nothing while the world decided who he was: the husband who left, the man the suicide pointed back toward, the keeper of Sylvia Plath's silenced voice. Then, months before his own death, he broke that silence in the strangest way imaginable, not with a defence but with a direct address, eighty-eight poems spoken to Plath herself as though she might still answer. He does not argue. He reaches back past the myth her death had hardened into and finds the actual hours: a borrowed room, a colour she could not stop seeing, the weather of a marriage before its ending swallowed everything else. The present tense keeps her reachable, alive on the page, walking toward a February no poem will name. To read it is to overhear a conversation thirty-five years held in, finally said aloud to someone who can no longer hear it.

title: Brideshead Revisited
author: Evelyn Waugh
extract: I should like to bury something precious in every place where I've been happy.
blurb: Two undergraduates lie in the long grass under the elms, a bottle of cool golden wine beside the wild strawberries, and one of them carries a teddy bear named Aloysius and treats Oxford as a garden made only for pleasure. That summer is the bright lie at the heart of [Evelyn Waugh](/authors/evelyn-waugh)'s novel, because Charles Ryder is telling all of it backward, as a middle-aged officer billeted in the requisitioned house years later, and the beauty arrives already shadowed by its own loss. Brideshead is a great Catholic family scattering from its faith through drink and exile and unhappy marriage, and the deeper argument is that grace works like a fisherman's line: a twitch upon the thread can pull a soul home from the ends of the earth. Charles loves the place, loves Sebastian, then loves his sister, and is granted neither. What makes the house unbearably lovely is the same thing that makes it impossible to keep.

title: The Affluent Society
author: John Kenneth Galbraith
extract: Here, in an atmosphere of private opulence and public squalor, the private goods have full sway.
blurb: Picture a family out for a Sunday drive in a brand new, chrome-bright car, gliding past crumbling pavement, sagging wires, and a river too fouled to swim in, before pitching camp for the night in a park with no working toilets. [John Kenneth Galbraith](/authors/john-kenneth-galbraith) built an entire argument about American wealth out of that one damning scene: a country that had finally beaten scarcity, and somehow felt no richer for it. He gave the comfortable ideas that let this pass the name conventional wisdom, a phrase this book invented and the culture never gave back. And he found the mechanism underneath: production, he argued, does not satisfy our wants so much as manufacture them, each new want summoned by the advertising built to sell it, a treadmill with no finish line. What lingers is the quiet devastation of his real subject, not poverty, but a nation so busy buying that it forgot to build the schools, the parks, the clean water, that no family can buy for itself alone.

title: The Cantos
author: Ezra Pound
extract: What thou lovest well remains, the rest is dross.
blurb: Open _The Cantos_ at any page and it comes at you in pieces: a line of Greek, a Chinese character set whole into the margin, a snatch of Provençal song, a banker's ledger, the names of American founders. [Ezra Pound](/authors/ezra-pound) spent nearly fifty years building this, calling it "a poem containing history," and he meant the whole of it, dynasties and usury and myth crammed into one fracturing verse. The center is Pisa, 1945, where he wrote eleven cantos from memory in a US Army cage while awaiting trial for treason, and where the vast machine turns suddenly, achingly tender: "What thou lovest well remains, the rest is dross." The poem never resolves. Near the end he writes "I cannot make it cohere," then two lines later insists "it coheres all right." He lets both stand. That refusal to tidy the wreckage is the truest thing a man ever made who tried to hold the entire world in his hands and could not put one piece of it down.

title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker
extract: Welcome to my house! Enter freely and of your own will!
blurb: A ship runs aground at Whitby with every sailor dead and the captain lashed to the wheel, and nothing aboard but a foreign count in his crates of native earth. [Bram Stoker](/authors/bram-stoker) builds his novel from the wreckage of ordinary documents: diaries, letters, telegrams, the wax cylinders of a phonograph, as though the modern world's whole arsenal of proof were needed to make anyone believe what has landed on English shores. It is not really about a monster in a cape. It is about the horror of a body that will not stay dead and will not stay itself, about blood passed mouth to mouth until the sweetest girl in the book, Lucy Westenra, rises from her own grave to feed on children and must be driven through the heart by the men who loved her. Stoker never once has to say the word erotic; every page insists on it anyway. Close the book and the count is still out there somewhere, patient, unkillable by daylight alone, waiting for an invitation.

title: Pedro Páramo
author: Juan Rulfo
extract: I came to Comala because I had been told that my father, a man named Pedro Páramo, lived there.
blurb: The dead in Comala have not stopped talking. They murmur up through the floors and the broken walls of a town the heat hollowed out long ago, and into that quiet, which turns out to be no quiet at all, walks Juan Preciado, sent by his dying mother to find the father he never knew, a man named Pedro Páramo. She promised him a green paradise; he arrives to its ash. _Pedro Páramo_ tells itself from inside death, fragments and ruptured time and voices you cannot sort into living or gone, until you give up trying. At the centre of every whisper is the cacique himself, whose power over Comala was absolute and who let the whole town wither when Susana San Juan, the one thing he ever truly wanted, drifted past his reach forever. [Juan Rulfo](/authors/juan-rulfo) wrote almost nothing else. He did not need to: here is the discovery that longing outlasts the body, and finds nowhere left to go.

title: Aubade
author: Philip Larkin
extract: I work all day, and get half-drunk at night. Waking at four to soundless dark, I stare.
blurb: Work all day, get half-drunk at night, then wake at four to soundless dark and stare. From that bare opening [Philip Larkin](/authors/philip-larkin) builds the most clear-eyed poem in the language about the fear of dying, and he refuses every exit. Religion he calls a vast moth-eaten musical brocade made to pretend we never die; the philosopher's reassurance that no rational being can fear a thing it will not feel he answers flatly, because the not-feeling is exactly the horror, the sure extinction of sight and sound and touch and the mind that knows them. _Aubade_ borrows the shape of a dawn love song, but the only thing approaching at first light is the same dread it began with, dressed as an ordinary morning of telephones and postmen. What makes it bearable, strangely, is its refusal to lie to you. To read it at four in the morning is to find, in the one poet who will not pretend, a kind of company.

title: The Pillow Book
author: Sei Shōnagon
extract: In spring it is the dawn that is most beautiful. In summer the nights.
blurb: "In spring, the dawn." So her book begins, and so it goes on, a thousand small acts of attention: the mountain rim slowly paling and flushed with red, fireflies adrift in the summer dark, wild geese shrunk to specks in a far autumn sky, snow fallen on a winter morning. [Sei Shōnagon](/authors/sei-shonagon) served the young empress Teishi in the Heian court, and into a private sheaf of paper she poured everything she noticed: things that make the heart beat faster, things that should be small, hateful things, the exact pleasures and irritations of a refined life. What undoes you is the nearness of her. A thousand years dissolve, and here is a living woman, dazzlingly sharp, helplessly alive to beauty, telling you precisely what delights and annoys her. To read it is to be handed a whole sensibility intact, proof that the texture of a single day, noticed hard enough, outlasts the court that made it.

title: The Waste Land
author: T.S. Eliot
day: T.S. Eliot Wins the Nobel Prize
extract: April is the cruellest month, breeding Lilacs out of the dead land, mixing Memory and desire, stirring Dull roots with spring rain.
blurb: Everyone else calls April the kindest month; [Eliot](/authors/ts-eliot) calls it the cruellest, because spring drags the half-dead back into wanting, stirring dull roots that would rather sleep. From there the poem fans out into a city of voices that never quite meet: a clairvoyante laying out her wicked pack of cards, a typist and her indifferent lover, women murmuring in a London pub at closing time, the Thames-daughters singing from a river that no longer carries anything holy. Nothing binds them but their nearness, and that is the terror and beauty of it: a whole civilization handed to you in overheard scraps, church bells fading into a snatch of song, the Grail legend crumbled to a handful of dust. It should not cohere, and it doesn't, and somehow it became the truest thing the century said about itself. At the end, in a parched land still praying for rain, the thunder speaks in a borrowed tongue and a voice gathers what is left, these fragments I have shored against my ruins, and holds them out to you like broken bread.

title: Prometheus Unbound
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
extract: To suffer woes which Hope thinks infinite; To forgive wrongs darker than death or night;
blurb: Three thousand years chained to a crag in the Caucasus, his flesh torn each dawn, the Titan who stole fire for mankind has every reason to want his tyrant dead. Instead, [Shelley](/authors/percy-bysshe-shelley)'s _Prometheus Unbound_ opens with Prometheus recalling the curse he once hurled at Jupiter, wishing now that no living thing should suffer as he has. That single act of withdrawn hatred is the revolution: Jupiter falls not to an army but to the moment his victim refuses to mirror him, and the shapeless power beneath all things, Demogorgon, rises to sweep him into the abyss. What Aeschylus resolved by reconciliation, Shelley remakes into something stranger and braver, a universe transfigured from the inside out, beginning with one spirit's change of heart. The verse is dense, exalted, almost unsingable in its reach, yet Asia's "My soul is an enchanted boat" floats free as pure music. To forgive wrongs darker than death or night, the poem insists, is the only freedom worth the name.

title: Bastard Out of Carolina
author: Dorothy Allison
extract: I've been called Bone all my life, but my name's Ruth Anne.
blurb: The state of South Carolina stamps ILLEGITIMATE across Bone Boatwright's birth certificate, and her mother drives back to the courthouse year after year for a clean copy, as if the right piece of paper could unmake what the county has already decided about a girl born poor in Greenville. For a while the Boatwright clan is enough to save her: a sprawling tribe of hard-drinking, gospel-singing uncles and furious, tender aunts who love loud and hold their grudges forever. Then Anney marries Glen, and the beatings start, and then something worse, and [Dorothy Allison](/authors/dorothy-allison) will not look away from any of it, least of all the sexual violence a grown man visits on the child who keeps loving her mother anyway. She tells it in Bone's own plainspoken voice, poor white Carolina rendered with fury and not one ounce of pity. And the deepest wound is not Glen's hands. It is that Anney adores her daughter, and still cannot choose her over him.

title: The Alexandria Quartet
author: Lawrence Durrell
extract: A city becomes a world when one loves one of its inhabitants.
blurb: A woman's affair plays out across the white sea-light of Alexandria, and a young Irish schoolmaster believes he understands what he has witnessed; three further novels will prove him wrong. [Lawrence Durrell](/authors/lawrence-durrell) published the four books between 1957 and 1960, calling the sequence an experiment in relativity rendered as fiction. Justine and Balthazar give the same events from successive vantages, each disclosure dismantling the last; Mountolive widens the lens to diplomacy, espionage, the British presence in the Levant; Clea moves the whole apparatus forward in time. The cast moves through dust storms, brothels, and embassy ballrooms, and every character is, at some point, the deceiver and the deceived. Truth in Alexandria is never one thing, only the quartet of things one city contains.

title: Gone With the Wind
author: Margaret Mitchell
extract: After all, tomorrow is another day.
blurb: Red Georgia clay is still under Scarlett O'Hara's fingernails when she claws a shriveled radish from the ruined garden at Tara and gags it down, swearing to the sky that she will never be hungry again. [Margaret Mitchell](/authors/margaret-mitchell) builds her Civil War epic on that vow, not on hoop skirts and candlelight, though she gives you Twelve Oaks blazing white before the war and Atlanta blazing orange after it. The real subject is a woman too hard, too selfish, and too alive to die with the world that raised her. Ashley Wilkes is the man Scarlett loves; Rhett Butler is the man who sees exactly what she is and marries her anyway, gambling she will notice in time. Around them a civilization burns and remakes itself into something harder, and Mitchell loves Scarlett for doing the same, whatever it costs the people who loved her softer. By the time Scarlett understands her own heart, the door is already swinging shut, and all she has left is her old, ferocious faith that morning will bring a way through.

title: Fatelessness
author: Imre Kertész
extract: Even there, next to the chimneys, in the intervals between the torments, there was something that resembled happiness.
blurb: György Köves narrates Auschwitz the way another boy might narrate a first week at a new school: he learns the timetable, masters the work, sizes up the company, and registers each fresh deprivation as simply the next reasonable thing. He is fourteen. [Imre Kertész](/authors/imre-kertesz) was the same age when he was deported along that same route, and his novel rests on the most disturbing truth he carried home: that a person does not experience his own destruction all at once but absorbs it by degrees, each new horror settling quietly into a revised sense of the ordinary. So the boy, in the lulls between the day's torments, comes to know something he can only call happiness. The voice never rises, and that flatness is the whole argument. _Fatelessness_ withholds the comfort of outrage and offers instead a child telling it precisely as it was, refusing to perform for anyone the suffering they expect to hear.

title: The Gay Science
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
day: World Science Day for Peace and Development
extract: God is dead! God remains dead! And we have killed him!
blurb: Imagine a demon slipping into your loneliest hour to tell you that this life, every pain and joy and unremarkable afternoon of it, you must live again and again in the same sequence, forever. Would you curse the messenger, or fall down grateful? [Nietzsche](/authors/friedrich-nietzsche) calls this the greatest weight, and he sets it down here for the first time, the eternal recurrence posed not as cosmology but as the hardest question a person can be asked: could you love your existence so completely you would will every detail of it back? The book that holds this question is the one where the madman runs into the marketplace at dawn, lantern lit, howling that we have wiped away the horizon and killed God, and have not yet seen the blood on our hands. And yet its title means joyful knowledge, gai saber, the troubadour's art. Nietzsche wants thought stripped of every comfort to still come out singing. It ends on three Latin words, Incipit tragoedia, and the tragedy that begins is _Thus Spoke Zarathustra_.

title: Fear and Trembling
author: Søren Kierkegaard
extract: The knight of faith is the only happy one, the heir-apparent of finitude, while the knight of resignation is a stranger and a foreigner.
blurb: Four times a man retells the same story, and four times it fails to reach the bottom of it. God has asked Abraham for his son, and Abraham, saying nothing to Sarah, nothing to Isaac, nothing to the servants left waiting at the foot of the mountain, sets out to obey. _Fear and Trembling_, written under the name Johannes de Silentio, John of Silence, keeps circling this three-day journey because it cannot let go of one intolerable thing: from the outside, the man who would kill his child for God and the man of perfect faith look exactly alike. [Kierkegaard](/authors/sren-kierkegaard)'s Abraham is great not because he will give Isaac up but because he believes, absurdly, against all reason, that he will somehow get the boy back. That belief is what the book calls faith, and it offers no comfort. It is a leap over an abyss with nothing underneath. By the last page the trembling is yours.

title: Death in Venice
author: Thomas Mann
extract: Loneliness ripens the eccentric, the daringly and estrangingly beautiful, the poetic.
blurb: A sweetish smell of disinfectant drifts over the canals, and no one in Venice will say why. Gustav von Aschenbach, a German writer who has spent decades converting every impulse into prose of marble severity, has come here to rest, and instead finds his whole disciplined self coming apart over the face of a Polish boy at his hotel on the Lido. Tadzio never speaks to him. The longing lives entirely inside Aschenbach's skull, swelling as the city, quietly filling with cholera, keeps its own fever secret from its guests. [Thomas Mann](/authors/thomas-mann)'s terrible insight is that the artist's lifelong austerity and this final degradation are not opposites but the same hunger, routed differently. He even gives the obsession Socrates' own words on beauty, the dialogue of the _Phaedrus_ rising through the heat. And all of it moves in sentences of perfect composure toward the loss of all composure, a man dyeing his hair young while the boy he worships walks out into the gray-green sea.

title: Nicomachean Ethics
author: Aristotle
extract: Every art and every kind of inquiry, and likewise every act and purpose, seems to aim at some good.
blurb: You become a builder by building, [Aristotle](/authors/aristotle) writes, and a lyre-player by playing the lyre; and so you become brave only by doing brave things, just only by doing just ones, until the doing has quietly made you into someone. This is the book's most consequential claim, and its most consoling too: virtue is not something you know but something you practise into being, laid down one ordinary choice at a time. The man who freezes in the crisis was not unlucky. Courage was simply never the habit. The _Nicomachean Ethics_ takes up the oldest question there is, how a person ought to live, and answers it not with commandments but with the slow shaping of a character over a whole life. It gives two entire books to friendship, certain the good life cannot be lived alone, that you need another self in whom your own goodness becomes visible. Happiness, here, is never the reward for being good. It is what living well already is.

title: Pippi Longstocking
author: Astrid Lindgren
extract: Don't you worry about me. I'll always come out on top.
blurb: On the porch of Villa Villekulla stands a horse, and one red-headed girl in odd stockings lifts it clean over the railing before breakfast, because nobody has ever told her she can't. Pippi Longstocking lives alone with a monkey named Mr. Nilsson and a suitcase heavy with gold coins, her mother dead, her sea-captain father swept overboard and, by her own cheerful account, crowned king of cannibals on an island where he is waiting for her. She keeps no bedtime, attends no school, answers to no one, and meets every burglar, bully, and disapproving grown-up with the same delighted, unbudgeable confidence. [Astrid Lindgren](/authors/astrid-lindgren) wrote the fiercest kind of comfort here: a girl who lives without a single grown-up in sight and refuses to be lonely about it, who turns an empty house into a kingdom and shares every coin of it with the ordinary children next door. No one has ever needed anyone's permission less, and for as long as the book lasts, neither do you.

title: Crash
author: J.G. Ballard
extract: Vaughan died yesterday in his last car-crash. During our friendship he had rehearsed his death in many crashes, but this was his only true accident.
blurb: On a wet flyover near Heathrow, chrome and torn safety glass arrange themselves around a body, and the narrator finds, to his horror and then his fascination, that the wound excites him. This is a novel about people aroused by car crashes: about Vaughan, the scarred visionary who photographs collisions and dreams of dying in a head-on impact with Elizabeth Taylor, and the circle he draws into his fever, tracing the shapes a dashboard stamps into flesh. [Ballard](/authors/jg-ballard) writes it in cold, glittering, clinical prose, the language of a coroner in love, and the effect is hypnotic rather than lurid. He takes the century's romance with the machine to its final logic and finds the death drive waiting there, chromed and gleaming. Read it once and you cannot cross a motorway junction the same way again: every merging lane, every crumpled bonnet on the hard shoulder hums now with a terrible, intended tenderness.

title: Blindness
author: José Saramago
extract: If you can see, look. If you can look, observe.
blurb: The blindness, when it comes, is not darkness but a luminous white, a sea of milk that floods the eyes of one driver stopped at a traffic light and then, person by person, an entire city. The state does what states do and locks the infected away in a derelict asylum, then forgets to feed them. Among the quarantined is one woman who can still see, the doctor's wife, who faked the disease to follow her husband inside and now alone must watch what everyone else is spared. [Saramago](/authors/jose-saramago) gives no one a name, only their afflictions and their roles, so the crowd becomes every crowd. His sentences run on for half a page, commas stitching speaker to speaker without a single quotation mark, the grammar itself going gradually sightless. What she witnesses as the wards turn to filth and predation is unbearable, and the novel's terrible wager is that sight, here, is the curse and the conscience both.

title: The Road Not Taken
author: Robert Frost
extract: Two roads diverged in a wood, and I-- I took the one less traveled by, and that has made all the difference.
blurb: Two roads diverge in a yellow wood, and a traveler stands a long while where they part, sorry he cannot walk both. Everyone knows how it ends: he takes the one less traveled by, and that has made all the difference. But read the lines again. He admits the two paths are worn "really about the same," that the leaves that morning lay equal on each, and that the heroic sigh he imagines giving "ages and ages hence" is a story he is already rehearsing, before he has gone anywhere. _The Road Not Taken_ is the most misread poem in English, and that is its quiet genius: it catches a mind in the act of inventing the meaning of its own life. [Frost](/authors/robert-frost) wrote it to tease a friend who agonized over every turning they had not taken. The trap is that you will finish it feeling vindicated, and never notice you were the one being teased.

title: The Confusions of Young Törless
author: Robert Musil
day: World Day for the Prevention of and Healing from Child Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Violence
extract: There can be no real number that is the square root of something negative.
blurb: In a mathematics lesson at a remote Austrian military academy, a boy asks how a number that cannot exist, the square root of a negative, is allowed to govern real calculations. Told simply to accept it, he cannot, and that refusal becomes the whole engine of [Robert Musil](/authors/robert-musil)'s short, terrible novel. When Törless and two classmates catch a fellow student stealing, they lock him in an attic room and turn his punishment into a private, escalating theatre of cruelty, while Törless watches himself watching, unable to name what he feels or make himself stop feeling it. Musil is not writing a school scandal. He is lifting the floorboards of an orderly world these boys were raised to trust, and showing what waits underneath: unpoliced, patient, willing to call itself something else. Decades before disciplined young men in locked rooms would organize such cruelty on a continental scale, this novel had already found its logic. The confusions never resolve. Musil leaves you exactly where he left Törless, certain two irreconcilable things are both true, and still required to live between them.

title: The Street of Crocodiles
author: Bruno Schulz
extract: Let us say it bluntly: the misfortune of that area is that nothing ever succeeds there, nothing can ever reach a definite conclusion.
blurb: On a map his father keeps in a locked drawer, one quarter of the town glows blank white, the way old atlases marked the polar wastes: uncharted, disreputable, better left off the record. That white patch is the Street of Crocodiles, the town's cut-rate concession to the modern world, a district of washed-out daylight, tawdry shops selling nothing anyone needs, and desire that flares and goes nowhere. [Bruno Schulz](/authors/bruno-schulz) takes this shabby provincial street, based on his own Drohobycz, and transmutes it into something feverish and mythic, prose so sensuous it seems to grow like weeds through the pavement. Its deepest joke is also its ache: here nothing is ever finished, nothing reaches its conclusion, every gesture hangs half-made in the air, because the whole place is only a paper imitation of a real city. Read it and a drab street corner will never look ordinary again. Few writers ever made counterfeit reality this gorgeous.

title: Catch-22
author: Joseph Heller
extract: That's some catch, that Catch-22.
blurb: There is exactly one catch, and it is Catch-22: a man crazy enough to want grounding need only ask to be grounded, and the asking proves him sane enough to fly. The logic closes like a fist. Yossarian, an American bombardier on a speck of island near the war's end, has worked out that the people most determined to kill him are not the Germans but his own commanders, who keep raising the number of missions each time he nears the total that would send him home. [Heller](/authors/joseph-heller) spins this single paradox outward into a whole circus, a mess officer bombing his own base under contract, a colonel in love with tidy formations, men vanishing into paperwork. And then the laughter, which has been frantic, almost cruel, turns out to have been guarding something. The novel keeps returning to a wounded gunner in the back of a plane, withholding the worst of it, until it can bear to tell you everything. You will not stop laughing, and you will not be ready.

title: Candide
author: Voltaire
extract: We must cultivate our garden.
blurb: The best of all possible worlds, Dr. Pangloss keeps insisting, even as that world hangs him, shakes Lisbon to rubble, and flogs his hapless pupil across two hemispheres. [Voltaire](/authors/voltaire) wrote this little book in something close to fury and dressed it as a romp: earthquake, auto-da-fé, war, slavery, plague, each fresh catastrophe narrated at a sprint and with a perfectly straight face, until the comfortable doctrine that all suffering is secretly for the good lies in pieces on the floor. The marvel is how funny it stays while doing this, how lightly it carries its anger. Candide loses everything he was promised and keeps walking anyway. Then, after every grand system has failed him, arrives the quietest and most famous sentence in the book: we must cultivate our garden. Stop trying to justify the world; tend your own small corner of it. Read it in a single sitting, the way it was built to be swallowed whole.

title: The Prophet
author: Kahlil Gibran
extract: Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life’s longing for itself.
blurb: A ship is sighted on the horizon of Orphalese, the vessel that has come after twelve years to carry Almustafa home, and before he can board it the whole city gathers at the harbor to keep him a little longer, to ask him to speak on the things that make and break a life: love, work, children, joy, pain, death. He does not lecture them. He answers as though he has always known the answer and only now has the words for it, and reader after reader has found a piece of their own life inside his sentences: your children are not your children, they are the sons and daughters of life's longing for itself; work is love made visible. [Kahlil Gibran](/authors/kahlil-gibran) wrote it in the cadence of scripture but bound it to no religion, which is why it still gets read aloud at weddings a century later, not for its prettiness but because it says, in the plainest sentences it can find, what we mean to tell someone we love before they board a ship.

title: Siddhartha
author: Hermann Hesse
extract: I can think. I can wait. I can fast.
blurb: A seeker meets the Buddha himself, the fully awakened one, listens to a teaching that has no flaw in it, and then walks away. He cannot be given wisdom, Siddhartha understands; he must live it, every error of it, in his own body. So he plunges into the world he renounced: the courtesan Kamala teaching him love, the merchant teaching him greed, the dice and the wine teaching him despair, until a son he adores breaks his heart exactly as he once broke his father's. Then he comes to the river, and learns to listen to it. [Hesse](/authors/hermann-hesse) wrote this slim, luminous book out of his own collapse, and it carries the strange calm of someone who has stopped fighting the current. Its great gift is the river's secret, that time is not real and every voice of the world is one voice saying Om. Few books make peace feel so hard-won, or so close.

title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin
day: On the Origin of Species Published
extract: There is grandeur in this view of life.
blurb: Look long enough at a tangled bank, [Darwin](/authors/charles-darwin) writes near the end, at the plants and the singing birds and the worms working the damp earth, and you begin to see that every one of these elaborate forms was made by laws still acting all around us. That is the quiet violence of this book: it takes the orderly, purposeful world you walked in with and hands back one that improvises, wastes, and throws up beauty no intention ever planned. The argument never bullies. Darwin stacks barnacle on pigeon on island finch on fossil shell, spends whole chapters on the objections that frightened him most, concedes what he cannot yet explain, and reasons as though you were the rigorous skeptic he most needs to convince. He had held the theory for twenty years before he dared print it, and the dread is audible in the patience. By the last page, watching life branch and complicate without end, he can call it grandeur and mean it: from so simple a beginning, endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful.

title: Confessions of a Mask
author: Yukio Mishima
extract: What I wanted was to die among strangers, untroubled, beneath a cloudless sky.
blurb: In a reproduction of Guido Reni's Saint Sebastian, the martyr hangs lashed to a tree, arrows buried in his side, his head fallen back in an expression no one has taught the narrator to read as suffering. His body answers before his mind can object, and in that instant a schoolboy in wartime Japan learns the shape of a desire his country has no language to permit. What follows is a life built as performance. He worships a coarse, magnificent schoolmate named Omi from a distance he never closes, then courts a young woman, Sonoko, with a sincerity that is itself the most elaborate disguise, feeling the courtship and feeling nothing it is meant to mean. [Mishima](/authors/yukio-mishima) writes it all in prose cold and exact as surgery, a young man cataloguing his own concealment without once flinching. Do not wait for the mask to drop. His unbearable finding is that the confession is not the mask's undoing. It is the mask made flawless.

title: Gilead
author: Marilynne Robinson
extract: I told you last night that I might be gone sometime, and you said, Where, and I said, To be with the Good Lord.
blurb: Water comes down off a shaken branch onto a young couple laughing in the rain, and the old minister on his porch decides that water must have been made first for blessing and only afterward for crops and the wash. John Ames is seventy-six, his heart failing, and his son is seven, too small to remember him, so Ames sits down to write the boy a letter to be opened once he is grown, and the letter becomes this book. _Gilead_ is [Robinson](/authors/marilynne-robinson)'s argument, made in prose so quiet you find yourself holding your breath, that the ordinary world looked at hard enough is indistinguishable from grace: light moving on the river, the smell of a baseball mitt, the face of the young wife who came to him late. Ames cannot hold to a thought without turning aside to bless whatever has caught his eye, and that turning aside is the entire faith of the book. To read it is to be taught, sentence by sentence, how much of your own life you have failed to notice.

title: Long Day's Journey into Night
author: Eugene O'Neill
extract: None of us can help the things life has done to us.
blurb: By nightfall a foghorn is moaning out on the Sound, and inside the summer house the four Tyrones have talked their way back through every betrayal they have ever handed one another. Mary drifts upstairs and returns changed, the morphine pulling her out of reach while her husband and sons pretend not to see; James, the matinee idol who traded his talent for a sure thing, counts the cost of every lamp left burning; Jamie drinks; Edmund, the youngest, coughs and waits to hear how bad his lungs really are. [Eugene O'Neill](/authors/eugene-oneill) set down his own family here, sealed the manuscript, and asked that it never be staged in his lifetime. What binds these four is not cruelty but love so wounded it can only come out as blame. The fog they each long for is the time before the harm was done, and the night the title keeps promising is what is left when even that fog will not hold.

title: Oresteia
author: Aeschylus
extract: Men shall learn wisdom, by affliction schooled.
blurb: For ten years a watchman has lain on the roof of Argos, waiting for the fire that means Troy has fallen and the king sails home. When the beacon finally leaps across the hills, it lights the way to a murder: Clytemnestra has drawn her husband a bath and laid out a robe stitched shut, and she has waited longer than he has. So begins the only Greek trilogy to reach us whole, three plays that set a killing in the first, its answering killing in the second, and on the third the question beneath both. What happens when every act of justice is also a crime, when blood can only call for more blood? Orestes avenges his father by killing his mother, and the Furies, older than the gods and deaf to his reasons, hunt him down. The wonder of the _Oresteia_ is that it refuses to end in more blood. It ends in a courtroom, the first one, the law invented in front of you because the only other road is a house that never stops bleeding.

title: The Book of Disquiet
author: Fernando Pessoa
extract: I was born in a time when the majority of young people had lost faith in God.
blurb: Nothing happens here, and that is its glory. After [Fernando Pessoa](/authors/fernando-pessoa)'s death a trunk turned up stuffed with loose fragments in no order, never finished, never meant to cohere into a book; the volume you hold was assembled out of that disorder, and it stands as his masterwork. He hands the writing to Bernardo Soares, an assistant bookkeeper who lives above a Lisbon tobacco shop and to whom nothing ever happens. Soares neither loves nor travels. He watches: the light crossing his office wall, the fog settling over the Tagus, the small traffic of the Rua dos Douradores, and he sets it down with a precision so exact that his cramped life swells until it holds everything. To read it is to sit inside a lucid, sorrowing mind that has decided the outer world is mostly noise it need not answer. You finish having recognised your own most private hours, the ones when you, too, only watched.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde
extract: There is only one thing in the world worse than being talked about, and that is not being talked about.
blurb: A single sentence can ruin a life, and [Wilde](/authors/oscar-wilde) proves it. Lord Henry Wotton lays out his glittering creed in a Chelsea garden, that youth is the only thing worth having and beauty the only truth, and a beautiful young man who has never owned a thought of his own takes every word as gospel. Dorian stands before his finished portrait and wishes that the picture might grow old in his place, and the picture obliges. He moves through decades of pleasure, betrayal, and worse without a line on his face, while the canvas locked in the attic curdles into something monstrous, the one honest record of his soul. The genius is that Lord Henry, who commits no sin himself, is the most corrupting presence in every room; his epigrams are the pleasure of the book and its slow poison, the same wit Wilde performed in drawing rooms and here puts quietly on trial. Beauty without consequence sounds like the finest of bargains, right up until you climb to the attic and see what it has cost.

title: Go Tell It on the Mountain
author: James Baldwin
extract: Everyone had always said that John would be a preacher when he grew up, just like his father.
blurb: On the morning of his fourteenth birthday, John Grimes works a dustrag across the front room of the Harlem apartment and watches the grime settle back the instant he lifts it, dirt ground so deep into the walls and the skin of his family that no labor will ever clear it. His stepfather Gabriel preaches with an authority that never bends toward love, and the long central movement breaks open the prayers of the saints around him, each carrying a Southern inheritance of whippings, shame, and flight that John is too young to read in their faces. That night he falls to the threshing floor of the Temple of the Fire Baptized, and [Baldwin](/authors/james-baldwin) writes salvation with such bodily force you feel the boards beneath his back. Is it grace, or the only door out of a house Gabriel has made unlivable? The whole book breathes in King James cadence, the tongue Baldwin himself preached in as a teenager, and it is unbearable to watch a boy reach for deliverance in a language no one ever gave him freely.

title: Austerlitz
author: W.G. Sebald
extract: We take almost all the decisive steps in our lives as a result of slight inner adjustments of which we are barely conscious.
blurb: In the waiting room of Antwerp's Centraal Station, beneath a dome built to shrink a traveller to the size of an insect, a stranger begins talking about fortresses and does not stop for three hundred pages. He is Jacques Austerlitz, an architectural historian who has spent years studying the walls men build to keep other men out, never asking why his own life has the same starved, sealed-off shape. W. G. [Sebald](/authors/wg-sebald) tells it in sentences that run on for pages, threaded with grainy, uncaptioned photographs that could be evidence, or could be nothing. What Austerlitz slowly uncovers, past fifty, is that he was born in Prague and sent alone to Wales in 1939, four and a half, given a new name by the minister who raised him, so completely he forgot he'd ever owned another. His mother was sent to Theresienstadt. His father wrote from Paris until, one day, the letters stopped. This is a novel about a man who spent his life studying walls, and never once asked what he was walling out of himself.

title: Lord Jim
author: Joseph Conrad
extract: He was an inch, perhaps two, under six feet, powerfully built.
blurb: Eight hundred pilgrims sleep below deck on a steamer crossing the Indian Ocean when something underwater strikes the hull, and a rusted bulkhead begins to bulge against the sea. Jim is the young first mate who has rehearsed heroism his whole life in daydreams, and in the one moment it is asked of him for real, his body jumps into a lifeboat without him. The ship does not sink. He is left alive, stripped of his certificate, a coward by one leap he can never take back, and [Conrad](/authors/joseph-conrad), who first went to sea at sixteen, knew the unbearable thing this book knows: that you are not the brave figure of your own imagining, only the person you were in the second your body chose for you. Marlow narrates in long, circling sentences that close on Jim from every angle and never quite hold him. He flees east to a river settlement that crowns him Lord and offers a second chance to prove what he is. You read on dreading, and half hoping, the moment it comes for him again.

title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes
extract: The life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.
blurb: A crowned giant rises over the landscape, his torso composed of hundreds of small human figures, sword in one hand and crozier in the other. [Thomas Hobbes](/authors/thomas-hobbes) engraved this frontispiece onto his 1651 treatise of political philosophy, written in Paris exile during the English Civil War while Cromwell's armies redrew the map at home. Outside the commonwealth, Hobbes argued, men live in a state of nature where every hand is against every other and the life of man is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. Only the social contract, surrendering all rights to an absolute sovereign, can save the species from war of all against all. Reason, fear, and the appetite for peace stitch the great body together; the giant is the multitude, made one.

title: Slouching Towards Bethlehem
author: Joan Didion
extract: The center was not holding.
blurb: San Francisco, the cold spring of 1967, and the missing children of America were gathering in the Haight to call themselves hippies. [Joan Didion](/authors/joan-didion) went to find them and came back with the coldest, clearest report anyone filed on a generation coming loose from its moorings. She borrowed her title from Yeats, from the rough beast slouching toward Bethlehem, because that was the atmosphere she felt in the panhandle: not a revolution, not a siege, but a center that was not holding, a society that had forgotten to teach its youngest the rules of its own game. What makes the essay unbearable is her refusal to editorialize. She simply watches, records the flat sad talk of runaways and drifters and the smallest children, and lets the detail do the indicting. Read it once and you will never again mistake the Summer of Love for a party, or forget the youngest faces she found at the end of it.

title: Clarissa
author: Samuel Richardson
extract: A feeling heart is a blessing that no one, who has it, would be without.
blurb: Two people sit writing letters about the same events, and the horror is that you believe them both. Lovelace is the most charming correspondent in English fiction, witty, quicksilver, confessing his schemes with such relish that you almost root for him even as he closes a trap around a girl of eighteen. Clarissa Harlowe writes from inside it: hounded by a family who would sell her to a man she cannot bear, then manoeuvred toward a rake who has decided her virtue is a fortress worth the siege. Across nearly a million words, [Samuel Richardson](/authors/samuel-richardson) lets you watch the slow machinery of ruin grind, letter answering letter, and makes you feel how a world that calls a woman good only when she submits has already done the seducer's work for him. What undoes you is her clarity. She sees the danger, reasons against it, and the trap shuts anyway.

title: Letters to Lucilius
author: Seneca
extract: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
blurb: From a rented room above a public bathhouse, grunts and splashes and the cries of the man selling sausages coming up through the floor, [Seneca](/authors/seneca) sits down to argue that a steady mind can hold its quiet anywhere. That is the strange charm of these letters to his friend Lucilius: not a treatise handed down from on high but philosophy made to prove itself in the racket of an ordinary day, where the question is never abstract but always, given so little time, what is the right use of this hour? He is candid that he falls short, a rich man preaching simplicity who knows it. And under every page runs a fact that turns the Stoic calm from pose into practice: Nero, the emperor he had once tutored, now wanted him dead, and would soon order it. We suffer more often in imagination than in reality, he tells Lucilius, teaching a friend how to meet death while still, himself, learning the lesson.

title: The Dhammapada
author: Anonymous
extract: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
blurb: Hatred is never appeased by hatred; by love alone is it appeased. The Buddha is said to have spoken that line, and the centuries between have not dulled it. The _Dhammapada_ gathers 423 such verses, the most beloved distillation of his teaching, and it asks you to believe nothing. There are no miracles here, no god to petition, no reward dangled past death. There is only a claim, stated in the opening line and proved across every chapter that follows: the mind makes everything, your joy and your suffering both, and so the work of becoming free is work no one can do for you. What unsettles is how gently it says this. The verses on desire and anger, on the sage who has crossed the flood, were shaped to be memorized, and they behave like seeds, dry and complete, apt to open hours after you have shut the book. To read it is to be handed full responsibility for your own mind, and to feel, against all expectation, lighter for the weight.

title: The Passion According to G.H.
author: Clarice Lispector
extract: I'm searching, I'm searching. I'm trying to understand.
blurb: Expecting a servant's clutter, a Rio sculptor steps into the maid's vacated room and finds instead a scoured desert: white walls, a bare cot, three charcoal figures drawn on the plaster like a cave painting. Then the wardrobe door, and inside it a cockroach, and the slow horror of crushing it so that a white paste wells from the wound. From this nothing, a clean room and a dying insect, [Clarice Lispector](/authors/clarice-lispector) builds one of the strangest spiritual ordeals in fiction. G.H., who has only initials, stops being a person across a single afternoon, peeled down past name and self until she reaches the oldest living matter, the neutral thing that simply is, indifferent to being loved or named. The novel ends in a reverse communion that you will not forget and may not forgive. Lispector writes in a continuous, groping present, language sent back into the place where language gives out, and somehow it holds.

title: Because I could not stop for Death
author: Emily Dickinson
extract: Because I could not stop for Death, He kindly stopped for me;
blurb: Death comes as a suitor. He pulls up in a carriage, unhurried, perfectly mannered, and because the speaker has no time to spare he makes the time for her, handing her in beside a silent third passenger named Immortality. What follows is the strangest courtship in American poetry: a slow drive past children circling a schoolyard, past fields of grain that seem to gaze back, past a sun that does not set so much as pass them, until the horses pause before a house that is only a swelling of the ground. [Dickinson](/authors/emily-dickinson) set all of this to the meter of the hymns she sang as a girl, so the lines rock with the cadence of Sunday worship even as they decline its comfort. She let almost none of her poems out into the world while she lived. This one waited in a drawer to tell you, centuries on, that eternity feels shorter than a single afternoon.

title: Thus Spoke Zarathustra
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
extract: I teach you the Superman. Man is something that is to be surpassed. What have ye done to surpass man?
blurb: In a forest at the edge of the world, Zarathustra meets an old hermit still singing his devotions to God, and walks on astonished that the saint has not yet heard the news the book will carry down into the marketplace: that God is dead, and the work of becoming human has only now begun. [Nietzsche](/authors/friedrich-nietzsche) wrote his hardest thinking not as argument but as scripture, in parables and songs and a voice that swings between ecstasy and laughter, certain that logic would only tame what he had to say. He teaches the Overman, man as a rope stretched over an abyss, something to be surpassed rather than worshipped. And he sets down the heaviest question philosophy has ever asked: could you love your one life so completely that you would will every moment of it back, unchanged, forever. The book does not persuade so much as press, and what it presses for is a different way of carrying your days. Zarathustra ends alone, walking out glowing into his morning, having kept no last disciple.

title: The Power and the Glory
author: Graham Greene
extract: There is always one moment in childhood when the door opens and lets the future in.
blurb: The boat that would carry him to safety is at the quay, smoke up, when a child runs to fetch him, his mother dying and calling for a priest. So the whisky priest turns from the river and stays in the state that shoots men like him. [Greene](/authors/graham-greene) gives him no name, only a thirst he cannot master, a daughter he fathered in a village he was meant to serve, and the settled certainty that he is a coward unworthy of the office he cannot lay down. Through jungle and mud, toward a capture he does too little to prevent, the novel presses a single scandalous claim: that grace runs through this ruined man exactly as it would through a saint, that a Mass mumbled half-drunk is no less holy for the shaking hands that lift it. The lieutenant hunting him is the better man by every human measure, a true believer in a country swept clean of God, and Greene loves him too. The worthlessness is the point. The cracked cup pours the same blood.

title: Black Beauty
author: Anna Sewell
extract: The first place that I can well remember was a large pleasant meadow with a pond of clear water in it.
blurb: A black colt with a white star on his forehead grazes in a meadow in Victorian England, learns the bit and harness from kind hands, and begins the long descent through owners careful and cruel that will define his life. [Anna Sewell](/authors/anna-sewell) wrote this novel from her invalid's couch in the last years of her life, finishing it in 1877 a few months before her death, the only book she would publish. Black Beauty narrates his own life in the first person, from foal to cab horse, passing through the hands of squires, drunks, livery stables, and London's pitiless traffic. The book did what no pamphlet had managed: it ended the cruel bearing-rein and shamed a nation into kindness. The horse speaks. The century listens.

title: The Rings of Saturn
author: W.G. Sebald
extract: In August 1992, when the dog days were drawing to an end, I set off to walk the county of Suffolk.
blurb: Somewhere along the Suffolk coast, a sight as ordinary as a derelict herring fleet or a kitchen-garden gone to ruin sets the narrator of _The Rings of Saturn_ thinking, and the thought never returns to where it began. A walk becomes a descent. From the empty beaches it falls through the Congo atrocities Roger Casement witnessed, the skull of Thomas Browne passed hand to hand, the silkworm cultures that ate whole Chinese forests and then were gone. Photographs interrupt the page, grainy and unexplained, as if memory itself were leaking through. [Sebald](/authors/wg-sebald) writes in long, grave, patient sentences that seem to be in no hurry to arrive anywhere, and that is the point: he has trained his attention to receive only what is perishing. Saturn was the planet of melancholy, and its rings are the debris of a body that came apart. To walk beside him is to look at everything you love and feel, without warning, that it is already passing.

title: The Temple of the Golden Pavilion
author: Yukio Mishima
extract: Ever since my childhood, Father had often spoken to me about the Golden Temple.
blurb: Picture the Golden Pavilion on its still pond in Kyoto, doubled in the water, gold against the dark trees, so finished and so perfect that it leaves no room for the boy looking at it. Mizoguchi is that boy: a novice monk, ugly, friendless, his stutter a permanent wall between himself and the moment he is trying to live. [Mishima](/authors/yukio-mishima) drew him from the acolyte who really did burn the temple to the ground in 1950, and he uses that fact to ask something genuinely frightening. What if beauty at its highest does not console you but shuts you out, arriving in the mind at the exact instant you reach for an ordinary life and cancelling it? The voice that carries this is slow, scrupulous, almost loving toward its own ruin, a mind refined past the point of living. By the time the flames come, you understand them, and that is the unbearable part.

title: Household Tales
author: Brothers Grimm
extract: Looking-glass, Looking-glass, on the wall, Who in this land is the fairest of all?
blurb: A queen orders a huntsman to bring back a girl's lungs and liver, salts them, and eats what she believes is proof of murder. That single scene, kept intact from the older, harsher version of _Snow White_, tells you what this collection actually is: not the softened bedtime stories the name now conjures, but tales two brothers spent years gathering from the voices around them, certain the old stories were dying and someone had to catch them before they were gone. The stepsisters in _Cinderella_ hack pieces from their own feet to force the golden shoe. _Hansel and Gretel_ shove the witch into her own oven and slam the door. A stepmother cooks her stepson into a stew and serves him, unknowing, to his own father. Nothing here is gentled for children; the forest is where hunger, cruelty, and cunning settle their accounts, exactly and without mercy. What survives every softened retelling is not the moral. It is the shiver, the sense that under every neat ending the old blood is still there, waiting.

title: The Masnavi
author: Rumi
extract: From reed-flute hear what tale it tells; what plaint it makes of absence' ills.
blurb: Listen to the reed, [Rumi](/authors/rumi) begins, and the whole poem follows from that command: a length of cane, carved from the marsh and hollowed out, wails because it remembers the bed it was torn from. That cry is you. _The Masnavi_ understands the human ache as homesickness for God, the soul severed from its origin and singing all its life to get back. Across six books and some twenty-five thousand couplets, dictated aloud as Rumi walked, turned, and wept, his student Husam al-Din racing to catch each line, the poem never explains its mysticism; it enacts it. A tale of a king and a slave-girl breaks off into a tale of a grocer and a parrot, which dissolves into pure prayer, then doubles back, because a soul reaching for the divine never moves in a straight line. There is no last word that resolves it, only the reed still sounding, and a longing that, the deeper it goes unanswered, somehow draws you nearer to its source.

title: Dune
author: Frank Herbert
extract: I must not fear. Fear is the mind-killer. Fear is the little-death that brings total obliteration.
blurb: Arrakis has no rain, no rivers, only sand, and the sand hides two things worth killing for: the deadliest animal alive, and the only drug in the universe that lets a mind see through time. Duke Leto Atreides is handed this planet as an honor and walks his House into a trap the Emperor and the Harkonnens have spent years building. What survives the fire is his son Paul, fifteen, fleeing into the desert with his mother and into the hands of a people who have waited centuries for a messiah built to his exact measure. [Frank Herbert](/authors/frank-herbert) built this world whole: its ecology, its worms, its harsh discipline of water. Then he asked the one question the genre almost never dares to ask, whether the chosen one can see, with total clarity, that the holy war rising in his name is a catastrophe, and walks toward it anyway. That is the vertigo at the center of _Dune_, awe and dread fused into one boy's foresight, a warning wearing the robes of a prophecy.

title: Cold Comfort Farm
author: Stella Gibbons
extract: I saw something nasty in the woodshed.
blurb: 'I saw something nasty in the woodshed.' That is all Aunt Ada Doom will ever explain about the childhood horror she has used for decades to rule Cold Comfort Farm from an armchair, and no one in the family dares ask her more. Into this fog of gorse and doom-soaked prose arrives Flora Poste: orphaned, briskly broke, and armed with nothing but excellent manners and a settled conviction that unhappiness is usually a housekeeping problem. [Stella Gibbons](/authors/stella-gibbons) wrote this to murder an entire genre of gloomy rural romance, the kind where scythes gleam with significance and cows low out their sorrows in the yard, and she kills it not with argument but with a tidy woman and a diary. Seth abandons his broodings for the talkies, Amos takes his hellfire on the road, and even Ada, unmasked, wants nothing grander than a new hat and an excuse to leave. It is the rare satire that is also, helplessly, an act of love, and it will make you wish briskness itself could be sent round to fix your own family.

title: The Sound Of Things Falling
author: Juan Gabriel Vásquez
day: American Airlines Flight 965 crash (El Diluvio hill, near Cali/Buga)
extract: The first hippopotamus, a male the colour of black pearls weighing a ton and a half, was shot dead in the middle of 2009.
blurb: News of a hippopotamus, shot dead after escaping the ruined zoo of a dead drug lord, is what sends Antonio Yammara back into his own fear. He had been a young law professor in Bogotá, playing billiards with a quiet ex-convict named Ricardo Laverde, when a motorcycle pulled alongside them in the street and gunfire took Laverde's life and nearly his own. What follows is not a thriller but an act of haunted excavation: Yammara reopens the dead man's history like a wound, because understanding it might explain the dread that has colonized his marriage, his sleep, his city. [Juan Gabriel Vásquez](/authors/juan-gabriel-vasquez) writes the private cost of the Escobar years, the way a whole generation of Colombians learned to flinch at the sound of an engine behind them. The title comes from a black box recording of a falling plane. You will hear it long after the last page.

title: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening
author: Robert Frost
extract: The woods are lovely, dark and deep, but I have promises to keep, and miles to go before I sleep.
blurb: Snow is falling, and a man has reined in his horse on the darkest evening of the year, before woods that belong to someone back in the village, someone who will never know he stopped here to watch them fill. That is the whole event: a halt, a hush, no errand and no reason, only the pull of something lovely, dark and deep that asks for nothing and offers, in the same breath, rest and the kind of rest there is no waking from. [Frost](/authors/robert-frost) lets the rhyme do the seducing, each stanza handing its odd line forward into the next like a held breath, the snow and the meter coming down at the same pace. Then the turn, said twice: promises to keep, and miles to go before I sleep. He speaks it once as plain fact and once as a man talking himself back onto the road, and under that second saying you can hear how much of him wanted to stay in the snow.

title: Endgame
author: Samuel Beckett
extract: Finished, it's finished, nearly finished, it must be nearly finished.
blurb: "Finished, it's finished, nearly finished, it must be nearly finished." So Clov begins, and for the rest of the hour nothing finishes. Hamm is blind and cannot rise from his chair; Clov can walk but cannot sit; Hamm's parents, Nagg and Nell, surface from two ashbins in the corner to bicker and remember. Outside the two small windows the world has gone gray and still. The title is borrowed from chess, the phase when the outcome is already decided and only the last empty moves remain, and [Beckett](/authors/samuel-beckett) means it exactly: these four go on performing their rituals and small cruelties because to stop would take a certainty none of them can find. Nell says nothing is funnier than unhappiness, and she is right; the play is savage and very funny at once. Beckett makes one room hold the whole strange labour of an ending that refuses to end.

title: Picnic at Hanging Rock
author: Joan Lindsay
extract: Everything if only you could see it clearly enough, is beautiful and complete
blurb: A hot Saturday afternoon in the summer of 1900, and the students of Appleyard College picnic in the shadow of Hanging Rock, an ancient volcanic outcrop rising from the Victorian bush. At noon every watch stops. Three girls and a teacher climb toward the summit through the shimmering heat and are never seen again. [Joan Lindsay](/authors/joan-lindsay) tells it in prose as still and sun-drugged as the afternoon itself, all drowsy warmth and the drone of insects, so that a schoolgirl outing curdles by slow degrees into something older and stranger than any crime. What makes it unbearable is that she refuses to explain. No body, no answer, no rational floor beneath your feet, only the rock, indifferent and immense, and the growing sense that the tidy European world of corsets and Latin lessons was always a thin skin stretched over a land that does not care to be understood. You will close the book and still be standing at the base of the rock, looking up.

title: The Book of Job
author: Anonymous
extract: The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
blurb: Heaven makes a bet. God lets an accuser strip a blameless man of his children, his wealth, and his health, to see whether he will curse God for it, and what follows is the oldest unflinching cry against undeserved suffering ever set down. Job's three friends come to console him and stay to accuse: surely he sinned, surely the world is just and he has earned his ruin. Job will not say it. He sits in the ash and demands an answer from the silence, and the silence holds, chapter after chapter, until God speaks at last from a whirlwind. What comes is not an explanation but a question, vast and unbearably beautiful: where were you when the morning stars sang together, when the foundations of the earth were laid? The whirlwind does not solve the problem of pain; it dwarfs it. And the book, astonishingly, takes the side of the man who refused every easy comfort and demanded the truth instead.

title: A Christmas Carol
author: Charles Dickens
extract: Marley was dead: to begin with.
blurb: Marley was dead, to begin with. His partner seven years in the grave, Ebenezer Scrooge spends his evenings alone in a cold counting house, treating kindness as waste and pleasure as debt, until the dead man's chain comes dragging up the stair. [Dickens](/authors/charles-dickens) built it as a ghost story, but the terror runs backward. The three spirits who come for Scrooge do not threaten him with hell. They walk him back through his own life: the boy left alone at school, reading by a low fire while the other children went home for Christmas; the young woman who loved him and watched him choose the ledger over her. Scene by scene the cruelty is given a source and a cost, until the last and most fearful spirit shows him a neglected grave with his own name cut into the stone. That is why Scrooge waking on Christmas morning, breathless and laughing and good, is among the most joyful figures in fiction. The warmth is no trick of the season. It was earned out of everything that first went cold.

title: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
author: Thomas Gray
extract: The curfew tolls the knell of parting day, the lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea.
blurb: The curfew tolls the knell of parting day; a plowman trudges home, the light leaves the fields, and one man is left among the slanting headstones of a country churchyard as the dark comes on. What [Thomas Gray](/authors/thomas-gray) does here had scarcely been done before. He turns the full ceremonial weight of elegy, the grand form built for the great and the mourned, upon the people beneath the rudest stones, the farm laborers no chronicle will ever name. He wonders what they might have been: some mute inglorious Milton, some village Hampden who once faced down a petty local tyrant, and he asks whether a life lived unknown is a loss or a mercy, a sparing from the world's worst temptations. Then comes the quiet miracle. The poem turns, and the man grieving strangers begins, without quite saying so, to grieve himself, to picture the hour some kindred spirit reads his own stone. Few poems have made such tenderness out of the fear of being forgotten.

title: Peter And Wendy
author: J.M. Barrie
extract: All children, except one, grow up.
blurb: Peter Pan cries on the nursery floor because his shadow will not stick, and Wendy Darling kneels in her nightgown and sews it back onto his foot. That single mend is enough. Within the hour she is out the window with her brothers, sprinkled with fairy dust, flying over London toward an island that rearranges itself to fit whichever child is dreaming it that night: lagoons, pirates, a crocodile ticking down the seconds to Hook's death, lost boys who fell from their prams and were never reclaimed. Peter rules over all of it and forgets nearly all of it too, eventually forgetting he ever had a Tinker Bell, and forgetting his own adventures by the time he has finished telling them. [J.M. Barrie](/authors/jm-barrie)'s real subject is what that forgetting costs: Wendy grows up, grows old, and Peter simply goes on, coming back for her daughter when she can no longer fly, and her daughter's daughter after that, so long as children are, in the book's own last and chilling word for them, heartless.

title: Notes on "Camp"
author: Susan Sontag
extract: The whole point of Camp is to dethrone the serious.
blurb: Fifty-eight numbered jottings, dedicated to the memory of Oscar Wilde, and by the last one you cannot unsee the thing they name. [Susan Sontag](/authors/susan-sontag) set out to describe a sensibility no one had pinned down, the taste that adores a Tiffany lamp, a feather boa, an old movie too gorgeous to be any good, precisely because each is too much. Camp, she writes, is a love of the unnatural, of artifice and exaggeration, a way of seeing the whole world in quotation marks. The thrill is that the essay never flattens its subject into an argument. It performs it instead, aphoristic and sly, half in love with the extravagance it dissects, serious about the frivolous and frivolous about the serious. Read it once and you start noticing camp everywhere, in a friend's ironic devotion, in a diva's grand terrible gesture. The ultimate camp statement, she decides, is that a thing can be good because it is awful.

title: Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee
author: Dee Alexander Brown
extract: I was born upon the prairie, where the wind blew free and there was nothing to break the light of the sun.
blurb: Turn over the story you were taught to call the winning of the West and underneath lies this: a conquest, set down from the side that lost everything. Dee [Brown](/authors/dee-alexander-brown) built his history out of the councils, treaties, and recorded words of the people it happened to, the Sioux and Cheyenne and Nez Percé and Apache, and the pattern repeats until you can hardly bear it. A nation signs a treaty. A gold strike or a railroad wants its land. The soldiers come, the promise is unmade, the survivors are driven onto ground no one else wanted, and it begins again, patient and merciless, through Red Cloud and Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse and Chief Joseph laying down his rifle for the last time. It ends in the snow of December 1890, at a creek called Wounded Knee, where the Seventh Cavalry killed men, women, and children who had already surrendered their guns. What devastates is not one massacre but the grinding sameness of thirty years of them, and the plain, unanswerable dignity of every voice Brown lets speak.

title: The Year of the Death of Ricardo Reis
author: José Saramago
day: Ricardo Reis arrives in Lisbon; Saramago opening
extract: We are the dreams of a god who chose not to believe in us.
blurb: Here the sea ends and the land begins, and it is raining over the colourless city as a ship carries Ricardo Reis home to Lisbon. He has come to mourn Fernando Pessoa, the poet who invented him, dead these few weeks; and the dead man returns the visit, climbing the hotel stairs through the months the newly dead are allowed to linger, sitting to talk and growing fainter with each call, while the heteronym he once dreamed up goes on breathing. [Saramago](/authors/jose-saramago) holds this vertigo perfectly level and lets the question of which man is the more real come quietly loose in your hands. Around them Salazar's Lisbon hardens and the Spanish war begins to bleed across the border, until Reis's lovely Horatian creed of accepting fate without grief shows itself as something only a poem can afford. The prose runs on like a slow river, weather and thought and unmarked speech poured into one current, and the pull of it is the whole pleasure: stop fighting and drift.

title: In Memoriam A.H.H.
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
extract: 'Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all.
blurb: Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky. One section is set on a New Year's Eve, the bells carrying across the midnight snow as Tennyson asks them to ring out the grief that saps the mind. _In Memoriam A.H.H._ is the elegy he kept writing for seventeen years after Arthur Henry Hallam, the dearest friend of his youth, died without warning in Vienna at twenty-two. It runs to 131 sections, each sealed in a four-line stanza whose outer rhymes reach across the inner pair to close, the shape of a hand trying to hold what is no longer there. The years of its making were the years geology was quietly unmaking Victorian faith, and Tennyson refused to look away: nature is red in tooth and claw, and still he asked whether love could outlast what the mind now honestly knew. The famous verdict, that it is better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all, is nothing handed over cheaply here. It was won across seventeen winters, against everything that wanted it to be untrue.
